title: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly: Lions Thrash Cardinals For 60 Minutes
full_text:
How low can you go if you're the Arizona Cardinals ?
When does it hit bedrock and you can't go any lower? No doubt it was going to be a season full of struggles.  Having the toughest schedule in the NFL does that.
Regardless, the on-field product is still a tough pill to swallow. To put salt on the wounds, former offensive coordinator Drew Petzing's Detroit Lions offense was a fine-tuned machine, rolling through a Cardinals defense that had nothing to combat the dishing.
Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs handed Arizona its fourth straight game with 30-plus points allowed this season. The Cardinals fell to a 45-21 Lions rout on Sunday afternoon at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona.
The good, bad and ugly from today's loss:
There aren't too many positives that can come out of blowouts. Still, the Cardinals' tight end has been one of the few bright spots on this team over the past couple of weeks. Trey McBride, like he's always been since coming to the desert out of Colorado State, led Arizona's receivers with nine completions and a garbage-time touchdown to make the final score less eye-watering.
McBride, though, was far from the only tight end to produce for the Cardinals today. Second-string Elijah Higgins went 3-for-3, catching the Cardinals' largest completion -- a 38-yard strike to open the second half.
Out of the trio, no one had a better afternoon than third-string tight end Teagan Quitoriano, who caught his first two receptions of the season, both for touchdowns.
Heading into the afternoon against the Lions, the Cardinals' offensive line was averaging 1.5 sacks per game. Not a terrible metric by any means, and certainly livable, especially looking at the defenses they've played so far. Today, Arizona was brutalized up front, allowing a season-high five sacks.
The lack of protection caused the rushing attack to suffer mightily, leading to the Cardinals recording their lowest ground production of the season, 56 yards. Rookie running back Jeremiyah Love handled most of the carries, totaling 22 yards on 12 attempts.
The Cardinals' defense has become the NFL's pick-me-up for any struggling offense or team looking for a quick stat pad for its candidate for offensive player of the year. It's been a concerning area since the start of the season and has not instilled much confidence going forward.
Arizona held Detroit to three punts and negative 9-yards to open the first quarter. The Lions scored on their next seven drives before punting one final time in garbage time to avoid running up the score with two minutes left on the clock.
Lions quarterback Jared Goff went 19-for-30 for 271 yards, with three passing touchdowns and a goal-line rushing score. Gibbs returned to form, rushing for 151 yards on 25 carries and punching in a pair of touchdowns.
Detroit, following the recipe set by the San Francisco 49ers, relied heavily on tight end Sam LaPorta to attack Arizona's defense. The fourth-year tight end led the Lions' receiving corps with 88 yards on five catches and one very wide open 38-yard touchdown.

title: What Cardinals Said After Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals were blown out by the Detroit Lions in Week 5, though the scoreboard wasn't close to the biggest storyline in the desert.
The Cardinals traded Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans right as the ball was kicked off at State Farm Stadium, putting an end to a saga that started earlier in the weekend when reports first emerged about Harrison departing Arizona.
Harrison now lands in Houston while the Cardinals recoup some solid draft capital in return.
After the game, reporters were able to speak with some members of the team on the trade. Here's what they said:
"I just thought it was in the best interest of this club," said LaFleur in his post-game press conference.
Previously this offseason, LaFleur told reporters his job was to maximize Harrison's talent. Through four games, Harrison — the former No. 4 overall pick — had just five catches on the season.
"I'm not going to totally get into that right now. I really like Marvin Harrison. He's a good person. I wish him well. We did what we thought was in the best interest of the Cardinals," LaFleur said when asked what went wrong.
"Any guy that does not play to the level that I feel like they're capable of, I'm always going to put that on me and coaching in general."
The news caught many by surprise, as early Saturday morning was when reports first emerged of the Cardinals trading Harrison. When asked when Arizona came to that decision, LaFleur said:
"I'm going to keep the details tight with us."
The Cardinals were suddenly without one of their biggest names on the offensive side of the ball, and they clearly struggled in Week 5.
"I don't think it was a distraction at all. It's not why we didn't play well today," said LaFleur before he was asked if Harrison wanted to be here in Arizona.
"I'm not going to answer for Marv."
"It definitely happened fast. Obviously outside of football that's a person that meant a lot for me and I had a really good relationship with. You never want to see somebody leave. Obviously wish him the best on whatever he has coming up next for him, but yeah it's tough. We all have a really good relationship with him in the locker room so losing him is big," he said post-game.
The Cardinals opted for Jalen Brooks at their X receiver spot, who had two receptions for 16 yards against Detroit. Kendrick Bourne led all Cardinals receivers with five receptions for 70 yards.
"It's football, so it's just like an injury. When somebody gets hurt, next person has to step up and pick up the slack, so I think that's more what it is," Brissett said on replacing Harrison.
He was also asked if he believed the trade was a distraction.
"I wouldn't say a distraction. We found out Saturday and got to go play in the game Sunday, so got to ignore the noise and block out all distractions."
Brissett also added the team was addressed by both Harrison and LaFleur on Saturday morning.
"He told us... Marv and coach [LaFleur] ... We found out before ya'll did."
Brissett also mentioned plenty of players had strong personal relationships with Harrison, which made the move a bit tough.
"It's tough. It's a person we all have a relationship with outside of football. As much as everybody says the business is the business, that doesn't make it easy. That makes it toughest because it is part of the business," said Brissett.
"It's somebody I know I'll miss and a lot of guys in that locker room will miss. I'm sure a lot of us are rooting for Marv."
When asked why Harrison ultimately didn't flourish in the desert, he said:
"I can't answer that question."
Williams was one of few players media got to speak with in the locker room.
"Surprising, but at the end of the day it's business. We hope the best for him, he's a great player. For us here we just got to keep moving forward and do what we gotta do," Williams said when asked about the trade.
"It's Sunday. We've got a game to play and we're all professionals. We got a game to play. Like I said we all rock with Marv, we want the best for him. But the guys here, we have a game. We just focus on that."
Williams also mentioned the business is unpredictable, but nobody is going to feel bad for the Cardinals after they dealt Harrison.
"I think it all ties back to what I was saying about being professional with it. Just understanding it's unfortunate, it kind of sucks, whatever, but at the end of the day when you have a game on Sunday, you guys [media], fans, nobody is going to feel bad for us not playing good because we're upset about one of our teammates being traded," he said.
"Especially because that's the nature of how this business goes. It's unpredictable. It's one of those things you can't really prepare for, you got to just do what you do."

title: 4 Big Instant Reactions After Cardinals' Humiliating Loss to Lions
full_text:
Heading into a Week 5 matchup against a flawed Detroit Lions team, the Arizona Cardinals had a chance to improve their record 2-3 and keep their season hopes afloat.
Instead of an Arizona win, the Lions handed the Cardinals a beatdown, winning 45-21 at State Farm Stadium.
Four big takeaways from this embarrassing home performance:
One storyline going into the game was that former Cardinals offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is now the Lions' offensive coordinator this season. In his "revenge game", Petzing could call anything that he wanted to. From inside runs and outside zone runs to play action, screen passes, and drop-back passes, whatever it was, Petzing faced little to no resistance from the Cardinals defense.
The Lions' offense put up extremely good numbers against Rallis' unit. The Lions totaled 412 yards, averaged 6.3 yards per play, and went four-for-four in the red zone. The worst and most worrying stat is that the Lions were perfect on fourth-down conversions, going four-for-four.
Yes, going for it on fourth down has been a staple in the Dan Campbell era in Detroit, but the fact that the Cardinals couldn't get a stop is a very bad sign. If Rallis were relieved of his job, the Cardinals have senior coach Teryl Austin waiting in the wings to likely become the new defensive coordinator.
Austin has 22 years of coaching experience. Before joining Arizona this offseason he spent seven years with the Pittsburgh Steelers. During those years, the Steelers constantly had great defenses. Austin would be a good candidate if the Cardinals decide they want a change at the position.
Since he was drafted with the 36th pick in the 2017 draft, Baker has been an absolute staple of the Cardinals. Baker's great instincts and ability to make highlight plays have made him a fan-favorite. However, with the Cardinals being 1-4 and still having tough teams on the schedule such as the Denver Broncos, Los Angeles Rams and the Kansas City Chiefs, it is best to move on from Baker.
Even though Baker is 30 year sold, he can still play at a high level, as he showed in this game by sacking Lions quarterback Jared Goff while leading the team with 11 tackles on the day.
With the Cardinals trading Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans, they're showing their cards: they are open for business. Plenty of contenders could use Baker.
While it might be hard for Cardinals fans to say goodbye to the All-Pro safety, it is the right move.
In Cardinals land, people aren't fans of how quarterback Jacoby Brissett has played this season, especially last week against the New York Giants . This week, Brissett was fine. While the stats look good, three touchdowns, two of those came when the game was out of reach.
Sure, Brissett threw for 292 yards in the air, but against a Lions secondary that has shown some weakness, Arizona's signal caller should have done better.
However, the truth is, the Cardinals lack the infrastructure to support any quarterback, rookie or veteran. Their offensive line is in shambles, as shown in this game with the Lions getting five sacks. Their defense is porous, so the offense has to play catch-up. Head coach Mike LaFleur is still learning in his first year.
Even if the Cardinals had an upgrade, say Trevor Lawrence from the Jacksonville Jaguars, they still wouldn't be playoff-caliber. Before the Cardinals can think about who their next franchise signal caller will be, they need to plug the holes on their roster.
Ending on a good note, the second-year tight end had a great afternoon. Quitoriano caught two passes for two touchdowns. With Harrison Jr. no longer on the team, Quitoriano could be a good rotation player in the pass game.
Brissett and Quitoriano seemed to have great chemistry in this game. If things progress very well going forward, the Cardinals could have one of the best tight end rooms in the league with Trey McBride and Quitoriano alongside Elijah Higgins.
Overall, this Cardinals team is a mess. They still have a lot to figure out about where this team stands. Next week the Cardinals travel to SoFi Stadium to take on their division opponent, the Los Angeles Rams.

title: Cardinals GM Trends on Social Media For All The Wrong Reasons After Lions Loss
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals have lost a fourth consecutive game, dropping their record to 1-4 on the season after a 45-21 loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 5.
It was a highly anticipated matchup for a handful of reasons, ranging from the return of former offensive coordinator Drew Petzing to the buzzer-beater trade of Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans just as the game kicked off.
The Cardinals got off to quite the start at State Farm Stadium, scoring on their opening drive while forcing three consecutive three-and-outs from Detroit's potent offense.
However, Arizona quickly found themselves down 24-7 entering halftime and couldn't recover in the final two quarters.
"Fire Monti" was trending on X during the game, which was a mix of reaction to the product on the field, Harrison being traded and the overall direction of the team.
With the loss to Detroit, Ossenfort's overall record drops to 16-40 since taking over in 2023. Arizona stripped its roster to bare bones after Ossenfort took over and thought they had built a possible playoff contender before things collapsed.
I see that Fire Monti is trending. I was a believer in his vision at the beginning, but the results are speaking for themselves. He has to go.
Ossenfort parted ways with franchise quarterback Kyler Murray this offseason and hired another rookie head coach in Mike LaFleur, stalling any realistic timelines of competing immediately.
Public perception went from bad to worse after the Cardinals engaged in a long contract standoff with quarterback Jacoby Brissett, who was handed $15 million in guaranteed money to again be the team's starting quarterback.
Results haven't been close to ideal to begin the season, and with the Cardinals dropping to 1-4, the team's future is in a bind.
Monti Ossenfort should resign or be let go after this game. 16-40 as the Arizona Cardinals GM.
After the Cardinals fired Jonathan Gannon, many thought team owner Michael Bidwill would have sent Ossenfort packing as well. However, Ossenfort stuck around for a fourth season.
"I look at the roster, I think Monti's done a very good job," Bidwill said after firing Gannon.
"Three years ago, this roster looked a lot different. A combination of draft and free agency, injuries are obviously a factor. But when I look at the just the totality of the circumstances -- I wanted 17 games over the 18 weeks to make that decision.
"Monti and I wanted to give the benefit of those coaches and those players to see a whole body of work for the whole season. And at the end of last night, when we had a chance to speak. And then again, this morning, after sleeping on it, we decided this was the best direction to go."
Months later, with results still not coming, Ossenfort's seat is practically on fire.

title: Cardinals, Texans Trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. Got Done Thanks to 1 Key Change
full_text:
ARIZONA — Marvin Harrison Jr. is no longer an Arizona Cardinal.
Right as their Week 5 contest against the Detroit Lions began, news broke of their deal with the Houston Texans that sent Harrison and a seventh-round pick packing in exchange for a second and sixth-round pick — all of which are in the 2027 NFL Draft.
Harrison had been in trade chatter for weeks, though things suddenly escalated over the weekend when reports first emerged of Harrison's departure. Arizona would eventually tell Harrison to stay home to preserve his health, and the rest is now history.
What ultimately got the deal over the line?
NFL insider Ian Rapoport says Houston's willingness to change the year of their second-round pick made the difference.
"#AZCardinals GM Monti Ossenfort held firm on his price, wanting a second rounder this year. Once Houston went from a 2028 second to a 2027 second, it was happening," Rapoport said.
#AZCardinals GM Monti Ossenfort held firm on his price, wanting a second rounder this year. Once Houston went from a 2028 second to a 2027 second, it was happening. https://t.co/HYkdfwbTQH
Arizona's insistence on getting a 2027 pick as opposed to 2028 was likely for a few reasons.
The Texans, despite starting 0-4, are one of the better teams in the AFC and could very well be in a spot to contend for the Super Bowl next season, which would massively sway the value of Arizona's newly acquired pick.
It's also important to note Ossenfort, whose job security is already in question, might not be around to make that pick in 2028 (let alone 2027). Time is of the essence for Ossenfort, who feels his seat growing warmer with each loss.
The Cardinals were smart to maximize Harrison's trade value now, as getting a second-round pick for a wideout with just five receptions on the season was a win for Arizona. However, they do lose the promise Harrison brings in what the Cardinals were hoping to be a highly potent offense.
Houston, on the other hand, is looking to solidify their turnaround in a AFC that feels very much up for grabs, as numerous teams are reasonable bets to make it deep into the postseason. The Texans' win over the Tennessee Titans today kept them three wins back from the division-leading Jacksonville Jaguars.
As for Arizona, they're in the process of dropping to 1-4 on the season with a grim outlook of turning things around.
Harrison wasn't very involved in the Cardinals' offense, though it will be interesting to see how Arizona's attack changes moving into the future.

title: Cardinals Trade Marvin Harrison Jr. to Texans
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are now underway here at State Farm Stadium as Week 5 action begins, and Marvin Harrison Jr. isn't in uniform.
That's because he's been traded.
ESPN's Adam Schefter is reporting the Cardinals are sending a 2027 7th-round pick to the Houston Texans in exchange for a 2027 2nd-round pick and 2027 6th-round pick.
Trade: the Arizona Cardinals have agreed to trade WR Marvin Harrison Jr. and 2027 7th-round pick to the Houston Texans in exchange for a 2027 2nd-round pick and 2027 6th-round pick, per @rapsheet and me. pic.twitter.com/ziepfRIPr4
Harrison was made inactive by the Cardinals today as trade rumors swirled around the former No. 4 overall pick. Reports emerged earlier this weekend Arizona would be moving him to a new team after a disappointing start, though we didn't gain any clarity until just now.
The Cardinals will surely be asked about Harrison following the game, though Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans confirmed to Texans reporters the team did land Harrison.
According to Arizona Sports' John Gambadoro, a trade with the Cardinals and another team had already been agreed upon on Saturday night.
"The latest I have heard on Marvin Harrison Jr. The trade, it is done and agreed to in principle, could be completed as early as late tonight or first thing in the morning," he said.
No immediate team was reported by any of the prominent NFL insiders who initially broke the news, which was a first given how massive the circumstances are.
However, Jeremy Fowler was first to say the Houston Texans are the team believed to be in the running.
"As of Saturday night, multiple execs gauging the overall trade market as well as an Arizona player source believe Harrison Jr. will be a Houston Texan," he posted .
The Texans defeated the Titans 26-3 today to get their first win of the season. Houston now adds to their receiving corps that's headlined by Nico Collins.
Harrison's in his third NFL season but has been unable to sustain any success in the desert. Harrison arrived with immediate expectations to transform Arizona's offense, though Harrison's only been productive in spurts while battling a mix of injuries, drops and mental lapses.
There was hope the Cardinals hiring new head coach Mike LaFleur would fix the relationship, though Harrison's logged just five receptions for 85 yards and one touchdown thus far, taking a major backseat to others in Arizona's offense.
A change is likely best for both sides, and now it appears to be all but official.

title: Cardinals Make Official Marvin Harrison Jr. Decision for Lions Game
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals have officially made Marvin Harrison Jr. inactive for their Week 5 contest against the Detroit Lions.
Harrison is reportedly close to being traded to another team just four games into his third NFL season, as the disconnect between the former fourth overall pick and the organization grew to a point beyond salvation.
Harrison is inactive alongside Carson Beck, Starling Thomas, Andrew Wingard and Andrew Billings.
Harrison's been an afterthought in the Cardinals' offense under new head coach Mike LaFleur, which has been a bit surprising given how highly Arizona spoke of Harrison through the stages of the offseason and training camp.
To date, Harrison's logged just five receptions for 85 yards and one touchdown this season.
Now, Harrison's on the move — though we don't exactly know where. Early reports from Adam Schefter, Ian Rapoport and other top NFL insiders weren't able to pinpoint a landing spot for the Ohio State product.
Early indications suggest the Houston Texans are his next destination, though nothing is known for sure.
Arizona Sports' John Gambadoro suggests a trade is imminent, however.
"The latest I have heard on Marvin Harrison Junior. The trade, it is done and agreed to in principle, could be completed as early as late tonight or first thing in the morning," he said Sunday on X.
The latest I have heard on Marvin Harrison Junior. The trade, it is done and agreed to in principle, could be completed as early as late tonight or first thing in the morning.
Gambo also added, "I believe it is for two future picks but waiting for confirmation. I wonder if the lesser pick has the ability to be bumped up based on production. At this time, we all do not know for certain so just relaying some of the things I have checked on."
The Cardinals move into the future with Michael Wilson and Trey McBride remaining as their top targets in the passing game with Jalen Brooks, Simi Fehoko and Reggie Virgil as potential fill-ins for Harrison's presence as Arizona's X receiver.
If the Texans' landing spot is true, Harrison will arrive to a Houston squad that is 0-4 entering Sunday with Nico Collins established as their top offensive weapon. However, injuries have hindered Houston's corps of weapons on offense, and the team is clearly hoping Harrison can improve.

title: Falcons' Missed Opportunities Prove Costly in Overtime Loss to Ravens
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons had several opportunities to put away the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday Night Football, but missed chances on offense and costly mistakes on special teams ultimately contributed to a heartbreaking 30-23 overtime loss.
Atlanta held a late lead and appeared positioned to secure its third consecutive prime time victory. However, the Falcons struggled to turn favorable field position into touchdowns, missed multiple opportunities to score and allowed Baltimore to capitalize when the game was on the line.
For a team that had played well enough to put itself in position to win, the inability to finish drives proved costly.
One of Atlanta's biggest issues was its inability to capitalize on opportunities inside Baltimore territory. The Falcons repeatedly moved into scoring range but settled for Nick Folk field goals instead of touchdowns, keeping the Ravens within striking distance.
The missed opportunities were particularly frustrating because Atlanta had chances to create a two-possession advantage and put additional pressure on Baltimore. Instead, the Ravens remained in the game long enough to mount a late comeback.
One of the most memorable moments came in the third quarter when Atlanta attempted a red zone trick play. Matthews reported as an eligible receiver and became the intended target on a pass from Michael Penix Jr.
The play had the potential to catch Baltimore off guard and produce a critical touchdown. However, Penix's pass sailed over Matthews, resulting in an incompletion and another missed scoring opportunity.
Here is the pass to Matthews. Penix throws him open but ball goes through his hands. #Falcons pic.twitter.com/6FbtFJZvlM
Rather than adding seven points to its lead, Atlanta failed to execute a creative play that could have changed the complexion of the game.
The Falcons also committed three costly special teams penalties, disrupting field position and creating additional challenges for the offense. Against a Baltimore team capable of generating explosive plays, those mistakes made it even more difficult for Atlanta to establish control.
Falcons offensive lineman Chris Lindstrom acknowledged that Atlanta could put the game away but failed to take advantage.
“Just that when you have an opportunity to put a team away, you gotta do it. And we didn’t do that. And so we gave them an opportunity, and what great teams do is they take advantage of it,” Lindstrom said.
Head coach Kevin Stefanski shared a similar assessment of the team's performance.
“Credit to Baltimore,” Stefanski said. “Obviously we didn't do enough to win that game. We had missed opportunities, and when you're playing a good football team, the margins are razor thin like we knew they would be; we've got to come through on some of those plays.”
Despite Atlanta's missed opportunities, the Falcons still had a chance to secure the victory late in regulation. Baltimore instead drove 71 yards in six plays, with Tyler Huntley connecting with Devontez Walker for a touchdown with 40 seconds remaining. Derrick Henry then scored on a direct snap for the two-point conversion to tie the game at 23.
Atlanta's defense could not produce the stop needed to preserve the lead, sending the contest into overtime.
The Falcons also lost Penix to a rib injury late in regulation, forcing backup quarterback Tua Tagovailoa to take over. Baltimore scored on its opening overtime possession when Huntley crossed the goal line on a one-yard quarterback sneak.
Tagovailoa then threw an interception to Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton, ending Atlanta's hopes of responding.
The loss was a reminder that winning against quality opponents requires more than simply creating opportunities. Atlanta had chances to extend its lead, finish scoring drives and deliver a decisive defensive stop, but failed to do enough in critical moments.
The Falcons will now prepare for the Chicago Bears, who rank first in the NFL in rushing yards per game. Atlanta must clean up its mistakes and become more efficient in the red zone if it hopes to rebound. Against Baltimore, the opportunities were there. The execution needed to finish the job was not.

title: Michael Penix Jr. Reveals Why He Couldn't Return for Falcons in Overtime
full_text:
ATLANTA – Michael Penix Jr. sat on the Atlanta Falcons sideline, towel draped over his head, as Tua Tagovailoa threw a game-clinching interception.
For the first time in 329 days, Penix had returned to the field where he tore his ACL. But as the Falcons tried to claw their way down the field with the fourth quarter ticking away, he found himself walking off it with yet another injury.
Penix, whose Falcons led the Ravens in prime time for nearly the entire game, took a big hit from Tavius Robinson. He left the field after the training staff tended to him, but returned for one play before the Falcons were forced to punt, sending the game into overtime.
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski confirmed Penix suffered a rib injury, something the oft-injured quarterback struggled with in college, but he could not comment on its severity. The quarterback will get imaging to better assess the extent of his ailment on Monday, but Penix said it is too soon to know if there are any similarities between his issues in college and what he has now.
“It’s frustrating, but the biggest thing is I want to be out there, especially in a big moment in a game like that,” the quarterback said. “I felt like I needed to be out there.”
Penix said afterward he did not feel the injury would be a long-term issue for him and even believed there was a chance he could have returned in overtime. Had the Falcons started with the ball, he expected to lead the offense back onto the field.
Instead, he felt his body get “cold” during the Ravens’ 14-play touchdown drive that sucked 7:03 off the clock. He tried to fight through the pain, but he wasn’t where he needed to be health-wise to go back out onto the field.
“I did not feel like I was going to be able to give our team what we needed to be able to help us win that football game, because of the pain I was feeling,” Penix said. “As I was sitting there, what I was going through, it started getting worse and worse.”
Sunday was a frustrating development for a Falcons team that had felt it had turned a corner with Penix under center. For at least three quarters, it felt like they would keep rolling. Penix didn’t complete a pass until the Falcons’ fourth possession, but he took off after that point. He started 0-of-4, but completed 19 of his next 28 passes for 240 yards and a touchdown, with 13 of those 19 completions going for either a first down or a touchdown.
Penix was especially effective when the Falcons needed him most, finishing 9-of-15 for 163 yards and a touchdown on third down, the most completions and yards in a game in his career. He found wide receiver Drake London five times in those situations, and he connected with his favorite target for 86 of his 118 receiving yards on third down.
London was one of six Falcons to catch a pass, and with Penix as its conductor, the offense was humming. Atlanta held a lead for nearly the entire game and was building on their positive momentum from the two previous weeks.
By all appearances, Sunday was set to continue the Falcons' offensive success from their last two weeks, until it wasn’t, and that momentum came crashing down after a single hit to the ribs.
The Falcons had chances to put Baltimore away on Sunday night, and this loss goes beyond a fourth-quarter quarterback injury. The defense faltered late, allowing Derrick Henry and the Lamar Jackson-less Ravens to pile up 200 yards on the ground, while the offense missed far too many opportunities in key moments.
“There are plays that we can make; there are calls that we can give our guys to be better,” Stefanski said. “In a game like that, all those little plays add up to being a big play.”
But for Penix and this team, this is all the NFL world will be talking about. Just two games after returning from a torn ACL, the quarterback is back in the training room, with his immediate future in question.
“I just pray he's alright,” running back Bijan Robinson said. “I know the whole team does.”
Still, he remains confident that he will be out there for his team next Sunday when the Chicago Bears come to town.
“Knowing me, I’m going to be ready to go next week,” Penix said, “because I’ve sat out enough in my career.”

title: Falcons Winners & Losers After Blown Second-Half Lead Against Ravens
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons lose a tough overtime game to the Baltimore Ravens, 30-23, in a tightly contested matchup at Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
Atlanta showed flashes of its potential on both sides of the ball, with several players stepping up in key moments while others struggled to capitalize on opportunities. With impressive individual performances and areas for improvement, here are the winners and losers from the Falcons’ Week 5 game against the Ravens.
Jessie Bates III was one of Atlanta’s biggest defensive standouts, making his presence felt throughout the game. The veteran safety helped the Falcons' defense deliver a critical takeaway after Sydney Brown punched the ball out, and Bates recovered it and returned it for a touchdown.
It marked Bates’ fifth defensive touchdown, but all four of his previous touchdowns came on interception returns.
Bates also made a crucial play on Baltimore’s first second-half two-point attempt, breaking up Tyler Huntley’s pass after the Ravens scored on a screen to Derrick Henry. His ability to make game-changing plays in multiple phases of the defense was instrumental in Atlanta’s effort.
Whether creating turnovers or preventing points, Bates continues to demonstrate why he is one of the most important players on Atlanta’s defense.
Atlanta’s defensive front deserves recognition for its ability to pressure the quarterback and disrupt Baltimore’s offensive rhythm. The Falcons recorded four sacks, with Kendal Daniels, Samson Ebukam and Jared Ivey each contributing one. Zach Harrison and Cameron Thomas combined for another half sack.
The defensive front also generated 8 quarterback hits and consistent pressure, making life difficult for Huntley. Brandon Dorlus was particularly disruptive, applying pressure throughout the game.
Atlanta’s ability to generate pressure created opportunities for the secondary to make plays, including the defensive touchdown that helped Bates reach the end zone.
Although Baltimore found some success on the ground, the Falcons’ pass rush showed how disruptive this unit can be when it consistently wins at the line of scrimmage. The defensive front remains one of Atlanta’s biggest strengths moving forward.
Drake London and Kyle Pitts provided two of Atlanta's biggest offensive bright spots, giving the passing game much-needed production.
London led the Falcons with seven receptions for 116 yards, doing much of his damage on third down. His ability to move the chains and deliver in critical situations helped Atlanta sustain drives and create opportunities downfield. London remains a reliable target for quarterback Michael Penix Jr., particularly when the offense needs to convert in high-pressure situations.
Pitts also delivered an encouraging performance, finishing with five catches for 42 yards and a touchdown. His scoring reception appeared to involve a ball that went through tight end Austin Hooper's hands before Pitts secured it for the touchdown.
Pitts’ red-zone production was particularly valuable, while London’s third-down production highlighted his importance to Atlanta’s passing attack.
The Falcons need consistent contributions from their receiving corps to complement their rushing game. London’s production and Pitts’ touchdown were positive developments, giving Atlanta two players capable of making a significant impact through the air.
After an outstanding game from the Falcons’ quarterback, Ravens defender Tavius Robinson hit him and forced a fumble. Penix returned to the field one play later but did not return for overtime.
Instead, Tua Tagovailoa threw an interception that ended the game.
Atlanta's biggest concern was its inability to stop Baltimore from breaking off several significant gains on the ground. The Ravens finished with 208 rushing yards on 35 carries, averaging 5.9 yards per attempt.
Justice Hill delivered one of the game's most damaging plays when he broke loose for a 47-yard run in the second half that set up a TD. Derrick Henry also had a big day, totaling 102 yards on 24 carries.
While Atlanta made important stops, those explosive runs let Baltimore gain chunks of yardage without consistently sustaining long drives. The Ravens also used their passing game's versatility, with Henry scoring on a screen pass from Huntley in the second half.
The gut-punch came on the overtime possession, when the Ravens rumbled downfield for the go-ahead touchdown. A gassed Falcons defense couldn't slow Henry and that rushing attack, which accounted for nine carries on the 14-play drive.
The production is particularly concerning because Atlanta entered the matchup with the NFL’s No. 1 run defense. Allowing that many yards is a significant challenge for a unit that had established itself as one of the league’s best at stopping the run.
The Falcons did show flashes of strong run defense, but limiting explosive plays must become a priority. Better tackling, gap discipline, and execution will be necessary to keep opposing offenses from consistently creating big gains.
Zachariah Branch had a disappointing day in terms of his opportunities to impact the game. The rookie had not recorded a punt return, limiting his chances to change field position on special teams.
His offensive involvement also included a costly negative screen pass that resulted in an eight-yard loss. He later caught a 23-yard screen pass, the longest gain of his career.
Branch possesses the speed and explosiveness to become a difference maker, but Atlanta needs to find ways to maximize those abilities while avoiding negative plays
The Falcons will need to be more deliberate in their use of Branch moving forward, particularly when attempting to get the ball into his hands in space.
Jake Matthews experienced a difficult moment during his 200th career start. The veteran offensive tackle missed a touchdown opportunity, marking his first missed touchdown of the game, according to game observations.
Jake Matthews Dropped The Open Big Man Touchdown 😂 That’s A Miss. 😬 pic.twitter.com/HDCzVqdIYV
Matthews has been one of Atlanta’s most dependable offensive linemen, making the moment all the more notable. Reaching 200 starts is a significant milestone, but the missed opportunity overshadowed part of what should have been a memorable occasion.
One mistake does not diminish Matthews’ overall body of work or his importance to Atlanta’s offensive line. However, the Falcons need to capitalize on scoring opportunities, especially in a matchup where possessions and momentum can shift quickly.

title: 5 Bold Predictions for Atlanta Falcons vs. Baltimore Ravens
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are the consensus pick against the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday Night Football. Even with a healthy Lamar Jackson, who is out for the game , the Falcons still might have been the popular pick as one of the most dominant teams over the last two weeks.
The Falcons find themselves in unfamiliar territory as frontrunners, as the love poured in from national media after back-to-back prime-time blowouts. We'll find out if the Falcons can handle the prosperity on NBC at 8:20 on Sunday, but until then, here are five bold predictions for the Falcons against the Ravens.
OK, so this doesn't feel like that bold a prediction, but much has been said about the lack of atmosphere at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. That's a combination of less-than-mediocre play over the last decade and a pricing structure that put lower-bowl seating into the hands of non-Falcons fans.
Atlanta is a transient city, full of transplants who have gravitated south through the years and brought their loyalty with them, but the Baltimore Ravens do not have a huge presence in the city like, say, the Pittsburgh Steelers, Chicago Bears, Philadelphia Eagles, or any team from New York.
Neutral fans tuning into the game tonight are going to see as loud a Falcons crowd as they've seen in a long, long time.
The Falcons are fifth in the NFL in quarterback pressures , but they're only 22nd with seven sacks. The Ravens have only given up seven sacks this season, tied for ninth-best in the NFL.
But most of those numbers have been accomplished with Lamar Jackson at quarterback. He's out, and it's time for the good pressure to pay off on Sunday. Atlanta has been playing with leads the last two weeks, setting up more pass-rush opportunities. That happens again on Sunday night.
The Falcons get at least three sacks of Tyler Huntley.
As the national media has been gushing about Bijan Robinson (rightfully so), everyone has taken notice, including the Baltimore Ravens. Drake London has 290 receiving yards in his two games with Michael Penix Jr. at quarterback.
The Ravens will crowd the line to try to stop Robinson. All-World safety Kyle Hamilton will keep a close eye on London. That's going to leave Kyle Pitts Sr. plenty of room to operate. Juwan Johnson of the Saints went for 4 catches and 66 yards against the Ravens in Week 2, and the Cowboys' Jake Ferguson had three catches for 24 yards and a touchdown in Week 3.
Pitts goes for 100+ yards and a touchdown.
Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry finished last season with four straight 100-yard games. He began this season with 144 yards against the Colts. He hasn't broken 100 yards since. He rushed for 73 yards last week in a win over the Titans, and his season low is 68 against the Saints in Week 2.
The Falcons have the No. 1 rushing defense in the NFL by some distance. They'll be looking to hold Henry to a season low, but why not dream a little bigger?
The last time Henry was held under 50 yards was in a 44-10 loss to the Texans in Week 5 last year. Week 5 last year, Week 5 this year?
Henry breaks 50 yards, but is kept under 75.
The Falcons are a near-unanimous pick from the national media and FalconsSI staff alike . This is a team unaccustomed to the spotlight, but they are built to avoid the massive highs and lows they've experienced over the last three seasons.
They're better in the trenches. They're better at quarterback. Dare we say they're better at running back?

Can they handle being frontrunners?

The story on the other side of the ball is that the Falcons have been the league’s best rushing team the last 2 weeks against a defense that struggles to stop the run. As long as Penix and the offense can limit mistakes, the Falcons should run away with this one.

title: Falcons Make Roster Moves Ahead of Ravens SNF Showdown
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have announced several roster moves ahead of their Sunday Night Football matchup against the Baltimore Ravens at Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
Linebacker Yasir Abdullah has been placed on injured reserve due to a hamstring injury, while defensive end Za’Darius Smith has been downgraded to out for Sunday’s game with a concussion/neck injury. Atlanta has also signed safety Jammie Robinson to the 53-man roster and elevated defensive ends Bralen Trice (his third and final elevation before needing to be signed to the active roster) and Drake Jackson from the practice squad.
Abdullah was ruled out for Sunday’s matchup with a hamstring injury before being placed on injured reserve. The linebacker appeared in all four of Atlanta’s games this season, recording two tackles and one pass defended. His absence leaves the Falcons with one less defensive option as they prepare for a physical matchup against Baltimore.
Robinson’s promotion adds depth in the secondary and on special teams. Atlanta previously elevated him from the practice squad for Week 4's Monday night matchup against the New Orleans Saints, before signing him to the active roster ahead of Sunday night’s contest.
The safety appeared in six games for Atlanta last season after joining the practice squad in November. Before arriving in Atlanta, Robinson spent two seasons with the Carolina Panthers. He was a fifth-round pick in the 2023 NFL Draft and has appeared in 27 career games. Robinson also made an impact on special teams last season, blocking a punt against New Orleans in Week 18.
The Falcons also elevated Trice and Jackson to bolster their defensive front. Trice has appeared in two games this season, recording one tackle and one pass defended. Sunday will mark his third and final standard practice squad elevation of the season, meaning Atlanta would need to sign him to its 53-man roster to make him eligible for additional game appearances through future elevations.
Jackson joins the game-day roster as another option along the defensive line. He appeared in two preseason games for Atlanta this year, recording one assisted tackle, but has yet to record a regular-season defensive statistic for the Falcons.
These moves follow Atlanta’s Week 4 win over New Orleans. The Falcons will look to carry that momentum into Sunday night’s primetime matchup while managing injuries and maintaining defensive depth.
With Abdullah sidelined, Robinson joining the active roster, and two additional defensive ends available, Atlanta will need contributions across its defense and special teams as it prepares to face Baltimore on Sunday Night Football.

title: 3 Keys to Victory for Atlanta Falcons against Baltimore Ravens
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have an opportunity to extend their winning streak when they host the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday night. With Lamar Jackson ruled out because of an ankle injury, Atlanta will face Tyler Huntley at quarterback and look to capitalize on Baltimore’s change under center.
The Falcons have several advantages entering the matchup, including a dominant run defense, a productive backfield tandem, and a pass rush capable of disrupting opposing quarterbacks. Here are three keys to victory for Atlanta.
Stopping Derrick Henry will be one of Atlanta’s biggest priorities. The Baltimore running back has rushed for 374 yards and seven touchdowns on 89 carries through four games, averaging 4.2 yards per attempt. His combination of power, speed and ability to break tackles makes him a threat to change the game with every carry.
Fortunately for Atlanta, its run defense has been outstanding. The Falcons rank first in the NFL in rushing defense efficiency, allowing just 2.7 yards per carry through four weeks. They will need that physicality against Henry, who can wear down defenders and create additional yards after contact.
Atlanta must approach Henry as a collective effort. The first defender needs to slow his momentum, while teammates rally to finish the tackle. Maintaining gap discipline, taking proper angles and limiting missed tackles will be essential.
The Falcons also need to prevent Henry from establishing himself early. Forcing Baltimore into third-and-long would allow Atlanta to focus more attention on Huntley and give its pass rush additional opportunities. If the NFL’s top run defense can limit Henry, it will significantly improve Atlanta’s chances of controlling the game.
Atlanta’s backfield has been one of its biggest offensive strengths this season. Bijan Robinson has recorded 494 rushing yards and four touchdowns, while Brian Robinson Jr. has contributed 194 yards and four touchdowns through four games.
Bijan has been especially impressive in primetime. He rushed for 194 yards and two touchdowns against Green Bay before following that performance with 145 yards and two touchdowns against New Orleans. His ability to produce explosive runs and consistently gain yards has helped Atlanta establish its offensive identity.
Brian has complemented that production with a physical running style, including three rushing touchdowns against New Orleans. Having both backs involved makes Atlanta more difficult to defend and prevents opposing defenses from concentrating exclusively on Bijan.
The Falcons must continue establishing the run early against Baltimore. Consistent production on first and second down will create manageable passing situations for Michael Penix Jr. while helping Atlanta control the clock.
If both Robinsons continue producing, Atlanta can keep Baltimore’s defense on the field and limit the opportunities available to Henry and the Ravens’ offense.
Atlanta must take advantage of Huntley’s opportunity as Baltimore’s starting quarterback. Although Huntley has experience in the Ravens’ offense, consistent pressure could force hurried decisions and disrupt the timing of Baltimore’s passing game.
Cameron Thomas has been an important contributor to Atlanta’s pass rush, recording 19 pressures through the first four games. Maason Smith has also provided an interior presence, generating seven pressures and helping collapse the pocket.
Za’Darius Smith, Samson Ebukam and the rest of Atlanta’s defensive front will be equally important. The Falcons need contributions from multiple rushers rather than relying on one player to consistently win individual matchups.
The defensive line must also remain disciplined. Huntley can escape pressure with his mobility, so Atlanta’s defenders need to maintain their rush lanes and prevent him from extending plays.
If the Falcons stop Henry on early downs, they can force Baltimore into predictable passing situations and unleash their pass rush. Turning pressure into sacks, hurried throws, and turnovers could give Atlanta’s offense valuable opportunities.
Ultimately, Atlanta’s path to victory starts with controlling the line of scrimmage. If the Falcons contain Henry, continue their productive rushing attack, and pressure Huntley with a collective defensive effort, they will put themselves in a strong position to secure another victory.

title: Falcons vs. Ravens Predictions Find Atlanta in Unfamiliar Territory
full_text:
Atlanta Falcons fans might be rubbing their necks after suffering whiplash from the sudden turnaround. Left for dead after an 0-2 start with journeyman quarterback Cooper Rush at the helm, the Falcons are now the talk of the town after bullying the Green Bay Packers and New Orleans Saints in consecutive weeks on national television.
They'll get a third straight week in front of a big audience when they take on the Baltimore Ravens on NBC's Sunday Night Football at 8:20 p.m. EST.
The Ravens are missing several key players, including quarterback Lamar Jackson , edge rusher Trey Hendrickson, and newly acquired Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens. The Falcons find themselves in unfamiliar territory: heavy favorites.
While Jackson has been doubtful most of the week, it should be noted that all of these predictions were made before he was officially ruled out on Friday afternoon by the Ravens.
NFL Network has all five of its analysts picking the Falcons , with Brooke Cersosimo saying this about Atlanta: "Is anyone better in prime time than Bijan Robinson? Not in my book, though Derrick Henry might have something to say about that. But God bless the schedule-makers for giving us Bijan thrice in night games over the first five weeks."
ESPN analytics writer Seth Walder is a long-time Falcons detractor, and he's not ready to get on the bandwagon, but he's the lone holdout of his co-workers. Pamela Maldonado and Eric Moody both pick Atlanta .
With Jackson out and Tyler Huntley under center, the Ravens will lean heavily on running back Derrick Henry. Earlier this week, Henry said Bijan Robinson was the best in the game right now, but defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich knows Henry can carry a team.
UUlbrich's unit is No. 1 in the NFL against the run after the season's first month.
"This is a great challenge," Ulbrich said this week. "We've had some success. Not saying it's been perfect by any means, but we've had some success versus the run so far this season. You want to be the best. You want to play the best.  Derrick Henry is one of the best maybe ever in that way. Just the physicality, the toughness, and then the speed that you're not ready for as he runs by you and the stiff arm, etcetera.
"But like the commitment by the offense, the organization, the offensive line to run the ball and play that that style of football. I'm excited about that.”
Falcons fans have been burned more than once when the spotlight is on their team, but they're flying high right now on both sides of the ball. They're coming home to Mercedes-Benz Stadium, and they're eager to prove in front of a national audience that this team has turned a corner and can thrive as frontrunners.

title: Falcons Get Final Word on Baltimore Ravens QB Lamar Jackson
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons will face the Baltimore Ravens without one of the NFL's biggest stars on Sunday night, as quarterback Lamar Jackson has officially been ruled out with an ankle injury. Tyler Huntley will get the start for Baltimore when the two teams meet in Week 6.
Jackson has not practiced this week after suffering the injury during the Ravens' Week 5 victory over the Tennessee Titans. His absence is a significant development for Baltimore, which will have to adjust its offensive approach without its two-time MVP quarterback.
Jackson's ability to create explosive plays as both a passer and runner has been central to Baltimore's offensive identity. Without him, the Ravens will turn to Huntley, who has experience starting games and familiarity with the team's offensive system.
Huntley has a career record of 7-9 as a starter, including a 5-6 record with Baltimore and 2-3 record with the Miami Dolphins. He will make his 12th career start for the Ravens, giving the team an experienced option despite the challenge of replacing Jackson.
Huntley also saw action against Tennessee after Jackson exited with the injury. He completed eight of nine passes for 63 yards without a touchdown or interception, helping Baltimore secure the victory.
The backup quarterback's mobility gives the Ravens another option to execute designed runs and extend plays outside the pocket. Baltimore could lean more heavily on its rushing attack, particularly with Derrick Henry serving as a key component of the offense. Huntley will need to protect the football, make quick decisions, and take advantage of opportunities in the passing game.
For Atlanta, Jackson's absence presents an opportunity to build on its recent success. The Falcons are coming off a convincing 45 -24 victory over the New Orleans Saints and will look to carry that momentum into Sunday night's contest.
Atlanta has historically struggled against Baltimore, holding a 2-5 all time record against the Ravens. Baltimore won the last two meetings, defeating the Falcons 26-16 in December 2018 and earning a 17-9 victory in December 2022.
The Falcons will look to reverse that trend while taking advantage of Baltimore's quarterback situation. Atlanta's defense must remain disciplined against Henry and prevent Huntley from finding a rhythm, particularly if the Ravens attempt to control the game with their running attack.
Jackson's absence changes the complexion of Sunday's matchup, but Baltimore still has playmakers capable of creating problems. The Falcons will need to control the line of scrimmage, limit explosive plays and capitalize on the opportunity to secure another important victory.
The Ravens and Falcons are scheduled to kick off Sunday, October 11, at 8:20 p.m. ET in Atlanta.

title: 4 Major Issues Ravens Must Still Fix On Defense
full_text:
The Ravens may have forged a new identity under rookie head coach Jesse Minter Sunday night, finding a way to comeback and beat the Falcons in Atlanta in primetime despite lacking their highest-paid player on offense and defense.
Baltimore was without two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson and without $30M/year pass rusher Trey Hendrickson and trailed throughout the game, and still came away with the win, 30-23, in overtime . Minter funneled more manpower to the line of scrimmage than ever before this young season to try to tamp down elite running back Bijan Robinson, and it worked expertly. And, yes, while doing that will leave you a little exposed on the back end , this secondary is also supposed to be the strength of the team, and a young quarterback just back from his third ACL surgery shouldn’t be able to repeatedly convert on third-and-10 or longer as Michael Penix did throughout the course of this game (Atlanta was 9/17 on third down in regulation despite being in long situations).
Tavius Robinson’s late sack, which effectively knocked Penix from the game and forced washed back-up Tua Tagovailoa into the contest, proved huge, but if this defense is going to be Super Bowl quality there remain significant areas that must be improved and cleaned up.
“Obviously, you kind of know when you play a lot for the run you may give up a few things in the passing game,” Minter said late Sunday night. “But again, I thought we could have played some third downs better, from both schematical (approach) and just playing the plays. But man, I am just really, really proud of our guys.”
Hybrid defensive back Kyle Hamilton, who put the game away by picking off Tagovailoa in overtime, kept it real as always: “I don't think we played well, for real. The third-down stuff was crazy … Third down, we have to do better. But it obviously feels a lot better fixing those mistakes with a win. I might be a little too cynical or critical, but we can be better."
Here’s what needs to improve:
Minter will always want to flood the field with defensive backs, and he played a 3-4 base throughout the first half t o mitigate Bijan Robinson and it worked expertly (17 carries and just three for five yards or more), but Penix converted seven first downs passing against Minter’s dime defense on 14 dropbacks and did so from these distances: 3 yards, 6, 10, 10, 10, 11 and 15.
Penix had a 101.7 rating throwing against dime Sunday, Baltimore has faced 95 dropbacks vs it (21 is NFL average; Rams are second with 71 and they play Monday). The Ravens rank 20th in opposing QB rating vs dime (89.5) and 20th in completion percentage (66%) and 21st in yards/attempt (8.3).
Baltimore’s dime coverage is even worse on third-and-fourth down, allowing a 94.4 rating and 9.5 yards/attempt. Minter needs to find the right mix back there or be willing to use more nickel. Overall the Ravens are just 14th in the NFL in opposer passer rating; outside of Dak Prescott have not faced a top QB.
The hope is that Hendrickson’s return will mean everything. That’s always been the hope.
After his finger surgery, the Ravens need him to look like his Week 1 version. The Ravens are just 20th in pressure rare through five gams and Minter continued to have to blitz on one of every three plays, which is not his comfort level or preference. His blitz rate was around 22% with the Chargers.
Ravens edge players had just two total QB hits in Sunday night’s game despite Penix not really trusting his repaired knee to take off and run nearly as much he did coming out of college as a first-round pick. Merely re-inserting Hendrickson needs to be a cheat code for Minter; if this becomes a scheme-reliant thing we’ve got problems. Former All-Pro defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike is back to being a menace on the inside following neck surgery and getting him and Hendrickson going at the same time will be vital.
Top receivers continue to take games over against this secondary. I strongly believe lack of pass rush in critical moments has a lot to do with that, but they also are going to need top corners Nate Wiggins (who has problems with Drake London Sunday) and Marlon Humphrey to make plays on the ball.
The Ravens have been thrown on 171 times – ninth-most in the NFL – and their cornerbacks do not have a single interception. They don’t have many pass breakups. They don’t get their hands on the ball much at all and haven’t for years.
Here’s what No. 1 receivers have done against them since Week 2 (Carnell Tate of the Titans hasn’t looked like a top wideout against any other team, but he’s as good as it gets for that suspect operation):
London (ATL): 7/11, 118 yards, 7 1st D
Tate (TEN): 9/12, 145 yds, 6 1st D
CeeDee Lamb (DAL): 7/8, 112 yds 5 1st D
George Pickens (DAL): 7/11, 82 yds, 4 1st D
Chris Olave (NO): 8/10, 86 yds, TD, 6 1st D
Minter has a lot more on his plate than ever before having to run a sideline and manage a game, which is brand new to him, and also call the defense. His early-game plans have generally been stout but as games go along this defense tends to wilt, the fourth-quarter collapse gene is still in there and the second half in general has not been good enough.
The Ravens are 26th in the NFL allowing 2.64 points/drive in the second half. QBs – again, not very good ones by and large – complete 69% of their passes (21st) with a 102.7 rating (21st). Baltimore allows 5.6 yards/play (20th) and 129 passing yards (26th) and they rank just 18th in third-down defense in the second half.
In the fourth quarter the Ravens are allowing 5.9 yards/play (26th) and 94 passing yards (31st) and 3.83 points/drive (tied for 31st) and a 42% TD rate (30th). Atlanta rolled up 126 yards in the fourth quarter Sunday and this remains a very real issue; the Ravens holding them to two field goals after marching down the field late was vital.
The Ravens have allowed 46 points in the fourth quarter, tied (with the Eagles) for second most in NFL (only Washington is worse).

title: Critical Takeaways From Wild Ravens Comeback, OT Win In Atlanta
full_text:
The Ravens overcame a bevvy of injuries, including two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson missing the game, rallied to force overtime with a two-minute drive, went ahead in overtime and sealed a huge win over the Falcons with Kyle Hamilton's interception.
Rookie head coach Jesse Minter and novice offensive coordinator Declan Doyle managed the game expertly, knowing what they were up against with Atlanta boasting the best rushing attack in the NFL to go with the top rushing defenses and the best pass rush in terms of pressure rate. Backup quarterback Snoop Huntley is very limited in the downfield passing game but saved his best work for late in two TD drives and secure a 30-23 win at Mercedes-Benz Stadium to surge to 4-1.
Baltimore’s pass rush was tepid for most of the night, the secondary gave up repeated big plays on third downs (four of third-and-10 or longer), and went 9/19 on that down in regulation, but got key goal-to-go stops late again. Tight end Mark Andrews, who has been in major decline for years, had a rough game that took points off the board but caught a key pass in overtime.
The offense, which finally cut down on its penalty issues, mustered it's crispest drive of the night to tie the game at 23 in the dying seconds, with Huntley (24/32 for 201 yards with a rushing TD and two passing TDs) looking at ease and finally using the middle of the field, throwing a short TD pass to Devontez Walker, then Derrick Henry converted a Wild Cat two-point conversion that sent the game to overtime.
"Snoop is just one of the coolest dudes," Minter said after the game. "He doesn't get rattled."
Here are the key takeaways from Week 5:
The Falcons pass rush was a problem most of the night and the Ravens had trouble sustaining things, but the drive to tie the game was masterclass - going 71 yards in six plays in 1:51. The operation was smooth and in sync.
Minter opted to take the ball after winning the toss in overtime and the Ravens reconstructed offensive line continued to take the game over. They had a helluva second half and, facing a defense that came in allowing 2.7 yards/carry, the Ravens got Henry over 100 yards and they ran for 209 yards as a team.
The Ravens mustered a 14-play drive in overtime that erased over seven minutes from the clock to give them their first lead since 3-0. Atlanta backup QB Tua Tagovoalia had to replace Penix late in the game after he took a big hit and Hamilton read him perfectly to end the game with a pick after the Falcons had started to drive.
"It could be a launch point to really get us going," Minter said of the way his team finished the game.
The overpaid tight end was horrible a few hours after the best tight end on the Ravens roster the last two seasons, by far, Isaiah Likely, comminated Washington for the Giants as he has been doing all season. Andrews cannot separate anymore, he can’t run routes downfield, he is good for about eight yards a catch and he continues to drop easy passes early in games.
Andrews basically cost Baltimore 14 points in the first half of this game. And really 16 because he needed to make a better effort on a two-point conversion that came his way, too.
He dropped a touchdown pass early in the game, a play that simply has to be made, and then had a terrible fumble deep in Baltimore territory that was returned for a touchdown. General manager Eric DeCosta has a nasty habit of letting the wrong people walk, and giving Andrews $13M when he couldn’t land a fourth round pick for him back after his terrible drop in the 2024 playoffs to spite Likely will have major ramifications for this season as he runs low on anyone besides Zay Flowers to make plays downfield. Likely making about the same money as Andrews is even sillier.
The Ravens’s pressure peaked early in the game and they were unable to pressure jittery young QB Michael Penix Jr., coming off his third ACL surgery, as the game worse on, especially on obvious pass-rush situations. He had far too much time to operate in general on second-and-long and third-and-long and the Ravens need $30M edge rusher Trey Hendrickson back from his finger surgery ASAP.
Atlanta went up, 14-6, late in the first half when Penix picked up 13 yards to Kyle Pitts on second-and-16, the Drake London for 25 on third-and-three, and Jahan Dotson for 36 on third-and-six, and then Pitts for a touchdown on third-and-five.
In the fourth quarter, Penix had all day to hit London for 14 yards on third-and-two from the Atlanta 18 and then he hit London again for 19 yards on a third-and-15 in which no one could get anywhere close to making the QB concerned.
The Ravens vaunted secondary got picked apart. Minter doesn’t want to blitz but he had to Sunday night (43%) with very shaky results and Penix converted a third-and-10 inside of six minutes that was a backbreaker. There was not nearly enough winning going on up front and Baltimore’s fourth-quarter defense will remain among the worst in the NFL until some real closers emerge.
It would take a commitment from the offensive and defensive game plans to be synced to keep this game close given Baltimore’s injury issues, including, of course, no Jackson. It would take a willingness from young offensive coordinator Declan Doyle to keep it simple here and he did.
The best way to stop Falcons dominant running back Bijan Robinson is to keep him off the field and prevent him from getting a volume of plays on the ground to get going. That’s what we got. Jesse Minter played a loaded line of scrimmage, as was required, and Baltimore’s makeshift offensive line helped them sustain possession.
The Ravens ran 40 plays in the first half. They ran the ball 19 times. They were using over 41 second of wall clock time per play in the first half and that helped them keep the ball for 19:28 in that opening half. So even without scoring any touchdowns they were very much in the game at 14-9.
Atlanta held the ball for nearly as much time in the second half, however, with Baltimore’s defense wilting. But overall Minter applied heavy attention to the line, sticking with heavy fronts, and they bottled up Bijan Robinson (17 rushes for 86 yards) outside on one long blast on an outside zone play.
"Overall, I thought we played Bijan very well," Minter said.
Minter boasted about hunting explosives with Huntley this week but thankfully that was just talk. Well done.
You don’t want Huntley, with a 5.9 yards/attempt average for his career, trying to be something he’s not on the road against a defense that is getting a lot of pressure and with an offensive line that has never played together before. Minter cut down on the motion, the ball was designed to come out quickly and too the flats and with the offensive line so experimental in the interior, the Ravens attacked the perimeter of the field as they needed to .
He leaned into the screen game and horizontal passes, and the designed screens for Derrick Henry we told you were coming, one of which went for a touchdown. And the biggest offensive play of the game came in a “Pony Package” with Henry and running back Justice Hill on the field with Hill taking a draw 47 yards to set up Henry’s touchdown .
The Ravens got a defensive stop on the opening drive of the first half, to keep the deficit at 17-9 and not greater, continuing a recent trend of holding teams to three at critical times even after giving up some yards previously.
The Falcons got cute and called a pass to a tackle eligible rather than just hammer the ball on the ground. Safety Malaki Starks and corner Marlon Humphrey were excellent in run support in goal-to-go defense in general on the night and it was going to take defensive backs being very active in that regard to corral Atlanta’s rushing attack.
Humprey, who had a rough start to the season and missed most of practice with a calf injury, provided sound tackling and also had a great blitz on a fourth-and-short play to force a pressure and get Atlanta off field late in the third quarter.
Vega Ioane…

title: Ravens Inactives For Sunday Night In Atlanta
full_text:
The Ravens activated top receiver Zay Flowers and top-paid corner Marlon Humphrey for their Sunday night game at Atlanta, with both players listed as questionable. Baltimore is an underdog for the first time this season and is facing a Falcons team playing very good football.
The Ravens already ruled out two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson on Friday. His ankle injury could keep him out for Week 6 in Cleveland as well, and will be monitored closely this week. And top pass rusher Trey Hendrickson, signed to a $30M/year deal this offseason to jumpstart a poor pass rush, was also ruled out after having a procedure on his finger prior to Week 4 and he is expected back shortly as well.
The Ravens made a risky trade for Eagles offensive lineman Cam Jurgens early in the week, knowing he remained in concussion protocol and would not play Week 5, but head coach Jesse minter indicated on Friday that they believe Jurgens could be back next week. Jurgens will back to center with Baltimore, while some believe he was about to be benched by the Eagles , after the Ravens opted to deal two picks including a 2028 second-round selection for him in a deal that drew skepticism around the league .
Flowers has been the only consistent cog in the downfield passing game, with twice as many receiving yards as anyone on the team. But his production with back-up Snoop Huntley is above half of that it is with Jackson in terms of yards per catch and air yards per target, and the Ravens simply must alter the scope of their game plan and offensive attack against a Falcons defense that has the top pressure rate in the NFL and is also No. 1 against the run (2.7 yards/carry).
The Ravens also made receiver Elijah Sarratt (fourth-round pick) inactive for Sunday night as well as defensive lineman Aeneas Peebles. Guard Andrew Vorhees (foot) was also inactive.
Last week, with Hendrickson out, undrafted rookie free agent linebacker Ethan Burke, a Baltimore native, stepped up and made an impact after being limited to special-teams duty previously. He stands to see more work tonight and the Ravens will very likely be leaning on much heavier run fronts than we have seen so far this season against Atlanta’s potent rush attack. Bijan Robinson is generally considered the most complete back in the NFL and Brian Robinson has proven to be a powerful drive finisher as well.

title: Ravens Three Keys to Victory vs. Falcons
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens are slight underdogs to come out on top in their road interconference matchup against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 5 of the 2026 regular season.
Coming off the team's first regular-season home victory under new head coach Jesse Minter, they'll be playing in primetime for the first time on Sunday Night Football. With a win, they'll improve to 4-1 before hitting the road for their first primetime game against the Atlanta Falcons next week.
In this showdown between two teams looking to take control of the top spot in the standings of their respective divisions, the Ravens can emerge victorious if they follow these keys.
The Ravens are going up against a Falcons team that has the top-ranked run defense and the second-ranked rushing offense through the first four weeks of the season. However, some of those figures are a little inflated because of how the last two weeks transpired, as they can against Green Bay Packers and New Orleans Saints defensive fronts that were missing multiple key starters and banged-up offensive lines on the other side of the ball.
To pull off an upset despite being without their highest-paid and most integral players on both offense and defense , quarterback Lamar Jackson and outside linebacker Trey Hendrickson, the Ravens will have to own the line of scrimmage in the trenches . Defensively, they can't get blown off the ball along the defensive line and provide unimpeded paths to the second level for star running back Bijan Robinson. On the offensive line, they need to be able to impose their will and open lanes in the ground game for Derrick Henry and provide backup quarterback Tyler Huntley with ample time to throw in key moments.
With Jackson under center, the Ravens were able to dig themselves out of moderate to long down-and-distances because of his uncanny ability to extend and make plays downfield. They won't have that kind of leeway, as their margin of error with Huntley is much smaller because, while he's an impressive dual-threat in his own right, it's not to the same electrifying and seemingly inevitable degree as the two-time league MVP, who is truly one-of-one.
This means the Ravens need to turn their discipline sliders all the way up and try not to get in their own way to the same or even a similarly high rate that they've been doing as one of the most penalized teams in the league over four weeks , especially on offense. A Huntley-led offense can't operate from a negative game script or afford to fall behind the sticks consistently because he's at his best throwing at the short and intermediate levels of the field.
Falcons third-year quarterback Michael Penix Jr. has been a big catalyst for the renewed success of their offense, not because he hands the ball off better to Robinson than Cooper Rush, but for his ability to deliver an accurate ball in rhythm and push it downfield. Most of the time, when the former goes deep, it's on passes outside the numbers and hashes and rarely over the middle of the field unless he has a target streaking wide open.
This tendency could lead to opportunities for the Ravens' defensive backs to jump and undercut some of those intended passes for clutch turnovers on interceptions, maybe even a pick-six if they catch it in stride with nothing but green grass in front of them. With a trio of Georgia natives in the secondary , it'll be especially meaningful if either cornerback Nate Wiggins or safeties Kyle Hamilton or Malaki Starks makes one of those big plays in this game.

title: Four Ravens X-Factors For Clash vs. Falcons
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens will continue the 2026 regular season with the first leg of a two-game road stint against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 5 on Sunday Night Football , and the difference in the game could come down to how an individual player performs when it matters most or over the course of the game by capitalizing on their opportunities when presented with them.
With a win, the Ravens improve to 4-1 and could tie for or sit atop the AFC North division standings, but a loss would, at worst, tie them for second place with either the Pittsburgh Steelers or the Cincinnati Bengals if they both win on Sunday.
Here are four players who could wind up tilting the scales in favor of the Ravens and first-year head coach Jesse Minter.
With franchise quarterback Lamar Jackson out with an injury for his game, the former Pro Bowl reserve will be making his 17th career regular-season start and his 12th in place of the two-time league MVP. While the Ravens likely plan on having the offense flow through and leaning heavily on five-time Pro Bowl running back Derrick Henry, there will be times when they will need Huntley to step up and make a play with either his arm or his legs in crucial situations. He has shown an ability to rise to the occasion in his previous starts, especially the two most recent from last year, where he averaged just under 150 passing yards, a passing touchdown and just over 56 rushing yards in massive wins over the Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers.
The second-year pro has seen his playing time on defense increase each week since he made his 2026 debut in Week 3 after fully recovering from the torn ACL that ended his promising rookie season last December. Although he won't be supplanting four-time Pro Bowl veteran Roquan Smith or fourth-year breakout Trenton Simpson in the starting lineup, he'll almost certainly see another uptick in his defensive snaps going up against such a dominant and potent rushing attack as the one they'll face in Atlanta and star running back Bijan Robinson .
After losing veteran blocking specialist Durham Smythe for the rest of the season to a torn Achilles, the Ravens signed another veteran, Nick Vannett, from the practice squad to the active roster for depth. However, the fifth-round rookie could still wind up seeing an uptick in offensive snaps played for the third week in a row, particularly as a blocker, where he can fill the role Smythe did as a lead blocker in the backfield at times and an underneath target on play-action passing plays.
Since the Falcons' running game is heavily predicated on stretch and outside zone concepts, being able to set a strong edge and stay gap sound will be paramount to the success of Minter's unit in this game. Robinson is the Ravens' best run defender on the edge and leads the team with two sacks and six quarterback hits. With fourth-time Pro Bowl veteran Trey Hendrickson out for a second straight game while he recovers from finger surgery , he will be instrumental to their game plan both on early downs and as a pass rusher in obvious passing situations, whether he's lined up inside or on the edge.
