title: Five Pivotal Ravens Matchups to Watch vs. Falcons
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens' Week 5 bout against the Atlanta Falcons could ultimately be decided by battles between specific position groups or individual players outperforming their counterparts on the other side of the ball.
It'll take place in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium under a national spotlight as it'll mark the Falcons' third straight primetime game of 2026 and the first for the Ravens. With two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson out for this game with an ankle sprain , they're entering this matchup as slight underdogs.
If the Ravens prevail, they will improve to 4-1 and could be in a two-way tie for first in the AFC North standings, depending on how the Cleveland Browns fare on the road against the New York Jets this week. Here are the five matchups that can either make or break this game.
While Falcons All Pro running back Bijan Robinson has garnered most of the headlines for the offense's success on the ground, their offensive line has been the driving force propelling him to back-to-back monster games. Even after franchise left tackle Jake Matthews left last week's game, they didn't miss a beat and kept steamrolling the New Orleans Saints defense.
The Ravens are going to need their vaunted interior defensive line, featuring a pair of Pro Bowlers in Calais Campbell and Nnamdi Madubuike and rising star Travis Jones, to step up in a big way in this game. They've gotten blown off the ball far too often by some of the worst rushing offenses in the league in the first month of the season as they've been gelling and getting healthier after long ramp-ups during training camp and preseason. They'll need to dominate at the point of attack to keep their linebackers clean and get penetration into the backfield themselves.
In a similar way that limiting Robinson is a total team effort for the Ravens' defense, guarding Baltimore's homegrown two-time Pro Bowl receiver won't solely fall on the shoulders of one or two Falcons defensive backs. Since Flowers lines up in a multitude of spots , ranging from all three receiver spots to even in the backfield to create and exploit favorable matchups, face off with any of the players in their secondary.
With a Jackson out, offensive coordinator Declan Doyle might not try to push the ball down the field to Flowers in the same ways as with backup signal caller Tyler Huntley, who is more proficient at throwing underneath and at the intermediate level. Thankfully, Flowers is even more dangerous moving horizontally in space than he is as a traditional vertical threat, meaning that he is just as likely to turn a shallow or quick pass. The Falcons have allowed a 100-plus-yard wide receiver in three straight games, and they don't have anyone on their team who can stop Flowers from extending that streak.
Whether they're mostly kept clean by their compatriots in the trenches or not, the responsibility of getting both Robinsons, Bijan and Brian, on the ground at, behind and beyond the line of scrimmage will fall to likes of Roquan Smith, Trenton Simpson and Teddye Buchannan more often than not. They'll need to be both disciplined and decisive when shooting and filling gaps created by the Falcons' offensive line. Bijan, in particular, can make a defense pay dearly for not being gap-sound on any given down and turn a play that should be a loss of yardage or minimal gain into an explosive play and even a house call.
Despite not having two of their best returning players due to injury and off-field behavior, Atlanta's front seven has surprisingly been one of the best in the league thus far this season. Since recently acquired two-time Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens won't be making his debut this week, the Falcons will be going up against a reshuffled Baltimore offensive line that will be starting first-round rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane
 out of position for the second week in a row and one of either Andrew Vorhees or Emory Jones Jr.
Atlanta won't have sack leader and former Raven Za'Darius Smith available after he was downgraded to out with a concussion/neck injury , but defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich's unit still has several of the league's leaders in pressure rate both on the edge and along the interior. The Ravens will likely look to get the ball out of Huntley's hands quickly in the passing game while leaning heavily on star running back Derrick Henry to carry a lot of the offensive load on the ground, so being able to own the line of scrimmage when they need to will be key.
The Ravens traditionally have their outside cornerbacks play sides, but head coach Jesse Minter should make an exception in this case and have Wiggins follow the Falcons' top wideout early and often because he's the best man for the job. Four-time Pro Bowler Marlon Humphrey is listed as questionable with a hamstring and calf injury that kept him out of practice for most of the week and had him as a limited participant in Friday's session. Fellow 10th-year Chidobe Awuzie struggled in relief of Humphrey in last week's win over the Tennessee Titans, leaving Wiggins as their best possible option to limit, if not neutralize, London's impact in this game.

title: How Can Ravens Stop Bijan Robinson? Film Analyst Greg Cosell Suggests A Radical Change
full_text:
The goal of Ravens head coach Jesse Minter most weeks is to defend the run with as little manpower as possible.
That needs to change in a very fundamental manner tonight in Atlanta. And after watching every snap the Ravens and Falcons have played this season, longtime NFL analyst Greg Cosell from ESPN/NFL Films who studies every matchup, agrees with me that Minter will have to delve into some looks we have not seen all season in an attempt to mitigate the Falcons dynamic run game, specifically Bijan Robinson, the best back in the NFL, running outside zone stretch plays (7.4 yards/carry).
Minter enters Week 5 having used a four-man front just five times all season and being in nickel or dime (five or more defensive backs) over 90% of the time. That won’t work against this Atlanta scheme and offensive line and a pair of running backs (Brian Robinson also) and requires a total rethink of how they plan to operate up front, especially knowing the offense is limited with Snoop Huntley at quarterback and not Lamar Jackson and with new center Cam Jurgens on the concussion list and carrying serious injury red flags.
In fact, Cosell believes that with top pass rusher Trey Hendrickson out (he is not good against the run, anyway) that Minter could look into using anchors Tavious Robinson and Zion Young on the edge in base looks and lean into perhaps three defensive tackles at times. Minter also has flexibility to deploy hybrid defensive back/linebacker Kyle Hamilton in a multitude of ways at the line of scrimmage.
“They could play a 5-2 front, too, you know, and get the wider defender for the outside zone run game,” Cosell explained in detail on “The Daily Flock Show” this week. “Because that's where it starts with the Falcons with Bojan Robinson and outside zone. I think Bijan Robinson is the best back in the league. So you've got to be able to stop outside zone.”
Minter wants to flood the field with defensive backs of all shapes and sizes and responsibilities but that’s not going to play here. Tight end Kyle Pitts is a glorified outside receiver and he still doesn’t look fully vested in Atlanta’s pass game, Drake London is a bigtime receiver but young quarterback Michael Penix Jr is still feeling his way back from his third ACL surgery and it’s doubtful coach Kevin Stefanski wants him dropping back a ton if he doesn’t have to.
Cosell believes that Minter will devise a plan to get both linebackers Teddye Buchanan and Trenton Simpson on the field at the same time on some early-down looks; Simpson replaced Buchanan as a starter after Buchanan suffered an ACL tear late last season, and is playing the best football of his career by far, with him popping off the film for Cosell, along with Robinson in the front defensive front.
Here’s how some of the new base looks might shape out in a 5-2 framework:
“Hamilton would then be a (box) safety with (free safety Malaki) Starks as opposed to the big nickel where (Jaylinn) Hawkins is the third safety,” Cosell suggested. “So I think you're going to see more of that. But again, it also depends on the personnel. the Falcons put out there.
“You know, if they run out of base personnel (one back and two tight ends), you'll see that. If they run out of 11 personnel, then Jesse Minter has to decide how he wants to play that. Now, they don't have a big-time receiving core. So, you might feel that you can still play in your base even if they put 11 out there depending on distance and field location.
“Nothing, as you know, is 100% in an NFL game. So, other than Drake London, you're probably not necessarily believing that there's someone like, ‘Oh, we better stop that guy or else.’ So we'll see. But if you can widen your front, you have a better chance of setting the edge and dealing with that outside zone run game.”
On the other side of the ball, how will the Ravens try to muster a passing attack without Jackson and with their OL issues? A full breakdown of the Ravens and Falcons game can be found below.

title: Ravens Must Try These 3 Things To Unlock Zay Flowers With A Back-Up QB Sunday Night
full_text:
Few wide receivers have carried a heavier load in the first month of the NFL season than Ravens’s sparkplug Zay Flowers.
He has been something of a one-man army once again in their downfield passing game , he is as connected with two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson as anyone has ever been and the “Zay And Pray” passing game is alive and well. But it’s time for a calibration. It’s time for a rethink. At least for a few weeks, as Jackson is out this week and he could very well be out next week too, and Snoop Huntley, when it comes to pushing the ball downfield, has almost nothing in common with Jackson’s intent and acumen .
Rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle is going to have to experiment even more to get Flowers unlocked on Sunday night against a Falcons defense that is stuffing the run without devoting extra man power to doing it, at the same time generating the NFL’s highest pressure rate (and, you guessed it, without blitzing to devote extra manpower to that endeavor, either).
Here is what Doyle is up against, whether he wants to admit it or not . He can try to amp Huntley up by opining about, “I do not think the mentality of how you want to run the offense changes at all,” but that’s baloney. We have an established body of work with Flowers and these two quarterbacks and the differences are stark:
Zay with Lamar : 14.4 yds/reception               7.5 YAC/rec                 10.12 air yds/target
Zay with Snoop : 6.5 yds/reception                 2.4 YAC/rec                 6.39 air yds/target
Here’s a snippet of what needs to happen to try to keep Flowers vested in the game plan and an elite weapon:
Flowers has been in motion 27% of the time this season. It was around 24% last season with Todd Monken. Even with some serious OL issues ( prompting a fairly desperate trade ) and the need to avoid pre-snap penalties, some simple motions for Flowers make all the sense in the world.
He won’t be latching on to deep balls. Putting him in motion before he catches a bubble screen seems to be something they should lean into. Making the defense at least wonder about a jet sweep or end around can’t hurt. At some point the Ravens are going to need a complimentary winner downfield - seems unlikely that will be Marvin Harrison Jr . though they have at least checked in on that situation - and maybe it's rookie Ja'Kobi Lane at some point when he is healthy, but they need to keep scheming it up in the interim .
I fully understand that Huntley is better off delivering the ball on a shorter distance and that his throws to the far reaches on the boundary tend to be a little late and turnover-worthy. And I know Flowers has been particularly devastating in the slot this season, where he’s been for 60% of his reps, nearly doubling his career average. But, well, Atlanta is without its best cover corner in AJ Terrell (on IR) and teams have thrown on in them in the slot 46 times (second-most in the NFL) and those targets are going nowhere, while outside throws are eating them up.
We still need Flowers on a fair share of crossers, but Doyle should be cognizant of these splits with his best receiver.
Opposing QBs throwing to slot vs AT L: 72.9 rating, 52% completions
Opposing QBs throwing to outside vs ATL: 114.7 rating, 70% completions
Flowers has been lined up in the backfield four times this season. That’s already twice as much as all of last season. Might need four times Sunday night alone.
We don’t want him doing anything running inside, but designed sprints behind the tackles and running wheel routes out of a pony package in a gun look with either Derrick Henry or Justice Hill on the field and maybe, maybe a Wild Cat look or two might be in order.
The Falcons’ run defense is ridiculous thus far, allowing just 2.7 yards/carry and this is another game where Henry might be running into a wall 25 times , bleeding clock and keeping things close but not generating much explosion. They need creativity and multiplicity in the run game more than ever with Huntley taking over at a time the run game is in a deep funk and the offensive line has major issues.

title: Ravens Are Aware Of Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Market, NFL GMs Say
full_text:
The Ravens are at least monitoring the trade market for former first-round pick Marvin Harrison Jr., according to multiple NFL general managers who are aware of the process, though many around the league believe the youngster will end up with Houston or Kansas City.
The Ravens made a bold move already this week, trading a fifth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to the Eagles for center Cam Jurgens, a player with a deep injury history; many NFL execs believe the Ravens paid too steep a price due his performance since back surgery , while longtime Eagles team president told us he heard from sources in the Eagles headquarters that Jurgens was getting benched.
Baltimore is giving off a strong signal that it is fairly desperate to win right now with two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson in the last guaranteed year of his deal and holding extreme leverage over the franchise in 2027, while a nucleus of older/injury prone players are likely in their final year with the team. The Ravens are aware that outside of Zay Flowers no one has delivered with even a modicum of consistency in their downfield passing game for two seasons and multiple GMs passed along their informed belief that the Ravens were involved in Harrison’s market at least to some degree.
“We hear they explored it,” said one GM who is also interested in a potential Harrison trade. “He’s probably going to Houston. Maybe it’s just a rumor but that’s what we hear.”
Another GM expressed a similar sentiment. The Cardinals informed Harrison, selected fourth overall in 2024, that they will trade him after Week 5 games are completed according to reports, though no agreement is formalized Arizona could find an offer from another team that exceeds what the team essentially has in its back pocket. And an injury to a superstar receiver for a contending team could reshape the market as well.
The Ravens are in a cap crunch after the Jurgens deal though a few simple restructures would amend that, and Harrison has a base salary of just $1.075M on his rookie deal, and is signed for next season with a fifth-year option for 2028. He had nearly 900 yards and eight touchdowns in his rookie season but has struggled to fit into the offense since and his play has slipped and there are also serious concerns about his overall mentality in the scouting community.
Because of all of that, the Cardinals are not expected to yield close to what they have already invested in the 24-year-old thus far in trade compensation.
Despite years of pronouncements about Rashod Bateman being a quality NFL receiver, he has been ineffective most of his career outside of 2024 and offers more as a blocker and decoy than anything else. He has never clicked with Lamar Jackson for any period of time, Devontez Walker has yet to show he can stay healthy enough and consistent enough to make a dent downfield and rookie third-round pick Ja’Kobi Lane already broke his wrist and likely faces a tough adjustment to the NFL game.
Flowers has twice as many receiving yards as anyone on the team despite running just 56 routes this season and is the only receiver on the team generating any yards after the catch. Baltimore is playing with back-up quarterback Snoop Huntley Sunday and perhaps for another week and needs to find ways to generate explosion in other ways with him, because he does not push the ball downfield .
Harrison was a highly-explosive receiver at Ohio State, his father is a Hall of Fame receiver and he has elite athletic traits. He played in college with Texans quarterback CJ Stroud for two seasons, the Texans are more desperate than most teams at 0-4, and they have dealt with significant injuries to their receivers.

title: Ravens Were Fleeced In Cam Jurgens Trade, Longtime Eagles President Contends
full_text:
The Ravens made a significant leap and paid a steep price trading for Philadelphia center Cam Jurgens this week, with longtime Eagles team president Joe Banner speaking for many working for teams around the league in saying Baltimore general manager Eric DeCosta overpaid for the player.
The Ravens were in a pretty dire situation at center, in part due to injuries to fringe players and in part due to their own mismanagement of the position , and it began with not getting an extension done with star center Tyler Linderbaum  well before he became a free agent and ignoring the position despite having  picks in the draft. Jurgens, 27, underwent back/nerve surgery in February 2025, has not been the same player since and Banner, who watched his film closely and was integral in the rise of that franchise along with current Eagles GM Howie Roseman, a former Banner protegee  and former coach Andy Reid, believes Jurgens was losing his grip on a starting guard job with the Eagles.
Therefore, giving up a second-round pick in 2028 and a fifth-round pick in 2027 seems quite desperate.
The fact that Jurgens cannot even play this week as he is still in the concussion protocol following a loss to the Rams Sunday, even further speaks to the quirky timing, with Roseman moving on from one of his highest-paid lineman at a time he is already down All-Pro guard Landon Dickerson and with superstar tackle Lane Johnson just retiring. Hence why DeCosta is drawing criticism around the league for this move.
“I think it's hard to disagree with that word,” Banner explained of that "desperation" on “The Daily Flock Show” this week. “It's obviously a very strong word, but I don't think it's an exaggeration or more provocative than it intends to be. That's at least my opinion. I mean, I obviously follow the Eagles as closely as any team in the league. So, at least I have a strong, informed opinion on what they do and who the player is.”
As to who that player is, since the nerve problems created pain up and down his legs that marred his 2025 campaign, there are real questions being asked around the NFL about how he will hold up. The Eagles clearly did not want him snapping the ball regularly despite being a former Pro Bowl center; he was struggling mightily at guard, and, making $16.5M this season with essentially $17.5m guaranteed for next season, Banner believes Roseman was eager to shed this salary despite his line woes.
“The Eagles were really highly motivated to make a trade,” Banner said. “Even with all their problems at the moment (on the line), I mean, I guess I can't prove this, but from talking to people in the building, my impression is that he's about to be benched. You know, he comes in Monday, all of a sudden he's got a concussion. I think they were actually benching him.”
Banner was the president of the Eagles from 2001-2012 and then ran the Browns for two years. He is still very plugged in around the NFL and has always had a strong pulse on the Eagles and has known their owner for quite a long time. He is not one to come off half-cocked and he went back and watched all of Jurgens’s snaps this season again before we chatted.
He knows and understands how Roseman operates as well as anyone and was adamant the Eagles are not waving the white flag on trying to win this season and simply start cashing in good players for draft picks. Banner just thinks it was over-the-top offer they couldn't refuse for a player they saw as steadily on the decline.
“The Eagles are in a real cap problem,” Banner explained. “So getting out of cap is a huge benefit to them. Cap number this year isn't very big but starting next year where it's guaranteed the cap number is very high. You know some people say, ‘Oh it's a great value.’ He's the fourth-highest paid center going forward from today in football. I mean he's not even close at this point in his career to the fourth-best center the league.”
The Ravens are now able to move rookie Vega Ioane back to guard and Jurgens brings leadership, a warrior-mentality and excellent communication skills to a position that was sorely lacking in it in Baltimore and should be a decent upgrade over the likes of Jovaughn Gwyn. That’s if he can return to form at center and stay healthy for a considerable period of time. So, yeah, people around the league are a little baffled.
“You got to the point where you're offering a two for a center who's, you know, really struggled recently and they somehow convince you that's not enough,” Banner exclaimed, “that you need you need to throw more into the pot.”

title: Fantasy Football Start or Sit Week 5: Dalton Kincaid, Keon Coleman, Khalil Shakir
full_text:
When the Buffalo Bills take on the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night, Buffalo is going to need big contributions from tight end Dalton Kincaid and wide receivers Khalil Shakir and Keon Coleman.
That's because the Rams are capable of putting a lot of points on the board and Josh Allen and Co. are going to have to play at the elite level we know they're capable of.
Kincaid is coming off a rough outing, with the tight end tallying just one catch for seven yards last week. On the opposite end of the spectrum, Shakir and Coleman had their best games of the year, with Shakir racking up seven catches for 82 yards and Coleman finishing with six catches for 116 yards and a touchdown.
First, here's a look at the Bills' final injury report . Now, a look at what we're doing with Shakir, Coleman and Kincaid in our fantasy football lineups on Monday night.
After a red-hot start to the season , Kincaid should be fit for a milk carton at this point, as the Bills tight end has just three catches for 45 yards and zero touchdowns the last two weeks.
As a result of his recent downfall in production, Kincaid ranked as TE11 overall going into Week 4, according to Fantasy Pros .
Normally, this would be a tougher decision, but the tight end spot is shallow this season, per usual, and Kincaid is capable of elite production in any given week.
The Rams actually present a tough matchup, with Los Angeles ceding the third-fewest fantasy points per game to tight ends in 2026. However, we've already seen Kincaid produce big numbers against a defense that is tough on tight ends after he dropped a buck 30 in Week 1 versus the Houston Texans, a team that has given up the fourth-fewest fantasy points to the position.
We also know Kincaid thrived in the last primetime game he played in, which came in Week 2, when he torched the Detroit Lions for seven catches and 95 yards.
Another positive for Kincaid's chances of producing is the fact that DJ Moore may not even play , and if he does he will be less than 100%, so the Bills might have to lean on Kincaid more.
We're rolling the Bills tight end out there in Week 5.
What a difference a year makes!
Coleman looked like he might be on his way out of Buffalo after last season, but he is currently in the process of reviving his career.
Coleman has proven reliable over the last three weeks, posting 13 catches for 216 yards and one score in that span. He ranks as WR19 over that three-game stretch, which amounts to flex production.
The Rams have been nothing more than a middle-of-the-road matchup for wide receivers in fantasy, so this isn't a scary one. Adding to that, there's the potential for a shootout and lots of yardage and scoring production.
As if all that wasn't enough, Moore could sit out or might not be himself if he does play thanks to his shoulder injury. That paves the way for more opportunities for Coleman.
We're starting the former second-round pick on Monday night.
Shakir had a nice bounce-back game in Week 4, but he racked up 51 of his 82 yards on just one catch and it was still only good enough for a WR28 finish.
We're not sure what timeline this is, but Shakir might be falling in the pass-catcher pecking order in Buffalo behind Coleman and that's troubling news for his fantasy football stock.
This is a promising matchup, however, as the Rams are an average team when it comes to fantasy points given up to wideouts per contest, and we know these two offenses are capable of a shootout.
We also know Moore may not play, and it's possible he'll be limited if he does suit up, which could lead to more targets for Shakir.
There's justification for starting Shakir, but his entire body of work this season (WR58 overall) just hasn't given us enough of a reason to suggest him as a starter here.

title: Five Key Things to Know About Bills at Rams in Week 5
full_text:
On Monday night, the Los Angeles Rams will be hosting the Buffalo Bills for the third time in five years.
Joe Brady’s team is coming off its first loss of the season, falling to the visiting New England Patriots, 29-26. Meanwhile, Sean McVay’s Rams rallied late in the fourth quarter at Philadelphia to stun the Eagles, 24-20.
Obviously, it’s a very big game for both teams for a lot of reasons. The Bills look to avoid a second straight loss after a 3-0 start, while the Rams are already two games behind the 4-0 San Francisco 49ers and lost to Kyle Shanahan’s club in Australia, 27-7, in Week 1.
It’s especially important since on Sunday at Foxborough, Mike Vrabel’s surging club rolled to a resounding 45-17victory over the visiting Las Vegas Raiders. Simply put, a second consecutive setback by Brady’s bunch and the Bills and Pats would own identical 3-2 marks.
This will actually be the fourth meeting in seven seasons between these interconference foes, and the third straight at SoFi Stadium. Two years ago, Josh Allen threw three touchdown passes and ran for three scores and it wasn’t enough to knock off McVay’s team as the Rams survived, 44-42.
The series dates back to 1970, with the Bills owning a 9-6 lead.
MASSIVE INT @Patriots turn Josh Allen over in the clutch pic.twitter.com/Li24JeV9ws
In 2024, Buffalo tied the NFL record for fewest turnovers in a season by a team (8). A year ago, after not giving up the football in their first three games, the club gave up the ball 25 times in their final 16 overall contests—including playoffs. They’ve committed seven turnovers in their last two games—compared to zero in the first two weeks.
Entering Week 5, only the defending champion Seattle Seahawks had allowed fewer total yards and fewer passing yards per game than Sean McVay’s club. The latter figure is somewhat surprising considering Chris Shula’s defensive unit has allowed a total of seven TD passes in four outing—two or more aerial scores in three of those contests.
What’s in a number? Buffalo’s Greg Rousseau entered Week 5 with an NFL-high six sacks, and tied for the league lead with three forced fumbles. He’s also Pro Football Focus’ No. 6 edge rusher. Meanwhile, the Rams have done a pretty good job of keeping quarterback Matthew Stafford out of harm’s way. Yes, he’s only been sacked six times.
After four weeks of play, only six players in the league had amassed more total yards from scrimmage (467) than Rams’ running back Kyren Williams. He’s second on the team with 21 receptions, good for 173 yards and one touchdown. He also leads McVay’s club with 54 carries, 294 yards on the ground, and three rushing touchdowns.

title: Four Players Who Could Make or Break Bills' Week 5 Visit to Rams
full_text:
There's no denying that the Buffalo Bills are feeling the pressure as they enter their Week 5 matchup on Monday Night Football against the Los Angeles Rams .
After the New England Patriots defeated them in Week 4, they went on to win against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. That two-game winning streak has them right on Buffalo's heels in a suddenly tight AFC East.
Even without the Patriots turning things around over the past couple of weeks, the Bills would be entering this game with plenty to prove. Not only did they have multiple turnovers in their loss to New England, but they had five turnovers in their win the previous week against the Los Angeles Chargers.
The Bills desperately need a win, and they're only going to be able to do that if they play at their very best against the Rams. With that in mind, here are four players who will make or break Buffalo as they travel to Los Angeles.
Buffalo's secondary has struggled mightily this year, especially at cornerback. Taking on the high-powered Los Angeles passing attack is the last thing they need while trying to find their footing.
Davante Adams and Puka Nacua are two of the best in the game, and they're going to make plenty of plays. The Bills will need their cornerbacks to step up and limit their production, but even more important will be C.J. Gardner-Johnson. He's their most dynamic safety and will be asked to keep the Rams from taking the top off the defense. It also wouldn't hurt to see him create a turnover as he did against the Los Angeles Chargers, which would be a huge help for Buffalo as they go on the road.
In 2024, James Cook was tied for the NFL lead in rushing touchdowns with 16. In 2025, he led the NFL in rushing yards with 1,621.
He's off to another strong start in 2026 with 421 yards and three touchdowns through four games, but he wasn't given the ball nearly enough against New England. Cook had just 14 touches and still managed 83 yards from scrimmage with a touchdown. Against the Rams, they need to feed Cook early and often to take some of the pressure off Josh Allen's shoulders, while also keeping the Rams' offense on the sideline.
Matthew Stafford is one of the NFL's most accurate passers and can tear apart a defense with ease. He's also in his late 30s and isn't exactly a mobile threat. That means he can be taken out of rhythm with pressure up the middle, which is where Deone Walker comes in.
The second-year defensive tackle has been a disruptive force this season and is one of several defenders who is thriving under Jim Leonhard. The Bills will need him to be at his best as they look to get back on track in this high-profile game.
Speaking of getting back on track, this would be the perfect time for Josh Allen to turn things back around. He was absolutely unreal during the first two games of the season, but has been turning the ball over far too often. He had three turnovers against the Chargers and then threw a pick on the final play against the Patriots to seal the game.
Allen is the emotional leader of this team and when he's at his best, there's no player who can touch him. That's the guy they need on Monday as they look for a big win in prime time.

title: Former All-Pro LT Has Always Seen Greatness From Bills' X-Factor Greg Rousseau
full_text:
Through four games of the 2026 NFL season, things have been a little shaky for the Buffalo Bills on the defensive side of the ball .
Surrendering an average of 26.8 points per game, which ranks 25th in the league, new coordinator Jim Leonhard’s young, inexperienced unit has undoubtedly endured some growing pains in more areas than one so far.
However, one spot the defense has been relatively successful at has been in the pass-rushing department , as the Bills are currently tied for the sixth-most sacks in the league with a total of 10 quarterback takedowns heading into Monday night’s matchup with the Los Angeles Rams in Week 5.
In fact, sixth-year veteran outside linebacker Gregory Rousseau even leads the NFL in total sacks with six . . . which is just two shy of his career-high prior to this year.
And, not only does Rousseau lead all players in that important category, but he’s also tops in the league in quarterback pressures (29), tackles for loss (8), and forced fumbles (3), as well.
Whether it be due to natural maturation or him simply being better suited for the new 3-4 scheme now being employed by Buffalo under Leonhard, the 6-foot-6, 266-pound former University of Miami Hurricanes’ defender appears to be in the middle of a career renaissance in 2026.
Players, both current and former, are beginning to take note of his current trajectory, too. Some even think the Bills’ pass-rusher is on the verge of superstardom.
Longtime New Orleans Saints’ and Miami Dolphins’ left tackle Terron Armstead, a former 12-year NFL veteran who was a 2018 All-Pro selection and a five-time Pro Bowler during his professional career.
According to Armstead, Rousseau’s current breakout performance through the first four weeks of 2026, which earned him the AFC Defensive Player of the Month award in September, isn’t that shocking.
It’s a path that the one-time 2019 ACC Defensive Rookie of the Year has seemingly been taking ever since he was just a young player going up against Armstead during their divisional matchups in the AFC East from 2022 to 2024.
In seven games between the two, which included six meetings in the regular season and one playoff outing, Rousseau—who’s affectionately referred to as “Groot” by teammates—tallied 23 total tackles and 4.5 sacks.
“When I played for the Miami Dolphins, and (I was) battling against the Buffalo Bills twice a year, Greg Rousseau was a guy that I always felt like was primed to break out at some point. Now, I didn’t know when it would happen, but he had everything—speed, size, strength, the awareness, (and) he was smart—and I’ve just been waiting on this season,” former NFL offensive lineman Terron Armstead said in an appearance on NFL Network’s GMFB on Friday morning.
“It’s happening right now before our eyes. We’re watching a star (be) born.”
Rousseau started off the season with three-straight games posting two sacks in the matchups against Houston, Detroit, and the Los Angeles Chargers, but he failed to bring down New England Patriots’ quarterback Drake Maye in Buffalo’s first loss of the season last week at Highmark Stadium.
Rousseau was awfully close to Maye on multiple occasions, though, so it wasn’t as if he had any sort of bad outing during the recent affair in the AFC East by any stretch of the imagination.
For that reason, Armstead believes that when the primetime lights come on at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, for Monday Night Football in just a few short days , it’ll be running back James Cook III and Rousseau—not quarterback Josh Allen—who will be the real players to watch out for on the road against the Rams.
“The Rams are getting healthy. Puka’s back. Matt Stafford’s getting more into that groove—him, Davante, (and) all the things—but Greg Rousseau is leading the NFL in sacks, tackles for loss, and quarterback hits,” Armstead added on Friday.
“We’re watching a star emerge. Greg Rousseau (and) James Cook can be the X-factors for the Bills to get this win against the Rams.”
Kickoff for the intraconference game, which will be broadcast on ESPN , is slated for Monday night at 8:15 p.m. ET.

title: Refs Miss Critical Penalty vs. Bills, NFL Fines Patriots' Player After The Fact
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills have had a rough week since their narrow loss to the New England Patriots last Sunday at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park.
Whether it be injuries that resulted from the game or simply just the reality of the ramifications that now come with the divisional loss, Buffalo’s players and coaches—whether they want to openly admit it or not—have likely had lingering thoughts of New England and third-year quarterback Drake Maye in the back of their minds over the past several days.
Now, to make matters worse, news broke Sunday afternoon that Patriots’ second-year running back TreVeyon Henderson was recently fined for an infraction on the game-sealing play against Buffalo last weekend . . . and it’s one he should’ve apparently been flagged for.
If fans’ memories are foggy, the sequence in question was a 12-yard completion to tight end Hunter Henry from the aforementioned Maye on 3rd-and-10 with 55 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter of the matchup.
Off play-action to Henderson, the third-year quarterback rolled to his right and found Henry in the flat for an easy pass-and-catch to move the chains and secure a critical victory in the AFC East.
Some fans and outside critics questioned Bills’ cornerback Maxwell Hairston’s effort on the play, thinking the former University of Kentucky playmaker could’ve attempted to stop the much larger Henry in his tracks before he was able to cross the first-down marker.
However, what might peeve Bills Mafia even more is to know that Henderson should’ve been penalized for a chop block on the play, which he has now subsequently been fined for.
Following the fake hand off, Henderson went low on Buffalo’s rookie linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr , who was blitzing on the play.
The Patriots’ runner went low and easily flipped Elarms-Orr into the air and onto the ground . . . which allowed Maye to remain unscathed and quickly find his open target.
And, now seven days later, ESPN reporter Mike Reiss posted the news on X prior to New England’s afternoon outing with the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday that the former Ohio State runner was slapped with a $12,537 fine for the illegal chop block.
Patriots RB TreVeyon Henderson was fined $12,537 for a chop block late in last week's win over the Bills. The infraction came with 55 seconds left in the fourth quarter, the play in which the team sealed the victory (a 12-yard Hunter Henry catch-and-run for a first down).
Ultimately, he wasn’t hit with an infraction during the game, though, which is clearly an issue. The NFL outlawed all chop blocks prior to the 2016 season .
Furthermore, if the league finds a play to be worthy of a fiscal punishment a week later, then shouldn’t that exact same play have been penalized during a very critical point in a divisional matchup last Sunday?
Surely, that should’ve been the case . . . yet, just as many things have gone the Patriots’ way in the past, the NFL’s referees somehow turned a blind eye to the massive miscue on Henderson’s part only later to have the league office hand down a miniscule “slap” on the wrist after the fact.
Had Henderson been penalized, then New England would’ve likely had to punt after being pushed back 15 yards on third down. Instead, nothing happened aside from a minor financial penalty being given to the Patriots’ playmaker.
Now, following back-to-back victories, the Patriots are right back in the thick of contention within the AFC and the AFC East.
They could even leapfrog Buffalo in the standings, which Bills ON SI ’s Randy Gurzi just reported on following Sunday afternoon's slate of NFL games.
It’s funny how that happens, isn’t it?

title: Bills' Rookie WR Set for NFL Debut as Josh Palmer Replacement on Monday Night at Rams
full_text:
He's waited patiently over the first four weeks , and his opportunity has finally arrived.
Buffalo Bills' fourth-round rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell will be on the active game day roster for the first time this season on the road against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 5.
"Skyler’s going to be up, and it was good because early in the week, he's taking DJ's [Moore] plays in practice as we kind of go through it," said Bills' first-year head coach Joe Brady after Saturday's practice in Orchard Park.
While Moore is officially questionable for the October 12 primetime matchup as he nurses an AC joint issue, the Bills have already ruled out veteran wide receiver Josh Palmer due to a shoulder injury that popped up during Friday's practice. With Buffalo down at least one body at the wide receiver position, Bell will have the opportunity to introduce himself on Monday Night Football.
"Got to go put on the show [for Monday night]. Whole world watching, so, I'm excited," said Bell.
After a disappointing 2025 campaign with the Bills, Palmer has been boom or bust thus far through the first four weeks in 2026. He has three receptions, two of which resulted in long touchdowns, over 102 offensive snaps.
Deployed for 40 percent of plays, Palmer has earned only nine targets as a receiver. Now, he'll miss his sixth regular season game as a Bill, and the extent of his injury is currently unknown.
"He got kind of twisted up yesterday in practice. We're still kinda going through some of the testing and whatnot," said Brady on Saturday.
During his final season competing for Connecticut, Bell showed versatility, explosiveness and production . He led all Division I FBS players with 101 receptions.
"I think I'm explosive. I'm dynamic. I got speed, and I try to make every play that come my way," said Bell.
Over 13 games in 2025, he gained 1,278 yards receiving and caught a team-high 13 TD passes. The slightly-undersized receiver wasn't confined to the slot, displaying the ability to win downfield and win 50-50 balls.
"Skyler's a baller. His feel for the game is amazing. His ability to burst after the catch," said Bills' veteran wide receiver Khalil Shakir last month.
Bell missed about two weeks of training camp due to a groin injury that emerged on August 8. It wasn't until the preseason finale that he saw his first game action . He made seven catches for 49 yards against the Pittsburgh Steelers on August 27.
"Like I've been saying all along it's not like he hasn't been getting work with Josh [Allen]," said Brady. "I've got all the confidence in Skyler and I'm excited for his opportunity."

title: Bills Suddenly in Danger of Losing AFC East Lead on Monday Night Football
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills started the season on fire , while the New England Patriots struggled out of the gate. The two met in Week 4, with the Bills sitting atop the AFC East with a record of 3-0 while the Patriots were 1-2.
There's still plenty of time left in the season, but a win could have essentially buried the Patriots. Instead, the Bills played a sloppy game and lost 29-26 to the Patriots. That allowed New England to improve to 2-2 on the season and gave them plenty of confidence.
That confidence was on full display in Week 5 as the Patriots ran the Las Vegas Raiders out of the building. Drake Maye looked like the quarterback who led them to 14 wins and a Super Bowl berth in the 45-17 win, throwing for 374 yards with four touchdown passes and one touchdown run.
Now sitting at 3-2, they're right back in the race for the division lead. In fact, they could take the lead in the AFC East if the Bills lose on Monday Night Football to the Los Angeles Rams .
Buffalo hits the road for their showdown against the Rams, flying to Southern California for the primetime game. They enter as slight underdogs, and the majority of the experts believe the Rams will come out on top in this one.
The Bills have the talent to go toe-to-toe with any team in the NFL, but they're also struggling to find their footing right now. They were able to win in Week 3 against the Los Angeles Chargers, but that was an ugly game with five turnovers from the Bills. Three of those were from Josh Allen, who had two interceptions and a lost fumble.
His ball security concerns were on display again in Week 4, with Allen throwing a costly interception on their final offensive play of the game. That allowed New England to run the final 1:05 off the clock, sending them into Week 5 looking for answers on both sides of the ball.
If there is any good news for the Bills, it's that Los Angeles hasn't been the dominant team we're used to seeing. They head into Monday's game with a record of 2-2, although they had an impressive comeback in Week 4 to knock off the Philadelphia Eagles.
Still, they've shown vulnerability during their first four games of the season and it will be up to Buffalo's coaching staff to ensure they take advantage of that. If they don't, they'll suddenly be tied with the Patriots, who have the head-to-head tiebreaker.

title: Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Idea Presents Bills With High-Risk, High-Reward Decision
full_text:
From fourth overall pick to trade bait in his third season, Marvin Harrison Jr.'s time with the Arizona Cardinals is coming to a close. Could he wind up in Buffalo to join the Bills passing attack?
Adam Schefter reported on Saturday that the Cardinals are finalizing a deal to trade Harrison, but the Cardinals haven't announced who they're trading the WR to. He reported that "no trade will be completed until after Sunday's games are played," as Arizona will likely wait to see if the current best offer can be topped.
Here are reasons why the Bills should and should not trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.
Earlier reports indicated the Cardinals were looking for a second round pick for Harrison, per Tom Pelissero .
Buffalo *just* traded a second rounder for DJ Moore, a player with much more experience and productivity in the NFL. Giving up another premium draft pick would not be wise, especially since he'd only have two more seasons on his rookie deal (assuming his fifth year option would be picked up).
Even on a rookie contract, since he was picked fourth overall, Harrison is still set to have a cap hit of over $9.6 million in 2026 and over $11.25 million in 2027. Currently, his projected fifth year option would be $17.2 million. Arizona has paid a portion of this year's salary already, but trade details would determine how much the team getting Harrison would pay moving forward.
The Bills don't have the budget to spend that kind of money. Buffalo already ranks sixth in total spending on WRs, and that's before DJ Moore's contract spikes up to an almost $29 million cap hit.
There's a reason Harrison went fourth overall not too long ago. Coming out of Ohio State, he was highly touted as one of the best WR prospects in recent history.
Clearly, those projections were off. He produced 885 yards on 62 catches his rookie season, well behind other players in his draft class like Malik Nabers, Brian Thomas Jr and Ladd McConkey. His eight receiving touchdowns did help save his statline in 2024.
His sophomore season saw a dip in all facets of his production. His number of targets dropped from 73 to 41, yards down to 608 and touchdowns cut in half to four. He also missed five games due to a combination of two heel injuries, a concussion and appendicitis.
However, the 6-foot-3 wideout could be the latest first round pick that simply needs a change of scenery to reach their ceiling. Geno Smith, Baker Mayfield, Chase Young and Sam Darnold have all done it in recent years, and pairing him with Josh Allen and Joe Brady could be what he needs to get his career back on track. If the risk pays off, Buffalo has their WR1 for the next decade.
When you look at the makeup of Buffalo's offense, there is a skillset that's missing. DJ Moore is the savvy route runner and No. 1 wideout, Khalil Shakir is the reliable slot option, and Keon Coleman is the big-body contested catch weapon down the field. What the Bills are missing is speed - someone that can stretch the field vertically.
Harrison is not that. He struggles to create separation and had the worst catch rate in the league in 2024, the only season he had enough targets to qualify for the ranking.
In addition to his redundant skill set, the acquisition of Harrison would also likely block the continued development of Coleman, who has emerged as a reliable passing game option to open the season. Putting another obstacle in front of Coleman just as he's beginning to hit his stride might permanently stunt the development of the wideout.
Harrison has a unique ceiling as an athlete that could help Buffalo's offense explode if reached. However, given the price a trade for Harrison is reported to command, and the inability to have a clearly defined role with the offense, the risk is not worth the reward. It would be best if Brandon Beane allocated his assets elsewhere if he were to add to the wide receiver room.

title: This Key Factor in Bills at Rams Matchup Could Determine Monday Night Football Result
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills have a tall task ahead of them this week.
Not only does the team have to travel all the way across the country to an unfamiliar environment for just its second road matchup of the season after a three-game home stand, but the Bills will also be forced with doing so under the pressure of the primetime lights of Monday Night Football .
Furthermore, the opponent is reigning MVP quarterback Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams, a team coming off a crucial conference victory in less-than-ideal conditions at Lincoln Financial Field versus the Philadelphia Eagles.
And, Buffalo will be doing so with the hope of not dropping two straight games of its own, as the team just fell short against the New England Patriots at Highmark Stadium in devastating fashion last Sunday .
However, with that in mind, if they can win at SoFi Stadium, then the Bills should be fine moving forward in the minds of many.
But, if they lose to the Rams, then there will undoubtedly be more than a few eyebrows being raised amongst the fanbase, as well as from outside observers , regarding just what type of operation first-year head coach Joe Brady is running in Western New York this fall.
Bills ON SI has already covered a few points of concern on Buffalo’s roster heading into Monday night’s intraconference affair, as well as some areas that the team might be able to exploit against Los Angeles .
There is one other phase of the upcoming matchup, though, that seems to be falling a little under the radar in terms of its importance toward the outcome of the nationally-televised meeting between the Rams and the Bills on Monday night in Inglewood, California.
Well, it’s special teams. And, more specifically, in the area of punt returns.
For those who might not remember, the last time the Bills traveled to SoFi Stadium to take on Los Angeles in December 2024, Buffalo fell short to its NFC counterpart by a mark of 44-42.
It was a high-scoring event from both offenses as Stafford and fellow quarterback Josh Allen combined for 744 yards of total offense and eight touchdowns between the two of them, but in the end it was the third phase of the game that ended up being the deciding factor that turned the tide in favor of head coach Sean McVay’s Rams.
Although the West Coast squad won by less than a field goal, which is ironic considering Buffalo’s recent troubles with two-point conversions , the tipping point in the contest came when linebacker Jacob Hummel blocked a kick from former Bills’ punter Sam Martin in the second quarter with just under 13 minutes remaining before halftime.
Backup tight end Hunter Long recovered the punt at Buffalo’s 22-yard line and subsequently returned the ball all the way to the end zone to put the Rams up 17-7 with 12:29 remaining in the quarter.
And, as a result, the Bills were never able to recover despite outscoring Los Angeles by a margin of 35-27 the rest of the way.
Former Rams’ defender Michael Hoecht, who is now on the other side with Buffalo this time around, remembers the outing fondly.
He wasn’t on the field for the particular sequence mentioned above, but it’s definitely not lost on him when it comes to just how crucial every aspect of that contest at SoFi Stadium was two winters ago.
“Personally, I’ve had the game circled on my calendar for a while. It’s obviously cool because I still know a lot of people in the building. But, I feel like (people) have heard this message from me before, you know—you can’t ride the wave of, like, (some) games are bigger than others—it’s just you’ve got to stay consistent,” Bills’ outside linebacker Michael Hoecht, who played 36 defensive snaps and 14 snaps on special teams for the Rams in that game two years ago according to Pro Football Reference , said following practice on Thursday .
“Special teams was the difference in the game. It was the blocked punt. So, I mean, you never know which play it is in the game that is going to decide it.”
And, although Hoecht added that he hopes he and his defensive teammates can—somehow, some way—be the ultimate deciding factors on Monday, there’s some further truth to the reference of the importance of special teams when digging a little deeper into Los Angeles’ statistics this season.
Through four weeks, Rams’ fourth-year punter Ethan Evans has had only one punt downed inside the 20-yard line and, in the three games that Los Angeles’ special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone’s unit has faced a punt return, the team has also allowed an average of 13.73 yards per attempt.
While that may not seem like a lot to some, the highest average in the NFL right now amongst players with at least five returns isn’t too far off from that number as Minnesota’s Myles Price has an average of 20.1 YPR .
Furthermore, three of the top five returners in the league, however, have average return rates ranging between 13.5 and 13.8 yards per attempt according to StatMuse .
And, in addition to that fact, in back-to-back weeks Los Angeles has allowed punt returns well over Price’s league-high rate as Denver’s Kolbe Katis managed to bring one back 28 yards in Week 3, while Philadelphia’s Britain Covey had a return of 41 yards just last Sunday.
So, when peeling back that extra layer, it’s clear to see that—whether it be protecting up front for rookie punter Tommy Doman Jr., or blocking for wide receiver Greg Dortch in the return game—it’s going to be prudent for Buffalo to stay consistent, as Hoecht mentioned on Thursday, during the punting portions of the evening, especially when Dortch is standing back there.
There could be a play made that breaks the game wide open for the Bills.

title: Bills' Final Week 5 Injury Report: DJ Moore Practices Saturday, Two Ruled Out for MNF
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills won't have wide receiver Josh Palmer available when they visit the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football, and wide receiver DJ Moore is officially questionable to play.
Buffalo was forced to add Palmer to the injury report on Friday after he banged up his shoulder during practice.
"He got kind of twisted up yesterday in practice. We're still kinda going through some of the testing and whatnot," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady.
Palmer and Moore are two of 15 players listed on the Bills' final Week 5 injury report. Ten of those 15 have been cleared for the October 12 road game.
Palmer and starting defensive lineman Ed Oliver have been ruled out. With Palmer unavailable, Buffalo will activate fourth-round rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell for the first time.
Meanwhile, Moore, slot cornerback Dee Alford and rotational defensive lineman Landon Jackson all carry questionable tags as the Bills head west.
"We got 48 hours to kind of keep working through with these guys," said Brady following Saturday's practice in Orchard Park.
Brady claimed he's comfortable with taking it up to kickoff with the three questionable players, and he dismissed the idea that their lack of practice makes them less prepared for the game.
"We're at the point, these guys are vets that have practiced and have taken a lot of reps with us. It's not like these guys were out for an extended period of time and they haven't gotten a lot of time on task with the defense or the offense."
Despite leaving two games early because of his AC joint sprain, Moore has been available for the Bills all four games thus far.
As a result, the veteran wide receiver has appeared in 91 consecutive regular season games dating back to December 2020. He has 12 receptions for 178 yards and one touchdown thus far in his first season with the Bills.
"DJ has already shown that he can go out there and go play in a game and have success without the [practice] reps," said Brady, who was Moore's offensive coordinator with the Carolina Panthers in 2020 and 2021.
It seems to be a pain tolerance issue for Moore, who reaggravated the injury during the Week 4 loss to the Patriots.
"Nothing different. It's just the same thing kinda going on," said Brady.
Our guess is that Moore takes an injection to manage the pain and suits up for Buffalo on Monday night.
While Alford may not be available after tweaking his ankle during the October 4 loss, the Bills' ailing secondary will welcome back starting cornerback Christian Benford after a one-game absence.
"Christian's good to go," said Brady.
Benford, who suffered a non-contact toe injury in the Week 3 win over the Los Angeles Chargers, returned to practice in a limited capacity on Thursday and Friday. He was upgraded to a full participant on Saturday.

title: Panthers' Power Ranking Spot, Super Bowl Odds Rise Despite Not Playing
full_text:
The bye week was kind to the Carolina Panthers. Aside from a miraculous, stunning Tampa Bay Buccaneers win on Thursday, it went exactly to plan. The New Orleans Saints and Atlanta Falcons both lost, leaving the Panthers in first place.
They also got healthier. Though this week will be key, there's a good chance Jaelan Phillips, Monroe Freeling, and Jalen Coker will be back. Tershawn Wharton, Taylor Moton, and Trevor Etienne have a chance of joining them.
Plus, their next opponent, the Philadelphia Eagles, saw one offensive lineman retire, traded another, and then lost in unfathomable fashion in London before flying back to face the Panthers this Sunday.
It was as good an off week as you could ask for if you're the Panthers. And while they didn't play, those good vibes are reflected in their rising Super Bowl odds and Power Ranking placement.
Teams rarely move in NFL Power Rankings when they're not playing. They didn't do anything to earn it. Sometimes, though, teams get worse around them, pushing them up. And with these Power Rankings from Sports Illustrated's Peter Dewey , the rising Super Bowl odds pushed Carolina up.
The Panthers' odds rose likely because their division title odds rose with the Saints and Falcons losing. Since these rankings are based on Super Bowl odds, the spot went up from 20th to 18th, but there is a caveat.
"Bryce Young and the Panthers went from +9000 to +7400 to win the Super Bowl during their bye week, as they're 2-2 and in the mix to win the NFC South for the second season in a row," Dewey began.
But, he added, " Their defense needs to show more -- even with all the injuries -- before I really buy this team in the futures market."
This is true, although it's going to be hard for the defense to do anything as long as both Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn are out. That's an untenable situation, and the other nine players on the field can only do so much.
It is likely that what the Panthers did on SNF versus the Detroit Lions is the blueprint. They're going to have to live with Akayleb Evans being picked on, but they can shut down the run, get timely pressure, and make fourth-down stops when necessary.
Until Horn and Jackson return, that might be the best we can hope for, and it's the sort of thing that should inspire those like Dewey and see the Panthers continue rising up the ranks.

title: The Panthers Defense Makes Absolutely No Sense — And That's a Good Thing
full_text:
I really don't know what to make of the Carolina Panthers' defense right now. There are times when I watch them and think they still have a long way to go, and then they'll turn around and make a play that completely changes the game. Four games in, I'm still trying to figure this group out.
The numbers don't really help, either. Carolina is giving up 387.2 yards per game, which ranks 29th in the NFL, and its 11.8% pressure rate ranks 30th. There's really no way around it. Those aren't good numbers.
Then I got to the numbers that surprised me. The Panthers have eight takeaways through four games, second-most in the NFL, and they've stopped opponents five times on fourth down, tied for the most in the league. I had to look at that twice because it doesn't really match what I've watched at times.
How does a defense give up that many yards, get that little pressure, and still keep finding ways to end drives? I don't really have an answer. They just keep doing it.
The first four games haven't made much sense. Chicago ran for 291 yards and put 59 points on Carolina in the opener, and after that game, I wondered how this defense was going to stop anybody. Seven days later, Atlanta scored three points.
Then Carolina went to Cleveland and gave up only 21. A week later, Detroit rolled up 452 yards of offense , and Jared Goff threw for 412 yards on 52 attempts. If you had given me those numbers before the game and asked who won, I'd take Detroit every time.
Even the way that game ended fits with everything else. Detroit had moved the ball all night and had one last chance to go win the game. Carolina needed one stop, and Lathan Ransom and Will Lee III combined to make it on fourth down.
Maybe that's why I'm having such a hard time deciding what I think about this defense. I don't like giving up nearly 400 yards per game, and I definitely don't like being near the bottom of the NFL in pressure rate. Keep doing that, and eventually it's going to hurt you.
But I also can't ignore eight takeaways and five fourth-down stops. Those have certainly helped the siege of injuries Carolina has dealt with on that side of the ball.

title: The Panthers Just Fixed a Problem That Haunted Them All Last Season
full_text:
There were plenty of things I wanted to see change with the Panthers offense this season, but one of the biggest was pretty simple. I wanted to see some plays where it didn't feel like Carolina had to fight for every single yard. Last year, there were way too many times when it felt like the Panthers needed almost everything to go right just to put together a scoring drive.
Apparently, Dave Canales felt the same way. Around this time last season, he talked about Carolina's "lack of big plays" and the need to create more of them in both the running and passing game. I remembered Carolina having that problem, but I didn't realize how much it had changed until I started looking at the numbers from this season.
Through four games, the Panthers have an explosive-play rate of 10.9% , which ranks sixth in the NFL. They were at 8.8% last season and ranked 23rd. Going from the bottom third of the league to the top six is a pretty big change, even if we're only four games into the season.
The Detroit game was probably the best example we've seen so far. Carolina put up 445 yards in the 32-26 win , and 11.4% of its plays were explosive. It felt like every time Detroit started getting comfortable, somebody on Carolina's offense made a play.
Tetairoa McMillan caught 14 passes for 192 yards and two touchdowns. Bryce Young threw for 329 yards, and Chuba Hubbard ran for 122 yards and scored twice. We've talked about all three of those guys plenty already, but when you put what they're doing together, you start to see why the explosive-play numbers have changed so much.
That's probably what feels the most different to me. Last season, one holding penalty or one sack could put Carolina in a spot where I didn't know how they were going to get out of it. When you're constantly asking an offense to put together long drives, eventually something is going to go wrong.
This year, there are more ways to make up for it. McMillan can make a play downfield, Hubbard can break a run and suddenly Carolina is on the other side of the field, and Young has been more willing to push the ball when the opportunity is there. Carolina doesn't have to be perfect for 10 or 12 plays anymore just to get into scoring position.
I wondered if maybe Detroit was making these numbers look better than they really were. It wasn't. Carolina's explosive-play rate was 12.9% against Chicago, 10.2% against Atlanta, and 9.5% against Cleveland. The Panthers have been above last season's 8.8% mark in every game they've played.
Four games is still four games, so I'm not ready to say this offense has everything figured out. We've seen it stall, and there are still times when Carolina makes things harder on itself than it needs to. But explosive plays were something Canales specifically wanted more of last season, and so far, he's getting them.
Last year, the Panthers were searching for big plays.
This year, they're finally expecting them.

title: Tetairoa McMillan's Most Impressive Stat So Far Isn't His 385 Receiving Yards
full_text:
I thought I had pretty much said everything I needed to say about Tetairoa McMillan after what he did against Detroit. When a guy catches 14 passes for 192 yards and two touchdowns, there really isn't much left to add.
Then I started looking through PFF's latest wide receiver rankings , and one number got my attention. McMillan has had 26 catchable passes thrown his way this season, and he's caught every single one.
I know what some people are probably thinking. He's a wide receiver; isn't that what he's supposed to do? Sure, but going four games without dropping a single catchable pass is still pretty impressive, especially with how much Bryce Young has been looking his way.
There's more to it than just the catches, too. McMillan has 385 receiving yards through four games and is averaging 2.35 yards per route run, which ranks 12th among NFL receivers, according to PFF. They also have him ranked as the No. 8 receiver in football right now.
I expected McMillan to be good this season. I'm just not sure I expected us to already be having this conversation four games in.
That's what I'm starting to wonder about with McMillan . He had 1,014 receiving yards as a rookie, so we already knew Carolina had something. I thought another step forward this season probably meant establishing himself as one of the better young receivers in the league.
He might already be past that.
PFF had McMillan ranked No. 23 among NFL receivers before the season. Now he's eighth, and obviously the Detroit game had a lot to do with that jump. But I don't think you can look at 26 catches on 26 catchable passes and say this is all about one huge game.
That's probably what I like most about that stat. The 192 yards against Detroit are going to get your attention, and they should, but 26-for-26 tells you something else. Young has given McMillan plenty of chances through four games, and McMillan hasn't wasted them.
We've talked a lot about how different Young has looked through the first four games, and he deserves that. But I also don't think it's a coincidence that his jump is happening while McMillan is making one of his own. It has to make Young's job a little easier when he knows that if he gives McMillan a chance, chances are he's coming down with it.
There are still 13 games left, so I'm not ready to start putting McMillan in the same group as the very best receivers in football. I do think we're getting closer to having that conversation, though, and I probably wouldn't have said that before the season.
I came into the year thinking McMillan could become one of the better young receivers in the NFL.
Four games later, I'm starting to wonder if I set the bar too low.

title: Nobody Drafted This Panthers Rookie & That Already Looks Like a Mistake
full_text:
Coming into the season, Lee Hunter was the rookie defensive tackle I expected to be talking about. The Carolina Panthers took him with the 49th pick, and so far, he's given them plenty to feel good about.
Aaron Hall was a different story. He went through all seven rounds without hearing his name called, signed with Carolina out of Duke, and came into camp just trying to find a way onto the roster. Honestly, I wasn't paying much attention to him at the time.
Four games later, I am now.
Hall has played in every game, already has 10 tackles, and has even made a start. Six of those tackles came in Carolina's 34-3 win over Atlanta, and he also has a fumble recovery. That's a pretty good start for a guy nobody drafted.
The funny thing is, maybe the Panthers aren't nearly as surprised by this as the rest of us. After Hall made the 53-man roster, general manager Dan Morgan said the rookie "kind of blew us away" with his ability to handle double teams, rush the passer, and play with a high motor.
Turns out Morgan might have been telling us something.
What really made me take notice was NFL.com's early All-Rookie team . Hunter made the first team at defensive tackle, which is already a pretty good development for Carolina, considering how much they invested in him.
Then I kept reading, and there was Hall on the second team alongside Kansas City first-round pick Peter Woods. Think about how different those paths were just a few months ago. Woods heard his name called in the first round, Hunter went in the second, and Hall sat through the entire draft without getting picked.
Now all three are on the same list.
That's what makes Hall's first four games such a good story. This isn't just an undrafted rookie hanging around at the bottom of the roster. He's getting snaps, he's already started a game and he's showing that he belongs out there.
Hall had a pretty good résumé at Duke, too. He finished his final season with 44 tackles and 2.5 sacks and was a two-time team captain. He also grew up in North Carolina and watched the Panthers during the Cam Newton years, which makes the way this has started even better.
And Carolina might have gotten a little lucky here. Every team had a chance to draft Hall. Nobody did, and the Panthers were able to bring him in without using a pick.
Nobody knows what Hall's career is going to look like after four games, but that's not really the point of this story. Going from undrafted in April to making an NFL roster was already an accomplishment. Now he's playing meaningful snaps and getting recognized alongside some of the best rookies in the league.
Hall didn't hear his name called during the draft.
He's giving people a reason to remember it now.

title: The Panthers Have Suddenly Become a Defensive Coordinator's Nightmare
full_text:
I remember when the biggest question around Bryce Young was whether the Panthers had given him enough help. Actually, I feel like we've been asking that almost since the day Carolina drafted him.
I'm not sure we need to ask it anymore. I've watched this offense for four games now, and I'm starting to wonder about something completely different. If you're playing the Panthers right now, who are you trying to take away?
I guess the obvious answer is Tetairoa McMillan. After what he did against Detroit, I'd probably start there, too. I'm just not sure that fixes the problem.
McMillan caught 14 passes for 192 yards and two touchdowns against Detroit. He became the first player in Panthers history with at least 10 catches, 175 receiving yards, and two touchdowns in a game, and he was named NFC Offensive Player of the Week.
Panthers.com broke down McMillan's huge night , including how Carolina kept moving him around instead of letting Detroit know exactly where he'd be. Dave Canales credited the staff for “putting him in different situations, getting matchups right.”
So yeah, I'm probably making sure I know where No. 4 is before every snap. But if I'm spending that much attention on McMillan, now I've got Chuba Hubbard to worry about.
Hubbard just ran for 122 yards and two touchdowns against Detroit. I've complained plenty about Carolina getting away from him too quickly, but if he's running the ball like that, you can't spend the entire game worrying about McMillan and let Hubbard keep getting five or six yards at a time.
And then there's Jalen Coker. He didn't even play against Detroit, but we're only a few weeks removed from him catching eight passes for 138 yards and two touchdowns against Chicago. Hubbard has also caught 10 passes with two touchdowns this season, and Darren Waller caught two touchdowns against Atlanta.
I don't remember the last time Carolina had this many answers on offense.
I know it's only four games. I've also watched this team go from getting embarrassed by Chicago to beating Detroit on Sunday night, so I'm trying not to decide too much about the Panthers from one week to the next.
Still, 121 points is 121 points.
According to Panthers.com , that's the most points through four games in franchise history. Carolina has also scored at least 30 points three times, something no Panthers team had ever done in three of its first four games.
I definitely didn't see that coming.
Young has thrown for 1,268 yards and nine touchdowns. McMillan already has 385 receiving yards, Hubbard is coming off his best rushing game of the season, and Coker hasn't even been available the last couple of weeks.
Maybe I'm making this too simple, but isn't this what Carolina has been trying to give Young all along?
For most of his career, we've talked about what he didn't have. The offensive line wasn't good enough. He needed another receiver. The running game disappeared. It always felt like we were talking about what Carolina needed to add next.
I'm having a harder time doing that now.
I'm not ready to put this offense up there with the best in the NFL after four games. That's too far for me, especially with how different this team has looked from one Sunday to the next.
But I also don't think what we're seeing is nothing. McMillan just took over a game, Hubbard ran for 122 yards, Young threw for 329, and Coker wasn't even on the field.
For once, I'm not asking whether Young has enough help.
I'm trying to figure out who defenses are supposed to stop first.

title: Bryce Young's Stunning Turnaround Just Reached a Level Nobody Expected
full_text:
Yeah, I wasn't ready for that one.
I've spent most of the last few weeks trying to figure out exactly how far I'm willing to go with Bryce Young. The MVP chants against Detroit were fun, and I've already said I'm done acting like every good game needs to come with a “let's see him do it again.”
Then I saw PFF's first-quarter All-Pro team . Young is the second-team quarterback, with only Lamar Jackson ahead of him.
I had to think about that for a minute because it really wasn't that long ago that Young was getting benched for Andy Dalton. He spent time running the scout team, and there were plenty of people wondering if Carolina had completely blown the No. 1 pick.
Now we're talking about him as one of the best quarterbacks in football.
My first thought when I saw the PFF list was whether we're getting a little carried away. Young just threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns against Detroit, the Panthers got a huge win, and everybody is feeling pretty good about where this thing is going.
Apparently, PFF isn't looking at it as just one big night, either. In its latest quarterback rankings, PFF called Young's game against Detroit a “scintillating outing” that capped what it described as an outstanding four-game start.
So I went back and looked at what he's actually done, and I don't know. PFF might have a point.
Young has thrown for 1,268 yards and nine touchdowns. He's second among qualified quarterbacks in passing yards and third in touchdown passes, so it's not like one huge game is making his numbers look better than they really are.
Young also has an 88.6 overall PFF grade , which ranks second among 33 qualified quarterbacks. PFF has also credited him with eight big-time throws and only one turnover-worthy play.
That's probably the number I keep coming back to. We've seen Young make some throws this season that I don't think he was making consistently before, but he also hasn't been putting the ball in danger very often.
Now, I'm not forgetting Cleveland. That interception at the end was unfortunate, and it helped kill Carolina's chance to win. I'm not going to pretend it didn't happen just because everything around Young feels good right now.
But I'm also not going to let one throw while his arm is being hit erase everything else he's done.
Young threw for 361 yards and three touchdowns against Chicago. Then it was 287 yards and three touchdowns against Atlanta, 291 against Cleveland, and 329 against Detroit.
That's at least 287 passing yards in every game.
Four games aren't enough for me to say Young is going to be an All-Pro when the season ends. There's way too much football left, and we've already seen how quickly things can change with this team.
I just don't know how much more we can ask from him right now.
That's probably where I've changed the most on Young. Earlier this season, I kept wanting to see the next game before I bought into what was happening. He'd play well, and I'd immediately start wondering whether he could do it again.
Well, he's done it again. And then he did it again after that.
Maybe it doesn't last. Maybe we get to November, and this PFF All-Pro team looks completely different. That's the risk of doing something like this after only four games.
The question is whether Young has played like an All-Pro quarterback so far, and after looking at the numbers, I don't think PFF's choice is nearly as crazy as I thought it was when I first saw it.
Two years ago, we were wondering if Carolina had drafted the wrong quarterback. A few weeks ago, we were wondering whether Young was finally breaking out.
Now we're debating whether he's an All-Pro.
I definitely didn't have that one on my Panthers bingo card.
