title: Snaps, Studs and Duds From Packers’ Statement Win Over Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Chicago Bears’ team song is “Bear Down, Chicago Bears.” On Sunday, it was “Beat Down, the Chicago Bears.”
The Green Bay Packers delivered an emphatic wire-to-wire victory over their rivals. It was total domination and no asterisks were required .
Here’s our weekly look at the snaps along with six studs and two duds.
The Packers played 61 snaps on offense.
Quarterbacks: Jordan Love played the first 59 snaps before Tyrod Taylor took a knee to run out the clock. Love had played every snap this season. After two games of quality pass protection, he will be feeling good headed into Sunday night’s game against the Cowboys.
Love was 25-of-31 (80.6 percent) for 367 yards and two touchdowns, good for a career-high 137.5 passer rating. It was only the second occasion in franchise history of at least 350 passing yards, an 80 percent completion rate and two touchdowns in a game (Aaron Rodgers vs. Washington in 2019).
AIR JORDAN ✈️ Jordan Love joins Ben Roethlisberger as the only players with 5 completions of 30+ air yards in a single game since ESPN began tracking the stat in 2006. pic.twitter.com/x9rY4KOKNu
Running backs: After last week’s game against Tampa Bay, coach Matt LaFleur said the best teacher is the bench for running backs with a fumbling problem. So, with two fumbles to start the season, Kaleb Johnson found himself on the bench until the game was in hand.
MarShawn Lloyd led the unit with 27 snaps. Pierre Strong, making his Packers debut after spending all of last season and the start of this season on the practice squad, played 25 snaps. Johnson got nine snaps at the end.
Lloyd led the way with 10 rushes for 31 yards and two touchdowns. The Packers need more of his first touchdown run, when he ran over Jaylon Johnson to gain the final 2 yards, because he’s too often taken down sideways and doesn’t fall forward for an extra yard or two.
Receivers: The Packers are running out of receivers. Skyy Moore, who had replaced injured Jayden Reed in the slot, dropped out after 11 snaps with an ankle injury.
As always, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden led the way. Watson played 49 snaps and Golden played 47 (with three more as the punt returner). Bo Melton became the next man up to Moore, who had been the next man up, with 30 snaps. J. Michael Sturdivant played only eight.
Among all receivers who were targeted at least four times this week, Watson was first with 4.77 yards per route and Golden was second with 4.56.
Melton played 16 on special teams and Sturdivant played 11.
Tight ends: Tucker Kraft played 47 snaps, with his 77 percent playing time a bit less than usual due to the score. Mark Redman, who has been invaluable as a blocker, played 21 snaps. Jonnu Smith also played 21 and Josh Whyle got 11.
The only statistical contribution was Kraft’s five catches for 64 yards.
Offensive line: The No. 1 line of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Laken Tomlinson, center Sean Rhyan, right guard Travis Glover and right tackle Anthony Belton went the distance. With Glover making his second consecutive start, Kevin Zeitler’s Packers debut was limited to six snaps on special teams.
According to PFF, Belton and Rhyan pitched shutouts in pass protection. Tomlinson allowed only one pressure. Glover wasn’t as good against Chicago as he was against Tampa Bay, but he’s still been an upgrade over Jacob Monk.
The Packers played 69 snaps on defense.
Defensive tackles: It was a vintage Jonathan Gannon rotation. Karl Brooks, who had one of the team’s eight tackles for losses, led the unit with 39 snaps, followed by Devonte Wyatt with 32, Javon Hargrave and Chris McClellan with 31 each, and Jonathan Ford getting 17.
Now what, though? Hargrave suffered a torn Achilles late in the game. Coach Matt LaFleur was crushed.
“That kind of takes the air out of the room a little bit, when you lose not only a great player but a great guy, a key piece to this team, and it kind of puts a little bit of a cloud on the day,” LaFleur said.
With Warren Brinson on injured reserve, it will be Anthony Campbell’s time after he missed the last three games with an ankle injury sustained in his NFL debut against the Jets.
Wyatt had his first two sacks of the season. The first was a cheap one, with Tyson Bagent slipping and falling. The second was a sack-fumble that was the cherry on top of the victory sundae.
Edges: It was a balanced snap count here, too. Lukas Van Ness played 40 snaps. After that, it was Brenton Cox with 35, Dani Dennis-Sutton with 32 and starter Barryn Sorrell with 31. The tenor of the game meant more snaps for Cox, who is one of the team’s better pass rushers. (More on that in a moment.) Sorrell, meanwhile, played 16 snaps on special teams, so that probably impacted his workload on defense.
Dennis-Sutton might wind up moving ahead of Sorrell on the depth chart at some point. While he’s routinely lost on bootlegs, you can’t deny his big-play production. He had one sack along with a tackle for loss when he read and destroyed a receiver screen.
Linebackers: How would the Packers replace premier starter Edgerrin Cooper? Zaire Franklin played the first 64 snaps before he was removed at the 2-minute warning. Ty’Ron Hopper played 39 snaps and Isaiah McDuffie played 34.
The rotation was the way to go because both players are key cogs on special teams. Hopper played 14 snaps on special teams, giving him a total of 53, and McDuffie played 16 snaps on special teams, giving him a total of 50.
Franklin had nine tackles, one tackle for loss and one forced fumble, McDuffie had five tackles and Hopper had an interception.
Nick Niemann and Kristian Welch didn’t play on defense but got 18 and 16 snaps, respectively, on special teams. Niemann had two solo tackles.
Cornerbacks: Brandon Cisse was one of two defensive players to play every snap. Keisean Nixon played 61; he sat out the eight-play final series. Carrington Valentine played nine snaps as the next corner and Kamal Hadden got seven snaps in the slot to end the game.
Benjamin St-Juste was limited to six snaps on special teams as he continues to be plagued by hamstring issues.
The corners were excellent given the limited challenge brought by the Bears. Cisse allowed only one catch and had one sack.
Safeties: Evan Williams was the other defensive player to play every snap. Xavier McKinney played 61, getting to watch the final eight from the bench as Kitan Oladapo took his place.
Williams continued his hot start to the season with 11 tackles and McKinney’s two interceptions gave him three for the season. It was the team’s first two-interception game since Rudy Ford in 2022.
QB Jordan Love: Is there a better deep-ball thrower than Love? It wasn’t as if his receivers had to make a bunch of circus catches. For the most part, the balls couldn’t have been placed any better had Love hit pause, run down the field, and put them directly into the receivers’ hands.
On passes of 20-plus air yards, Love was 6-of-8 for 258 yards and two touchdowns. He had as many deep completions as total incompletions in a ridiculous performance.
WRs Christian Watson and Matthew Golden: The numbers are absurd, with Watson and Golden combining for 12 receptions for 266 yards. It’s not as if the Bears have a bunch of stiffs at cornerback. Jaylon Johnson is a two-time Pro Bowler and Tyrique Stevenson is one of the best young corners in the game. Stevenson missed half the game with a hamstring injury, but the Bears are high on rookie Malik Muhammad, who was torched.
Ultimately, it didn’t matter. Watson and Golden are on pace to finish the season with about 3,000 receiving yards.
Edge Brenton Cox: Cox had only three tackles with zero sacks, quarterback hits or tackles for losses, but PFF credited him with six pressures. Really, he was the only player providing something resembling consistent pressure.
S Xavier McKinney and Javon Bullard: Bullard took a big Year 2 jump and has continued his rise. His deflected pass resulted in the first of McKinney’s two…

title: Packers Report Card: Three A’s But Two D’s From Beatdown of Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The grades are in for the Green Bay Packers after they played their best game of the season in a 31-7 victory over the Chicago Bears.
Yes, they played against two backup quarterbacks and a backup running back, and they were at home. Those are some pretty decided advantages.
A big day from Jordan Love and his top two receivers combined with some suffocating pass defense led to a rout at Lambeau Field that had to feel extra sweet for an organizatio n that had been on the bad side of the rivalry for the first time in more than 30 years.
The grades, as you might imagine, reflect the dominance that took place at Lambeau Field.
Christian Watson said earlier in the week there were holes in the defense that Green Bay’s offense could exploit. Matthew Golden chuckled while referencing that quote after the game .
As it turns out, Watson was right. Jordan Love sliced and diced against a hapless Chicago secondary that, save for a brief sabbatical in the second quarter, did not have any answers from Love’s aerial assault on their defense.
Love threw for 367 yards, including two long touchdown passes to Watson. His reworked offensive line kept him clean for most of the game, as Love was only sacked twice, both of which came on the same possession at the end of the first half.
Apart from that, it was Love throwing bombs all over the field to Watson, Golden and Tucker Kraft, who combined for 330 yards. Watson and Golden became the first Packers tandem to top 120 yards in a game in a decade.
“It’s flow state – feels like you’re flowing out there – just play after play we’re making those. It felt good to be able to do that at home,” Love said.
Love joined former Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger as the only players with five completions of 30 or more air yards in a single game since ESPN began tracking that stat in 2006.
“That’s just one of them feelings,” Watson said after the game. “That was a great display we had out there today. Big time game from the whole team. Honestly, I was excited for each and every person who was out there making plays. That was a big-time win.”
Kraft had his best game of the season with five catches for 64 yards, including a 46-yard completion in the third quarter that helped set up a field goal from Trey Smack.
If you only watch the highlight tape, you’d think the Packers were able to move the ball on the ground for most of the game. MarShawn Lloyd found the end zone twice, including an angry run when he ran over Chicago cornerback Jaylon Johnson en route to the end zone to give the Packers a 14-0 lead.
Lloyd’s second touchdown was the nail in the coffin that gave the Packers a 31-7 lead. Kaleb Johnson, who was kept on the bench until late in the game, popped an explosive run of 23 yards.
Despite the big plays, there was not much room for Green Bay’s putrid ground game, which remains anemic at this point in the season. Pierre Strong had five carries for 7 yards. Lloyd had 31 yards on 10 carries. Overall, the Packers ran for 70 yards with a 2.7-yard average.
They desperately need one of their running backs to find a way to give them some punch in the run game. Maybe Lloyd can use his touchdown runs as a potential springboard next week against a Dallas defense that is one of the worst in the league.
The Year 2024 returned and Xavier McKinney is back in the saddle. On a day when the Packers should have had some opportunities to make some plays on the ball facing mistake-prone backup quarterback Tyson Bagent, McKinney obliged.
His two interceptions helped him surpass his total from last season, as he now has three this season. He was not alone. Ty’Ron Hopper picked off Case Keenum at the goal line. Evan Williams and Dani Dennis-Sutton recovered fumbles.
As noted by Packers.com’s Wes Hodkiewicz, the Packers have equaled their interception total of seven in 2025 in just five games.
“I feel good,” McKinney said. “I try to stack the weeks, stack the days. Even when the result is not what I want it to be every time, but still keeping my same process. So, my main focus is just making sure that I’m the best version of me every day and guys around me get the best version of me every day, regardless of what the result may be. But as long as I keep my process the same, I know the results will come.”
The tests are going to get stiffer in the coming weeks. Dak Prescott is one of the league’s best and he’s coming to town next week. He’ll be followed by Detroit’s Jared Goff, Carolina’s rising Bryce Young and New England’s Drake Maye. There are a bunch of elite receivers on the agenda, too.
On this Sunday, however, the Packers were dominant. Bagent and Keenum were erratic. They combined for just more than 200 passing yards. Combine that with four sacks and three picks? It’s almost a perfect day against subpar quarterback play.
The biggest storyline of the game was how the Packers were going to stop the Chicago ground game that entered play this week as the best rushing attack in the NFL.
Some of the punch of Chicago’s run game was removed when Kyle Monangai was ruled out with a toe injury on Friday. D’Andre Swift, who topped 1,000 yards last year, was still active, but the dropoff from him to Roschon Johnson was significant.
With the Packers taking an early 14-0 lead, however, Chicago’s run game was held in check. Swift had just nine carries for 43 yards and a touchdown. The rest of Chicago’s run game was kept under wraps, with Tyson Bagent being the Bears’ second-leading rusher with 17 yards on three carries. Six horizontal runs to receivers gained 11 yards.
The assignment will be more difficult on Christmas when the Packers will likely face Monangai and Caleb Williams.
Sunday, however, the goal was to make Bagent beat them. The Packers were successful.
Chicago had 81 rushing yards on 24 carries, a 3.4-yard average. The Packers would take that every day and twice on Sundays.
Matthew Golden looked explosive on a 17-yard punt return that helped set up the Packers’ offense for the second of two failed two-minute drills at the end of the first half. Outside of that, it was a pretty rough day at the office for Cam Achord’s group.
The kickoff-coverage team had some nice moments, with Kamal Hadden running through Chicago’s returners, but it also allowed an explosive return immediately after taking a 31-7 lead. That ultimately did not end up mattering because Chicago’s offense was as bad as it was, but that will matter next week against Cowboys returner Kavontae Turpin and prolific quarterback Dak Prescott.
Trey Smack had his first rookie moments as a kicker. He missed an extra-point attempt early, and followed it up with two missed field goals in the fourth quarter. Again, it didn’t matter because the Packers led by 24 points, but it will matter when they start facing real quarterbacks next week.
Smack has been good for most of the year, so next week against Dallas will be a chance for him to bounce back. Sunday? It was one of the few black eyes on an otherwise spectacular day for the home team.
Daniel Whelan outdid himself with a 75-yard punt that was ruled a touchback. Hadden was in on three tackles.
The first half likely embodies what the 2026 Packers are, but also what Matt LaFleur is at this point as a head coach.
There are flashes of brilliance. LaFleur was able to scheme up 14 quick points on offense to start the game. Everything he called worked.
Then the second quarter hit, and nothing worked. The Packers’ final three possessions of the half lasted nine plays and resulted in zero points.
Furthermore, LaFleur kept two timeouts in his pocket after a first-down sack and fumble was recovered by Jordan Love with the Packers threatening to get into field-goal range. As a result, the Packers were penalized for an illegal substitution. Love was sacked on the next play, and a drive that should have ended in at least a field-goal attempt ended with the Packers getting booed off the field while having a lead.
When the second half began,…

title: ‘Eat Their Words’: Packers Make Statement In Blowout of ‘Little Bro’ Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers tried. They tried to play things off as Sunday’s game against the Chicago Bears being just another game, but one quote from Javon Bullard after the game was over said it all.
“They’re still little bro, man,” Bullard said. “They’re still little bro. Sometimes big bro got a show up and that’s what we did.”
Bullard had the most noteworthy comments of the week when he stated what was a simple goal. He didn’t care what time the game was played, but he had one thought in mind. Bullard said their goal was to kick Chicago’s butt.
“Yeah, kick their ass. For sure,” Bullard said after Sunday’s game.
“I mean, what was the score 31-7? S***, you tell me.”
Matt LaFleur tried to deflect the discussion surrounding his interactions with Ben Johnson from a season ago, which included the Chicago coach loudly yelling “F**k the Packers” in a postgame video that was posted on the Bears’ X account. He continued to toe that line after the game was over.
“Here’s what I’ll tell you: I think we all are moving in the same direction, and we all got each other’s backs. Players-coaches, coaches-players, players-players – and that’s what great teams do,” LaFleur said. “That is the essence of ‘team,’ is that you have each other’s backs, that you’re willing to stick together, not point fingers in times of adversity, and just keep moving forward, and really try to be reflective of.”
LaFleur deflected to the players, and the players’ message was loud and clear.
Bullard smirked. Evan Williams smiled. Tucker Kraft tried to choose his words carefully. Ditto for Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. They knew what had been said since last season ended.
“We definitely heard some of the things they were saying,” safety Evan Williams said. “That might of fed into a little extra energy on the field, but it’s a rivalry that’s expected. I’m just glad we were able to handle ourselves like we did.”
The words and body language of all of those players said a lot, while still leaving some to the imagination of those listening.
Zaire Franklin did not leave anything to the imagination. Earlier in the week, Chicago receiver Luther Burden noted that the Bears were up, the Packers were down and that they had a golden opportunity in front of him.
Chicago’s goal was to make the Packers “quit,” Burden said, while putting them down at 2-3 as the Bears improved to 4-1.
Franklin took exception to that comment along with a lot of the others that were made throughout the offseason in the aftermath of Chicago ending Green Bay’s season.
“Man, I feel like since I been here, it's just been a bunch of them saying a whole bunch of stuff about us,” Franklin said before taking aim at Burden’s comments specifically.
“Them making a whole bunch of comments about us, doing a whole bunch of stuff about us and only thing we've been doing is focusing on being the best version of ourselves. And that's the message that Coach LaFleur been preaching, just being the best versions of ourselves. It's not about them. It's about us. And we see all the little weird stuff they be doing in the media and all the different stuff they be saying.
“You got guys that never really made a real play in this league talking about making somebody quit. That's weird. We don't do that. He quit today, by the way. He ain't want to play anymore. But we focused on ourselves, man. We ain't really worried about that. We ain't play that in a team meeting or nothing. We just focused on ourselves, being the best version of ourselves and we put out a good performance today because of that.”
Burden finished the game with 49 yards on eight touches.
LaFleur’s words may not have thrown expletives in the direction of Ben Johnson’s team, but his demeanor certainly did.
One of the criticisms of LaFleur is his propensity to take his foot off the gas and try to start running the clock once his team has a lead. He wants to lean on his run game in those moments.
Sunday? That went out the window. LaFleur dialed up two play-action bombs with the team leading 31-7 attempting to go for the throat on every possession.
LaFleur can laugh it off saying that last year’s game was a teacher in a game is never truly over. He can point to the lack of effectiveness from his ground game as a reason to keep throwing the ball down the field.
We’re not buying any of it. LaFleur is smart. He knows the history of this rivalry. The Packers were 52-18 against the Bears in their last 70 games, including the postseason.
LaFleur also knows that he does not want to be the coach who allowed the rivalry to swing back in the favor of Chicago.
Of course he took things personally.
Of course his team took things personally with the way last season ended.
Of course they took things personally that they were an underdog at Lambeau Field against their oldest rivals, while facing a backup quarterback.
“That’s disrespectful,” Bullard said. “We came here to do what we were supposed to do. That’s disrespectful when a team come in here and we underdogs in our own stadium and we’re underdogs with a backup quarterback. No disrespect to any of those quarterbacks. Those guys have standing in this league. They play great in this league before, but we take that personal and I think was just a testament to how we felt about it.”
That’s what great athletes do. Every perceived slight is taken personally. Chicago’s comments over the last nine months leave nothing to the imagination. Even if the Packers want to take the high road playing the role of the big brother, which the Packers have done for the better part of 30 years.
Kraft said during the week that his goal was to talk with his pads, a line that was reiterated for most of the week by those around him.
What did the pads say on Sunday?
A final score of 31-7 as the team he helps captain punched the bully back who dragged them through the mud for the last nine months. No matter what they said during the week, it felt good for them to get back on the winning side of the rivalry.
“Extra good, sure. It definitely feels gratifying to understand of course what we went through last year,” Williams said. “All the hoopla of what this game is going to be and what it means as a whole I feel like our culture is just tuning that out and having a one play mentality but, yes, it does feel a little gratifying to make them eat their words.”

title: Bombs Away: Packers’ Christian Watson, Matthew Golden Explode vs. Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – All of the machinations at receiver for the Green Bay Packers this year, from the trade of Dontayvion Wicks and the departure of Romeo Doubs to the contract extension for Christian Watson, led to this moment in a big game.
In a rivalry showdown against the Chicago Bears with so much at stake, Watson caught six passes for 143 yards and two touchdowns and Matthew Golden caught six passes for 123 yards. With those two and Tucker Kraft combining for 330 receiving yards, the Packers rolled to a 31-7 victory.
It marked only the 10th time in Packers history in which two players had at least 120 receiving yards and the first time since Davante Adams and Jordy Nelson against the Titans in 2016.
The barrage of bombs started on the opening drive when Jordan Love threw a 42-yard touchdown pass to Watson. It was a busted coverage, with the corner turning Watson loose and Watson blowing past the safety for an easy pitch-and-catch score.
“Just saw that no one ran with me right away and then I saw the safety playing over the top, so I said I’m going to get as much width as I can from the safety and just hope he puts it out there and, obviously, he did,” Watson said.
The Packers led 14-7 at halftime but the Bears had the momentum.
On the first play of the second half, which oddly was delayed because the balls had to be run back onto the field, Love faked a pitch to MarShawn Lloyd and fired a bullet over the middle to Watson for 31.
Then came the biggest sequence of the game. On third-and-12, J. Michael Sturdivant got one step on Pro Bowl cornerback Jaylon Johnson and made a tumbling 43-yard touchdown catch. The play was nullified, though, by a dubious interference penalty on Sturdivant. So, on third-and-22, Love found some open space to launch one deep to Watson, who made a leaping catch against rookie safety Dillon Thieneman for a 53-yard touchdown.
“I saw the safety was running back to it, so I knew someone’s got to get there first,” Watson said.
He did, making a spectacular catch just behind Thieneman’s helmet.
“I was joking around with some of the guys after, that’s just one of those ones that you watch it back on tape, and you’re like, ah the DB should’ve broken it up or it should’ve been incomplete,” Watson said. “Sometimes, you just find a way. I was just tracking the ball. I wasn’t thinking too much. Just go get it and came down with it.”
Love chalked it up to a great player making a great play, and it put the Packers in front 20-7.
“That’s what it’s all about right there,” Love said. “I said, ‘Ball don’t lie.’”
Next, it was Kraft’s turn. Love booted left and threw the ball deep to the right to Kraft, who was open instantly when he made his cut toward the pylon. That 46-yard play set up a field goal to make it 23-7.
“We let the ball over our head too many times – four passes over 40 yards or more,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said. “Credit to Green Bay, they came out, we knew we were going to get their best shot and we sure did.”
On the second-to-last play of the third quarter, it was Love to Golden up the right sideline for 36. That set up what essentially was the clinching touchdown run by MarShawn Lloyd to start the fourth quarter.
Finally, on the first play of the ensuing possession, Love went deep to Golden for 50 more.
“I think it’s something that we saw throughout the game that was working and we kept doing it,” Love said. “We kept our foot on the gas right there. I think really just guys were making plays. It was going to make some contested plays and nobody was just wide open, but I think guys were making some great catches out there, great plays.
“But I love it. We kept our foot on the gas, Matt was dialing it up and that’s what it needs to look like.”
It was all gas – and all bombs – and no brake.
“I would say we probably should've went and scored again. Honestly,” Golden said. “It's a statement game. But I feel like we played really good and it was an important game for us. It was a division game and we know we needed to come out with the win.”
With the Sunday night and Monday night games to be played, Watson is fourth in the NFL with 472 receiving yards and Golden is sixth with 397 yards. Watson is fifth with 18.2 yards per catch and Golden is 10th with a 16.5-yard average. Only Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba has more receiving touchdowns than Watson, who has six.
Watson is on pace for a preposterous 1,605 yards and 20 touchdowns. Golden is on pace for 1,350 yards, giving them a combined total approaching 3,000 yards.
The Packers had finished the day with six completions of 30-plus yards – as many big plays as Love had incompletions. They had five such plays against the Vikings in Week 1 but a total of three the past three games.
The Packers have a two-man receiver corps. Jayden Reed is on injured reserve and his replacement, Skyy Moore, dropped out early against Chicago. Watson and Golden carried the load, combining for 266 yards – or 72.5 percent of the team total.
For the season, they have 871 yards. That’s 61.9 percent of Love’s total.
“I think the day they had today kind of just speaks,” Love said. “I think we talked about it a little bit last week, how good the offense can be. It just shows right there. Those are two guys that are dominant factors.
“We get flowing like this and they’re making plays and we’re able to take advantage of what the defense is doing, both those guys, they’re capable of doing great things. I think that’s just a little bit of show what’s possible. It just comes down to executing. We talk about it every week. You got to go out there and make plays, and they made those plays for us today. We’ve just got to keep on building on it.”

title: Were These the Real Packers? 3 Reasons To Be Truly Excited After Rout of Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers played four lackluster games to start the season and were fortunate to have a 2-2 record entering their rivalry showdown against the Chicago Bears.
All the missed assignments, boneheaded penalties, careless ball-handling and other assorted self-inflicted wounds disappeared on Sunday. The Packers crushed the Bears 31-7. It’d be almost impossible to overstate the importance of the game.
Just like that, the Packers are 3-2. While they’re two games behind the undefeated Vikings in the NFC North, they might emerge from Week 5 within the group of seven teams leading the race for a playoff spot in the NFC.
It’s rather startling, really. For all the horrendous football they played to start the season, the Packers are 3-2 and in a good spot.
Coach Matt LaFleur, for his part, wasn’t about to take a victory lap. There’d be no pounding on his chest, no “F*** the Bears” comments, no middle fingers directed to the doubters. Instead, the search for growth – the same message as the past four weeks, and one that obviously resonated – was the theme after the game.
“That’s what you have in mind all the time,” he said. “But it’s easier said than done. I was a little disappointed with parts of the game, if I’m being truthful. At the end of the half, obviously, and then we’ve got to establish a better run attack.
“There were moments where we ripped off some big runs, but it’s just got to be I would say a little bit more consistent to help us stay in conflicting situations where you don’t know if it’s going to be a run or a pass. It’s harder when you’re sitting there in second-and-9, second-and-10, second-and-11 when everybody in the stadium is probably thinking pass.”
Can the Packers keep it going? Or will this be a fart-in-the-wind performance, to borrow a line from Ron Wolf, and nothing more than a fired-up team beating up on a backup quarterback?
Here are three reasons to believe in these Packers.
The Packers really struggled offensively the first three games, and a big reason why was the mismanagement of the offensive line. However, general manager Brian Gutekunst deserves credit for pivoting to veteran Laken Tomlinson at left guard and offensive line coach Luke Butkus deserves credit for suggesting Travis Glover take over at right guard.
Nobody is going to mistake this Packers offensive line with the 2014 juggernaut that powered the Packers to the cusp of the Super Bowl. But Tomlinson has been an excellent replacement for injured Aaron Banks and Glover has solidified the void at right guard.
Given plenty of time for most of the game, Love was 25-of-31 for yards and two touchdowns. He had as many completions of longer than 30 yards as he threw incompletions. It helps to have time, obviously; he was sacked twice – both at the end of the first half.
“It’s something we’ve talked about throughout the course of the season so far, and I thought they did a great job,” Love said. “They gave me a lot of time on a lot of those plays. Especially the one to Christian [on their 53-yard touchdown pass on third-and-forever in the third quarter], I had all day back there.
“They did a great job. I thought our run game has been improving. We’ve got some big runs going and we’re playing complementary ball right there. That’s what it needs to look like. We got to keep stacking stuff, but I thought O-line did a great job in pass pro.”
At some point, Kevin Zeitler will take over at right guard, but LaFleur said Glover had earned the right to start again.
“I think it's been immense – an immense improvement in terms of it allows us to call our offense, and it's a hell of a lot easier calling plays when the guys are blocking for the quarterback up front,” LaFleur said.
If the line continues growing, which should be the case as Jordan Morgan and Anthony Belton grow into their roles as the starting tackles, this line will be plenty good enough to help the team win games.
Obviously, five takeaways isn’t something that can be replicated on a weekly basis. And, just as obviously, it helps that the Packers were playing against Tyson Bagent instead of Caleb Williams. And, also obviously, the Packers will face better receiver tandems the next two weeks than they did on Sunday against Rome Odunze and Luther Burden.
Still, this was complete dominance. The Bears were limited to 246 yards, 3.6 yards per play and 4-of-14 on third down. They were limited to three plays of 15-plus yards; two of those came in the fourth quarter, with the outcome determined.
“There’s no asterisks,” linebacker Zaire Franklin said.
While Chicago’s offense was depleted without Williams and running back Kyle Monangai, the Bears still had their powerhouse line, starting receivers, starting tight ends and 1,000-yard rusher D’Andre Swift.
“It’s very important,” said safety Xavier McKinney, who had two interceptions. “It gives guys confidence. It reassures guys in the locker room of who we say that we are and who we preach about who we are every day.
“I think it gives us confidence and I think it helps us up the level of urgency because we understand what the standard is. This is our standard. This is what we should do every week. We have the talent to do it. We have the coaches to do it. We have the building to do it. We just have to go out there and make sure we do it. We can’t just talk about it. We have to be about it. Today, we were about it and we have to continue that.”
The task will grow tougher next week against Dallas quarterback Dak Prescott and his premier receivers on Sunday night. The following week will bring a trip to Detroit and a matchup against Jared Goff, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams.
“Finish” has been the team’s mantra ever since it failed to finish at Chicago in Week 16 and again in the playoff rematch.
Against the Bears, it was 14-7 at halftime and a runaway in the second half.
“It’s always finish,” Love said. “The mindset for us, no matter what it is, we went into halftime, it was finish. We got a lead, we got to take control of that lead, we got to keep putting up points as an offense, defense keep flying around, keep getting us the ball back. It’s all about finishing.”
So, with the Packers up 23-7 late in the third quarter, Love went deep to Matthew Golden. The long completion set up MarShawn Lloyd’s touchdown run to start the fourth quarter.
With the Packers up 31-7 early in the fourth quarter, Love went deep again to Golden for a gain of 50. They didn’t turn that possession into points, but it had nothing to do with LaFleur taking the air out of the ball to run out the clock.
“We kept our foot on the gas,” Love said.
And because they did, the Packers didn’t just earn a measure of revenge for last year’s losses to Chicago. They made a statement that the version of the team that showed up on Sunday is good enough to compete with anyone.
“That we can be as good as we want to be,” receiver Christian Watson said. “We’ve just got to go out, execute, have faith in each other and just play some complementary football.”
LaFleur knows it’s just one game, really no different than the blowout loss to Atlanta a couple weeks earlier was just one game.
Now that the Packers have proven they can play a complete game, they have to prove they can do it again. And again. And again.
“It’s important to win every week,” LaFleur said. “It’s a week-to-week league, and we know that. Certainly, I think it’s more for the fan base and everything. I love the excitement around the rivalry and all that. It weighs in the back of your mind how last season ended a little bit, but it’s still about us and what we do moving forward and how we come in and how we prepare and the product we put out on the field.”
The win – and the dominance of it – proves that the team has been on the right track and hard work could dig it out of its early hole.

title: Packers Punch Back: Winners and Losers from Dominant Win Over Rival Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers needed a win against the Chicago Bears. It’s rare that the Packers have been the team in desperation in this rivalry for the last 30 years, but that was the reality following a sluggish and mistake-plagued start to the season.
The Bears entered play at 3-1 and winners of the last two games against the Packers. They spent plenty of times rubbing their nose in last year’s playoff loss, and mentioned a desire to make the Packers quit.
The Packers, conversely, were the team trying to punch the bully back. They were 2-2, facing a backup quarterback.
They could not afford another loss in the rivalry. They could not afford another loss on the season as they were beginning a stretch of four games against four potential NFC playoff contenders.
Perhaps there were some demons to be exorcised along the way, as well. The Packers’ two losses against Chicago last year included them holding second-half leads that felt insurmountable against a lifeless Bears’ offense.
After a hot start, the Packers led 14-7 at halftime. It felt tenuous, given the recent history between the teams, but they blew them out in the second half for a 31-7 win.
Here are our weekly winners and losers from Green Bay’s dominant win over the Bears.
Jordan Love entered the fourth quarter with more than 300 yards passing. He was spectacular at the beginning of the game, and only was not brilliant after the offense fell out of rhythm due to a subpar run game.
Both of Love’s predecessors owned the Chicago Bears. There is little doubt that Love wanted to silence some critics after Chicago had won two in a row in the rivalry.
Love was a sharp shooter throughout the game. He finished the day with 367 yards passing, two touchdowns and zero turnovers.
The Packers had a dramatic advantage at quarterback coming into the game. They needed Love to play to that advantage.
Death, taxes, and Christian Watson scoring touchdowns against Chicago at Lambeau Field?
That’s not quite accurate, but Watson did have two touchdowns last season against the Bears, and was the best player on offense for a vast majority of the game. Sunday’s scoring started on the back of Watson, who broke open for a 42-yard touchdown on a beautiful pass from Jordan Love.
Watson was not done there. After an offensive pass interference wiped out a touchdown pass from Jordan Love to J. Michael Sturdivant, Watson made a spectacular catch on third-and-22 for a 53-yard touchdown to give the Packers a 20-7 lead after Trey Smack missed the ensuing PAT.
Say it with us now... LET'S GO!!! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/zLLSOq0xW5
Watson has a knack for making big plays, as he’s scored five touchdowns in four games against the Bears dating back to last season.
He finished the day with six catches, 143 yards, and two scores.
His running mate, Matthew Golden did not find the end zone, but he found plenty of real estate in Chicago’s secondary.
He caught six balls for 123 yards, and was a consistent target for Jordan Love.
Due to the injuries to Jayden Reed and Skyy Moore, the Packers do not have a lot of proven pass catchers on their roster, especially at receiver. Golden and Watson have a heavy burden to carry. They certainly did on Sunday, and should have more opportunities next week against the Dallas Cowboys.
When you’re facing a backup quarterback, your defense has to make plays. The Packers wanted to make Tyson Bagent beat them, as a clear effort to slow down their ground game was given in the first quarter of Sunday’s game.
After Watson’s touchdown to open the game, Bagent loaded up on two pass plays on the ensuing possession.
One was dropped by Cole Kmet. The second was dropped by Javon Bullard, but picked off by Xavier McKinney on a diving interception that put the Packers in business for what ended up being their second touchdown of the game.
McKinney’s pick was his second of the season, which equaled his total from a season ago.
He wasn’t done. McKinney picked off Tyson Bagent late in the third quarter to give the Packers a chance to throw the dagger early in the fourth quarter.
Javon Bullard did not mince words earlier in the week when he mentioned the team’s stated goal.
“We’re trying to kick their a**,” Bullard said.
Bullard did his part to attempt to do exactly what he said. Tyson Bagent stared down his intended target on the second play after Christian Watson’s touchdown opened the scoring. Bagent threw the ball directly into the hands of Bullard, who is still looking for the first interception of his career.
Instead, he had to settle for a tipped pass that ended up in the arms of Xavier McKinney.
Bullard entered Sunday’s game with one of the toughest assignments. He’s a slot defender who had to defend Chicago’s powerful run game. His potential matchups in the passing game included Luther Burden III, Colston Loveland, and Cole Kmet.
Perhaps it was a byproduct of bad quarterback play, but none of those players did much to impact Sunday’s game.
Bullard is one of the league’s best slot defenders, and proved it on Sunday.
Lloyd has been through a lot in his two-plus seasons as a pro football player. His first two seasons were riddled with injuries that knocked him out of essentially all of the regular season games.
His third season, he’s been healthy, but has not gotten off to the start that he was hoping for. Green Bay’s run game has been the worst in football by a significant margin through four weeks.
Lloyd was the lead man of that group, and the team desperately needed to find some semblance of a ground game to help their offense.
After Xavier McKinney’s interception gave the Packers the ball back almost immediately after Christian Watson’s touchdown to open the game, they moved into the red zone looking for a score to put a stranglehold on the game.
On the first play of the second quarter, Lloyd got the ball moving to the right side of the offense and had Jaylon Johnson in his sights. He lowered his shoulder, powered through Johnson and into the end zone for what was arguably the most impressive touchdown of the season.
The rest of the game was par for the course for the Packers so far this season. The run game went dormant after a solid start to the game, but Lloyd’s touchdown alone does give them a glimpse of the talent the Packers continue to insist will help their run game.
Matt LaFleur can say all he wants that this win did not feel different. He can say that the game is about the players.
His behavior says otherwise. With the Packers leading 31-7 in the fourth quarter after an interception by Ty’Ron Hopper, LaFleur dialed up a deep ball instead of trying to run the clock.
LaFleur has taken plenty of heat this season after the way last season ended. A large portion of that heat has come because of how the Packers lost to the Bears, and how much their coach, Ben Johnson, had to say after the fact.
LaFleur responded by doing what every Packers’ coach has done for the most part since Mike Holmgren took over in 1992.
He beat the Bears, and beat them badly.
Furthermore, that killer instinct late in the game is something that he can take to other games. We’ve long speculated this team is missing an edge that trickles down from their head coach.
Maybe getting his nose rubbed in the dirt gave him a reason to punch back and find something he didn’t have before?
That remains to be seen, but for one game at least, LaFleur found something.
Zaire Franklin had a rough series in the second quarter. The Bears were starting to gain some traction in their run game, and Franklin likely felt like he needed to put an end to that to make Chicago throw the ball to beat them.
Franklin read a run on a second down that was dead to rights if he made the tackle, which would have put the Bears in an obvious passing situation.
D’Andre Swift made him miss, and rumbled for a first down to keep the drive going.

title: Packers Punch Their Bullies In Statement Victory Over Rival Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers didn’t just beat the Chicago Bears. They demolished Ben Johnson’s team, punching the wannabe bullies in the face early and often during a 31-7 victory at Lambeau Field.
Spin it however you want. The Bears will spin it as losing without their star quarterback and powerhouse running back. The Packers will spin it as a statement win, a season-changing win and a rivalry-changing win.
Both sides probably have a point. The reality is the Packers, who were 2-2 this season and 2-7 in their last nine games, needed this win. They needed it for the standings. They needed it for their psyche after last year’s epic collapses in Chicago. And they needed it to remind their rivals that, while the Bears definitely don’t suck, the Packers’ demise has been greatly exaggerated.
The Bears (3-2), well, they’ll forever have bragging rights following last year’s wild-card game and they’ll get a chance to turn the tables on Christmas, presumably with Caleb Williams and Kyle Monangai on the field.
With Green Bay leading 23-7 late in the third quarter, Jordan Love hit Matthew Golden on a bomb between two defenders for a gain of 36. Then, with the seconds ticking away and the Bears appearing shellshocked, Love hit Golden for 15 more to the 6.
As the teams changed sides of the field for the fourth quarter, receivers Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant ran onto the field to exchange high-fives with Golden. The fans, who booed the Packers off the field two weeks earlier in a blowout loss to the Falcons, stood on their feet and roared. A thunderous “Go Pack Go” chant rang out through the famed stadium.
On the first play of the fourth quarter, MarShawn Lloyd bounced a run to his left and high-stepped his way into the end zone. Love hit Golden on the two-point play to make it 31-7.
Bears coach Ben Johnson had enough of Tyson Bagent, who had thrown two interceptions to Xavier McKinney. Case Keenum made it a third interception when, on fourth-and-goal at the 9, he was picked off by linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper before getting buried by Lukas Van Ness.
“Roll Out the Barrel” rang out as the crowd celebrated the blowout. Then, it was a “Go Brewers Go!” chant.
On the first play of the ensuing possession, Jordan Love went deep to Golden for a gain of 50.
It was the football equivalent of Johnson yelling “F*** the Packers” after last year’s playoff game.
“That was a huge win,” Love said. “Just for where we’re at in the season, starting off, that was definitely needed a much-needed win against an NFC North opponent. So, yeah, it was a huge win.”
Love had 300 passing yards through three quarters and finished 25-of-31 passing for 367 yards and two touchdowns, good for a 137.5 passer rating.
Christian Watson and Golden each blew past 100 receiving yards – six catches for 143 yards and two touchdowns for Watson and six catches for 123 yards for Golden. Throw Tucker Kraft into the mix, they combined for 330 yards.
“I love it,” Love said. “We kept our foot on the gas, Matt was dialing it up and that’s what it needs to look like.”
McKinney had two interceptions as the Packers, the king of the unforced error in the first four games, had zero turnovers and only four penalties through the first 57 minutes, when defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon cleared the bench. They were plus-five in turnovers.
Earlier in the week, safety Javon Bullard said he wanted to kick the Packers’ “ass.”
Was that mission accomplished?
“What was the score 31-7? Shit, you tell me,” he said.
For the second consecutive week, the Packers went with veteran Laken Tomlinson at left guard and young Travis Glover at right guard. And, for the second consecutive week, the Packers ran the ball a little – the production was sporadic but Lloyd had two touchdowns – and Love benefitted from cushy pockets. Other than a pair of sacks during a deflating end to the first half, the Bears barely got within an arm’s reach of Love.
About the only black eye was kicker Trey Smack missing two field goals and an extra point. That’s what Brandon McManus did in last year’s playoff game. Fortunately for the Packers, Smack’s misses were irrelevant.
Also, defensive tackle Javon Hargrave was carted off after the 2-minute warning. After the game, a subdued LaFleur said Hargrave sustained a torn Achilles.
The Packers, following the advice of Evan Williams, bolted to a 14-0 lead.
“Yeah, anytime it’s a division game, you kind of got to get your piss hot for the most part, understanding that these are going to have long-term effects on the standings for where we want to be at the end of the year,” Williams said this week.
“And also carrying over from last year, understanding we also have a bad taste in our mouth from what happened. You can understand a 12-round fight. It’s going to be a fistfight for sure.”
The Packers struck first on a 42-yard touchdown bomb to Watson. The worst third-down offense in the NFL beat the second-best third-down defense for a pair of conversions.
The Packers struck second on Xavier McKinney’s interception. Javon Bullard made a leaping deflection of a ball intended for Luther Burden, with McKinney grabbing his second pick of the year.
They struck third when Lloyd posterized Pro Bowl cornerback Jaylon Johnson by running him over near the goal line for a 6-yard touchdown. Pierre Strong converted fourth-and-1 behind Mark Redman’s lead block.
The Bears eventually stemmed the bleeding, then embarked on a 16-play, 9-minute touchdown drive to cut the margin to 14-7.
When the Packers butchered their end-of-half possession, the Bears took all the momentum into the locker room for intermission.
They didn’t keep it for long.
On the first play of the second half, Love faked a toss to Lloyd and hit Watson over the middle for 31. Moments later, on third-and-12, Love threw a touchdown bomb to J. Michael Sturdivant against Johnson. It looked like a potential breakout moment for the undrafted rookie. Instead, Sturdivant was flagged for pass interference – a horrendous call in which Johnson appeared to get the NBA-style “star” call.
So, on third-and-22, the Packers could have opted to pick up a chunk gain to give Trey Smack a shot at a 55- or 60-yard field goal. Instead, Love found some space to step into a bomb to Watson, who made an incredible catch for a 53-yard touchdown.
Watson caught the ball behind the back of the helmet of safety Dillon Thieneman, survived a collision and hit the turf with a baseball slide.
Smack, however, missed the extra point, so it was 20-7.
The battle of the missed kicks worked in Green Bay’s favor when Cairo Santos missed a 43-yard field goal on the ensuing possession. On third-and-8 before the kick, Dani Dennis-Sutton, who was sucked on a bootleg early in the drive, spotted a receiver screen and buried Kalif Raymond for a loss of 3.
The Packers tacked on a field goal with 1:58 left in the third quarter, a drive springboarded by Tucker Kraft’s 46-yard catch on the first play of the drive. It was a beautiful design, with Love booting left and hitting Kraft, who ran a post to the right.
With 77,755 fans in attendance for one of the hottest home games in franchise history, the day started with a moment of silence for former Bears player and coach and NFL legend Mike Ditka.

title: Packers First-Half Studs and Duds: Their Piss Was Hot Against Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers need to make a statement after two late-season collapses to the Chicago Bears last year and a lackluster start to this season.
The game could hardly have started any better, with Jordan Love throwing a 42-yard touchdown pass to Christian Watson and MarShawn Lloyd scoring on a thunderous touchdown run to give them a 14-0 lead barely 15 minutes into Sunday’s showdown at Lambeau Field.
With the Packers leading 14-7, here are some studs and duds from the first half at Lambeau Field.
First, for reference for the first few subheads, here’s what Evan Williams said this week:
“Yeah, anytime it’s a division game, you kind of got to get your piss hot for the most part, understanding that these are going to have long-term effects on the standings for where we want to be at the end of the year. And also carrying over from last year, understanding we also have a bad taste in our mouth from what happened. You can understand a 12-round fight. It’s going to be a fistfight for sure. We wouldn’t want anything else.”
The Packers’ piss was boiling at the start.
The Packers won the toss and deferred. The Bears picked up one first down before punting – Tyson Bagent tripped his way into Devonte Wyatt’s sack for a loss of 11. The defense tackled physically, starting with Kamal Hadden’s big hit on the kickoff return and open-field tackles by Williams, Xavier McKinney and Zaire Franklin.
Starting at their 9, the Packers ran a flea-flicker screen to start the game. Tight end Tucker Kraft “lost” the block to Montez Sweat, only to turn around and catch a screen for a catch-and-run gain of 13. Jordan Love converted a third-and-3 to Matthew Golden for one first down and Kraft took a “Tucky Sneak” for a first down on third-and-1.
On the next play, Love went deep to Christian Watson for a 42-yard touchdown. He was 5 yards beyond safety Xavier Woods.
Say it with us now... LET'S GO!!! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/zLLSOq0xW5
On the second play of the ensuing possession, Tyson Bagent went to Luther Burden downfield. Javon Bullard made a leaping deflection, with Xavier McKinney making a diving interception. His second interception of the season – matching his total from last year – gave the offense the ball on Chicago’s 45.
MarShawn Lloyd, finally, is off and running. He had a 10-yard run on the opening possession and scored his first career rushing touchdown on the second possession. On the first play of the second quarter, Anthony Belton had a good block at the point of attack, setting up a one-on-one confrontation between Lloyd vs. cornerback Jaylon Johnson. Lloyd put his head down and ran over the two-time Pro Bowl cornerback.
MarSHAWN LLOYD LAMBEAU LEAP 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/TVSKwKFBVW
The Bears finally got their offense going with a long drive that consumed most of the second quarter. On third-and-5, Tyson Bagent hit tight end Cole Kmet for a first down. Zaire Franklin missed the tackle, though it wouldn’t have prevented a first down.
One play, on second-and-10, D’Andre Swift dodged Franklin in the backfield, turning a lost-yardage play into a gain of 9. Then, on third-and-8, with Bagent running around like a chicken with its head cut off, Franklin was flagged for defensive holding to give the Bears a first-and-goal at the 8.
Swift scored on fourth-and-goal to cap a 16-play scoring drive. Isaiah McDuffie was blocked at the line of scrimmage.
Kamal Hadden had two physical hits in kickoff coverage and J. Michael Sturdivant made an excellent open-field tackle on a punt.
Then, late in the half after a feeble three-and-out by the offense, Daniel Whelan uncorked his best punt of the season, a field-flipping 69-yard bomb. Nick Niemann made the tackle and the Bears were flagged for holding, so they started at the 10. That’s a 65-yard change of field position.
With the Bears in position to seize all the momentum going into halftime, Brandon Cisse had a sack on second down and broke up a pass on third down. On second down, Lukas Van Ness raced around tight end Colston Loveland to force Tyson Bagent to step up in the pocket. Cisse was there for the sack. Then, on third-and-10, Bagent’s pass was high; Rome Odunze almost made a circus catch but Cisse knocked the ball loose.
CISSE 🔥 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/S3IKO0l0aE
The Packers got the ball at Chicago’s 49 with 39 seconds remaining, giving them a chance to double-up with a score to end the first half and get the ball to start the second half.
Instead, Jordan Morgan was beaten twice for sacks by nemesis Austin Booker.
Green Bay’s 109 wins against Chicago are the most for any team against any division opponent. The Giants are right on Green Bay’s heels with their 108 wins over Washington.
In Jordan Love’s first seven starts against Chicago, he topped a 100 passer rating in five with 13 touchdowns and two interceptions. His 113.2 passer rating is the second-highest against the Bears behind Carson Palmer’s 122.8 (minimum 100 passing attempts).
The Packers have defeated the Bears at least once in each of the last 18 seasons. That’s the third-longest streak in Packers history behind their 25-year run against Detroit from 1992 through 2016 and 19 in a row against Detroit from 1930 through 1949.
This is Matt LaFleur’s 122nd game as coach, which ties the legendary Vince Lombardi for the fourth-most in Packers history. He’s won 78 games, which trails Curly Lambeau (209), Mike McCarthy (125) and Lombardi (89).
It’s been a disappointing start for the Packers, but they are 2-2 or better through four games for the 20th consecutive year, the longest streak in NFL history.

title: Packers-Bears Inactives: Will Kevin Zeitler Start? Another Surprise on O-Line?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Kevin Zeitler is active for the Green Bay Packers for Sunday’s rivalry showdown against the Chicago Bears, but he will not be the team’s starting right guard.
Based on pregame warmups, Travis Glover will join the No. 1 line alongside left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Laken Tomlinson, center Sean Rhyan and right tackle Anthony Belton for the second consecutive week. It marks the first time this season they will use the same starting line.
“I thought they did great,” coach Matt LaFleur said this week of the play of Tomlinson and Glover against the Buccaneers. “I know they each had a penalty, I know Tomlinson had two, but I thought all in all just the whole unit played – that was the best we’ve played together for one game. It wasn’t perfect all the time, but the thing that I liked too was I saw the guys straining up front, there was some physicality that we needed to see and so I thought they did a good job against a pretty good front.”
Glover at RG instead of Zeitler. pic.twitter.com/vAcxiy5ecA
More on the offensive line in a moment. But first, here are the inactives for both teams.
The Packers had to list only four inactives. All of them are linemen:
RG Jacob Monk will miss his second consecutive game with an injured quad. He returned to practice on Friday and was doubtful.
LG Aaron Banks will miss his third consecutive game with knee and toe injuries. He’s played only one-half of a game this season, 22 snaps against the Jets in Week 2. He also returned to practice on Friday and was doubtful.
G/C Donovan Jennings started the season as the next man up at left guard in place of Banks. Now, he’s a healthy scratch after the veteran additions of Kevin Zeitler and Laken Tomlinson.
DT Anthony Campbell will miss a third consecutive game with an ankle injury sustained at the Jets.
The bigger news is that Javon Hargrave, the veteran defensive tackle who is coming off a strong game against Tampa Bay, is active. He was added to the injury report on Friday with a toe injury and listed as questionable.
Rookie guard/center Jager Burton, who missed time this week following back spasms and was questionable is active, as well. He got the call over Jennings.
With Chris Brooks out, running back Pierre Strong is active. Strong was elevated from the practice squad three times last year but never played in a game.
“Man, I could just thank the Lord,” he said after practice on Friday . “Like you said, it was a while but God’s timing is better than everybody’s timing. I’m here now so got to continue to get better.”
Packers. Bears. A glorious Sunday at Lambeau Field for the 214th matchup. pic.twitter.com/MCaCmlAwb3
Out for Chicago are quarterback Caleb Williams and running back Kyle Monangai. Those are two of the team’s best players on offense.
Williams will miss a third consecutive game following a hamstring injury. He practiced on Friday and was listed as questionable but that was just gamesmanship from coach Ben Johnson.
Tyson Bagent will start for a second consecutive game. He threw one interception in a blowout win over the Jets last week but penalties nullified three others.
“I think you go into each week the exact same as far as; Wednesday, Thursday, Friday getting the plan down, being locked in, taking it extremely seriously,” Bagent said of the rivalry this week.
“But to say that this is just like any game just wouldn't be true. It's one of the greatest rivalries in all of sports. Easy for the fans to get up for, easy for us to get up for. It'll certainly be a different feel out there and that's why it's so important that we put in the amount of work that we need to this week, get acclimated in a smart way but also in a hurry so we can have our best foot forward going into this weekend.”
Even with a backup quarterback, they are 1.5-point favorites at FanDuel Sportsbook on Sunday .
The other inactives for Chicago.
Inactives for #CHIvsGB : pic.twitter.com/naxqaxFcTP
The Packers signed Zeitler to stabilize right guard, which had been a real problem with Monk starting there for the first time in his NFL career. Zeitler is in his 15th season and has made 213 career starts.
The question entering this week would be whether two weeks of practice and ramp-up after not being on a team for training camp would be enough for the 36-year-old.
“We’ll see,” coach Matt LaFleur said before Friday’s practice. “He’s been practicing the last two days. He’ll be out there today. A lot of it is just how comfortable he is, and we’ll go from there.”
How would that be determined?
“There’s a lot of communication with the player and certainly how they’re performing out there, as well,” LaFleur said.
So, what would Zeitler say as part of that conversion?
The veteran wouldn’t bite.
“I’m just keep going,” he said after Friday’s practice. “I’m going to let that be on the coaches. If they know what they see and everything and I know what I feel, we’ll keep attacking and when gameday gets here, we’ll make the call.”
As he spoke, it was unclear if Zeitler was talking like a smart veteran not wanting to let the cat out of the bag or if he knew he wouldn’t be starting.
With Glover starting, the Packers will use the same starting guard combination for the first time this season. The Packers will have the same starting five, as well.
Week 1 vs. the Vikings: LG Donovan Jennings, RG Jacob Monk.
Week 2 vs. the Jets: LG Aaron Banks, RG Jacob Monk.
Week 3 vs. the Falcons: LG Jager Burton, RG Jacob Monk.
Week 4 vs. the Buccaneers: LG Laken Tomlinson, RG Travis Glover.
Week 5 vs. the Bears: LG Laken Tomlinson, RG Travis Glover.
Said LaFleur: “I think there's no greater thing than continuity up front, and so the more people play together, the more that grows, and the more those guys are on the same page – getting off on the same snap count and being able to play off one another – I think that's critical. And so, yeah, I'm looking forward to that.”
The Packers’ line is coming off its best game of the season in the 34-year-old Tomlinson’s debut.
“I thought the O-line kicked butt last week and they did a lot of great things, especially in all the heat down there, and I was really pumped about that,” Zeitler said. “That’s a good thing. The more people playing well, the better.”
Zeitler said he felt “much better” mentally following a second week of practice. Physically, he’s feeling strong.
“Yeah, finally getting to practice again, you feel those feelings and those tiny muscles that haven’t fired in so long are firing,” he said. “So, overall, feel good.”

title: Packers-Bears Rivalry Is Real, It’s Spectacular And It’s Hit Pivotal Moment
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – It’s been a long, long time since the ancient rivalry between the Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears, which will be played for the 214th time on Sunday at Lambeau Field, had real fangs.
The feud’s been bitter, to be sure – recall Mark Lee’s ejection in 1985 and Charles Martin’s infamous cheap shot against Jim McMahon in 1986 – but it’s usually been a battle of bullies. The Packers and Bears have had long runs of dominance, with one team being really good and one team really bad.
Until last year, the Packers and Bears hadn’t qualified for the playoffs with winning records in the same season since 2010.
The Bears had a huge lead in the series until Brett Favre arrived on the scene. Then Aaron Rodgers stomped on the accelerator. Beginning on Nov. 22, 1992, when Favre led the Packers to a 17-3 win, through last year’s victory at Lambeau Field, which was clinched by Keisean Nixon’s interception, the Packers went 52-15.
Favre went 22-10 against Chicago. Rodgers went a remarkable 25-5, including the 2010 NFC Championship Game.
However, the Bears enter this game with wins in three of the last four meetings. Before that, they had three wins in the previous 29 matchups. Packers coach Matt LaFleur won his first 11 games against Chicago; the Bears have a chance to win three in a row for the first time in 20 years.
For a long time, this wasn’t a rivalry. It was bullying. When Rodgers screamed in the end zone that he owned the Bears, who was going to argue with him?
Bears coach Ben Johnson has replaced Rodgers as the dynamo in the rivalry. When he screamed “F*** the Packers” in the locker room after last year’s playoff win, who was going to tell him he was out of line? After years of being given wedgies and swirlies, the Bears were back.
Sunday’s game at Lambeau Field is as big as it gets. No, it’s not a playoff game, like last year. No, it’s not for the NFC North championship, as was the case in 2013.
Especially for the Packers.
Yeah, revenge is a factor after Green Bay’s all-time implosion in last year’s wild-card game. Yeah, the standings are a factor, with one win (or loss) feeling like it could be worth four or five for the Packers, who have looked like pretenders throughout their 2-2 start to the season.
“Definitely a lot of history,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “We always talk about the oldest rivalry in all of the NFL, so it goes back a long way, a lot of history in this game. So, yeah, it’s a good rivalry. Obviously, NFC North matchup and all these teams we take just a little more pride in these games. We gotta win these ones. They mean so much throughout the course of the season, so definitely going to be a good game.”
Love, who was abused by the Bears last season with nobody really having his back, will never be as outspoken as Rodgers. It’s just not in his nature.
So, leave it to his teammates to provide the real talk.
“Yeah, anytime it’s a division game, you kind of got to get your piss hot for the most part, understanding that these are going to have long-term effects on the standings for where we want to be at the end of the year,” safety Evan Williams said.
“And also carrying over from last year, understanding we also have a bad taste in our mouth from what happened. You can understand a 12-round fight. It’s going to be a fistfight for sure. We wouldn’t want anything else.”
It can’t be anything else. Because while playing a winning standard of football is important after four mistake-plagued games, and the standings are important given the difference between 3-2 and 2-3, where this game is of critical importance is for the rivalry. If the Bears shove the Packers into a locker again while playing without starting quarterback Caleb Williams, it could mark another run of one-sided dominance in the border battle.
Johnson, who started jabbing at LaFleur from the moment he was hired, is the driving force behind the rivalry’s renewed relevance.
“Some sh** don’t slide, and you don’t let that sh** go,” center Sean Rhyan said of Johnson’s locker room comments after last year’s playoff meltdown.
Jordan Morgan has been a part of the rivalry since he was drafted in 2024. This will be his first start at left tackle in the series.
“He’s dissing us. He’s dissing the Packers,” he said of Johnson. “A lot of people in here, I’m pretty sure, take that to heart. And we got a chance to prove to everybody on Sunday that we the best team.”
Added Williams: “That’s part of the rivalry. We understand how they feel about us, and we feel the same way, is what I’ll say. It’s a rivalry for a reason. We’re both competing to be the best in not only our conference, but the league. You get two powerhouses going up against each other, and on any given Sunday, you’re going to have those feelings spill out, for sure. I’m not going to quite say exactly what you want me to say, but it’s mutual. It’s mutual.”
Tight end Tucker Kraft missed all three games last season following his torn ACL.
“I talk with my pads, so I’ll just wait ‘til Sunday,” he said.
This will be Zaire Franklin’s first taste of the rivalry. He already knows this one’s different.
“It’s a lot of bad blood. A lot of bad blood,” he said. “A lot of genuine dislike, which is a little different than nowadays. Nowadays, most rivalries are just on social media and in the offseason, you’re hanging out. I don’t think nobody want to hang out with the Bears in the offseason. I think it’s a real issue between both sides.
“The beautiful part of it is we got nothing but space and opportunity to figure it out. Looking forward to it.”
New Packers guard Kevin Zeitler, who might make his starting debut, grew up in Wisconsin so knows what the rivalry is all about.
“Growing up in Wisconsin, obviously all about the Packers vs. Bears and everything, and it's cool to be a part of that now officially,” he said. “It's a very heated rivalry for obvious reasons and got to bring your A game.”
Safety Javon Bullard said this will be a primetime game, no matter the time.
“We’re playing the Bears. They don’t like us, we don’t like them,” he said.
“Sh**, once you respect the game in a way, you appreciate the rivalries,” he added. “Everybody got their game. I grew up watching these types of games. You’ve got Baltimore-Pittsburgh, you’ve got Seattle-San Fran, us and the Bears. So, it’s not just us. Everybody got their game and we treat every game like it’s the same game but, at the end of the day, they them boys from across the street so we’ve got to knock them off.”
For more than three decades, the Packers turned the so-called Monsters of the Midway into cute little stuffed animals. Led by Johnson, is there a new era in this agent feud? Or will the Packers restore order and punch the want-to-be bullies in the face?
The time for talk is done. It’s time to battle. It’s time to do the punching or be the punching bag.
“It’s something that doesn’t really have to be said,” Evan Williams said. “It’s just a type of energy that we understand how they feel about us, and we know how we feel about them. All of that is talk for me.
“For the most part it’s about who’s going to show up and who’s going to do their job violently. That’s really what it’s all about. As far as the energy goes, I feel like both sides understand how pivotal not only the game is, but understanding the type of energy the other side is going to bring. You’ve just got to put your hard hat on and be ready for a fight.”

title: Texans' Biggest Winners and Losers From Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade
full_text:
The Houston Texans took a big swing on the trade market after their Week 5 win over the Tennessee Titans by opting to acquire 2024 No. 4 pick Marvin Harrison Jr. and a seventh-round pick from the Arizona Cardinals in exchange for a 2027 second- and sixth-round pick.
It's a high-risk, high-reward investment from the Texans' front office. Harrison Jr., who was largely viewed as one of the best receiver prospects seen in some time when entering the league, now joins a new situation in Houston with hopes of bringing a jolt of playmaking to this offense, while also bouncing back from a disappointing start to his career.
And because of the Texans' newest addition to their receiver room, there are some clear winners and losers around the team that stick out now that this offense looks a little different than it did entering this past weekend.
Let's break down the Texans' newest splash trade by sorting through three winners and three losers from Harrison Jr.'s addition to the roster.
The clear winner of Houston's move to bring a new talent in at wide receiver is surely the guy that's going to be throwing passes to him–– especially when factoring in his existing chemistry with Harrison Jr. from Ohio State.
Stroud clearly saw something in Harrison Jr. that made it worth the Texans investing in him. Stroud spoke after the trade was announced where he told reporters he spoke to the front office about interest in a potential move for the Cardinals wide receiver, and in due time, he's now in Houston.
Now, the time comes for Stroud to try and unlock the same talent that Harrison Jr. looked like from his time at Ohio State. And there might be no better candidate to turn towards for that goal than the guy that helped form him into the can't-miss prospect he was viewed as entering the league.
Just over a month from when the Texans last made a trade for a new wide receiver to add into their offense–– coming from the New England Patriots in their deal to bring in Kayshon Boutte –– Houston has already decided to add a new set of hands into the building.
That tends to tell you how the Texans feel about their existing wide receiver group around Nico Collins. And in the case of Boutte, he hasn't exactly developed into a quality starter to line up opposite him on a weekly basis. In five games, he recorded 12 catches for 153 yards.
Now, Boutte will see Harrison Jr. enter the mix for an already deep receiver room, is due to see a bit less snaps because of it, and might have a less certain future in Houston once hitting the offseason when he's due for a new contract.
Some may argue that Collins is a bit of a loser in this scenario, considering Harrison Jr. might take away some targets and offensive responsibility from the Texans' No. 1 pass-catcher. But in my mind, it's quite the opposite.
If Harrison Jr. can develop into a quality sidekick to Collins in the receiver room, that'll only take less attention off of Collins for him to produce even better numbers than he's seen so far this year. It's an aspect this Texans offense has needed for some time, and there's a chance that the former No. 4 pick could bring that spark.
If Harrison Jr. still continues to disappoint like he has in Arizona? Then Collins is still a winner. He'll remain the No. 1 option in the receiver room as he has been, and will remain a key part of the Texans' future, knowing that he's the best source of production at the position that this franchise has had in some time.
The Texans have two noteworthy names in their receiver room currently signed onto expiring contracts for the 2026 season. The first of those is Kayshon Boutte, whom we discussed earlier, and the second is fourth-year pass-catcher Xavier Hutchinson.
And when adding a young, talented piece like Harrison Jr. into the position, it tends to add a bit more uncertainty for what Hutchinson's future in Houston could look like beyond this season.
Do the Texans really want to invest money into a pass-catcher who might fall down to fifth or sixth on the depth chart by next season? Hutchinson has continued to play well as a depth contributor this season, and even in 2025, but a heavy investment in Harrison Jr. could force Houston to make some sacrifices at the position.
Another clear winner of the Texans' newest move: the guy who's going to be calling plays for Harrison Jr. in offensive coordinator Nick Caley. Houston has long coveted a reliable No. 2 since 2024, when Houston has left without the likes of Dell or Stefon Diggs, and this trade now makes for Caley's first time having a potential complementary talent to Collins.
Now, Caley has a bounty of pieces to work with at both receiver and tight end; each of which brings something unique to the table that this offense could capitalize on.
The challenge for Caley now comes in the form of helping Harrison Jr. reach that same potential he was projected to have entering the league a couple of years ago.
If he succeeds in that effort, Caley will be viewed as a hero, and even a miracle worker . If he fails to do so, it'll make that second-round investment in his services look a whole lot more questionable.
The good news for Tank Dell is that his return to the Texans' lineup seems to be right around the corner . Houston opened Dell's 21-day practice window from injured reserve, that could allow him to return for a game as soon as Week 7, or Week 9 on the later side.
But now as Dell is going to return to the Texans' lineup, the competition for targets is going to be immense. Not only when battling for touches with Collins and Harrison Jr., but also the depth pieces that will now be fighting a little harder to get their opportunities like Boutte, Hutchinson, and Jaylin Noel.
For Dell to get back on the field for an NFL game makes him a winner in itself. But as for the impact he'll be making in this offense upon his return, it feels like that's taken a hit with Houston's latest trade.
