title: 5 Things DeMeco Ryans Said After Texans' Week 5 Win Over Titans
full_text:
The Houston Texans finally have their first win of the 2026 season in the books, as they took down their AFC South rival Tennessee Titans for a rout of a victory in Week 5, 26-3.
And after the game, Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans spoke to the media about how his team performed, and some other factors that might've stuck out in what was their best showing of the new season thus far.
Let's sort through five of the most noteworthy quotes that stuck out from Ryan’s post-game presser after Houston's win vs. Tennessee:
After a winless first four games, the Texans finally flipped the script in Week 5 for a much-different-looking result than what they've been used to. The offense showed signs of life, the defense looked the best it's been all year, and as a result, a dominant performance came to form.
So what was the big difference that DeMeco Ryans saw from the Texans that led to a winning result? In his mind, one major takeaway was his team's execution. But he didn't forget to give his flowers to his quarterback, C.J. Stroud, for an awesome day on his part.
"It was our execution. We executed really well and controlled the game," Ryans said about what was different for Texans in Week 5 win. "Offensively, they did an outstanding job of driving the football down the field. C.J. did an outstanding job of making play after play when we needed it. He was dealing."
C.J. Stroud ➡️ Jaylin Noel for the touchdown! @HOUvsTEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/yUJBMVAv0r
"He was throwing the ball to everyone who was open and making really great decisions with the football. He was able to get a rushing touchdown in there as well. He's been doing a great job all year, so I'm thankful to celebrate him. He's been leading our offense really well and is very deserving of everything.
The biggest change the Texans made in terms of game-planning from Week 4 to 5 was the pivot from defensive coordinator Matt Burke to DeMeco Ryans calling plays on the defensive side.
Clearly, seeing that the Texans allowed just three points from the Titans throughout the day, that shift seemed to work rather well. And after the game, Ryan’s made sure to give all the credit he could to his players on that side of the ball.
"The defense did an outstanding job today, taking the football away," Ryans said. "Jake Hansen did a great job getting the ball. Dom Robinson got one out. We were able to recover the fumble."
"Our d-line––they got after it when we needed them to. They put a lot of pressure on the quarterbacks. Our players did an outstanding job today."
Will Anderson was undoubtedly the Texans' defensive MVP for how he took on this outing against the Titans. He stuffed the stat sheet with a whopping three sacks on quarterback Cam Ward, which led to DeMeco Ryans giving a major hand to his All-Pro edge rusher's performance.
Will Anderson Jr. steps up and gets the sack on 4th and 20 👏 @HOUvsTEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/nOZadKuT2h
"Will is our guy," Ryans said of Anderson's three-sack day. "It's great to see what he's able to do every week. He's a tenacious player, relentless on every single snap."
"There's no better competitor or person than Will Anderson. To see him go out and dominate the game with three sacks was an outstanding performance."
The Texans got a select few recently injured names back in their lineup for Week 5. But none of those returnees were more important than Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair .
Al-Shaair made his presence felt against his former team in Tennessee, as had a game-high for total tackles (11), along with one QB hit and a pass defended. And there's no doubt that Ryans was thrilled to have his defensive captain back on the field.
"Azeez is our field general and our communicator. He's the man in the middle. When we have him out there, our guys are on the ball and moving fast," Ryans said.
"Azeez communicates really well, tackles well in the middle and makes the plays he needs to make. I'm really happy to have him back."
The most viral moment of DeMeco Ryans' presser came at the very end of it. After the Texans head coach was asked about a potential trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. for the third time after the game , Ryans let the world in on the front office's big move made over the weekend.
"You guys want to know, huh? All right. We traded for Marvin Harrison Jr," Ryans said. "See ya."
DeMeco Ryans with the ultimate mic drop. When asked about Marvin Harrison Jr. at the end of his presser after beating the Tennessee Titans: “You guys wanted to know, huh? Yes, alright, we traded for Marvin Harrison. SEE YA.” pic.twitter.com/n3dzY6SCXp
While the Texans' Week 5 win in itself is pretty exciting, so is this move to bring in a top-five pick from only a couple of summers ago. Expect to see Harrison Jr. in uniform with Houston heading into Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

title: C.J. Stroud Shares Thoughts on Texans' Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade
full_text:
The Houston Texans are the latest team to make a splash trade following the events of Week 5's NFL action, as they've decided to bring in wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. in a deal with the Arizona Cardinals , sending over a second and sixth-round pick in exchange for his services and a seventh-round pick.ound pick.
It was a move that was largely rumored in the hours leading up to the Texans' Week 5 game against the Tennessee Titans . And after Houston had taken care of business for a dominant 26-3 victory, the bombshell had been dropped by head coach DeMeco Ryans that the move for Harrison Jr. was made.
For Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud, bringing in Harrison Jr. is certainly a welcomed addition to their offensive side of the ball.
Not only is he another talented set of hands that Houston can lean on in their wide receiver room, but also because of the existing chemistry Stroud has with his former teammate from Ohio State.
Once the news surfaced around the Texans making a move to go and get Harrison Jr., Stroud made it apparent on just how excited he was to get his new receiver in the fold––calling Houston a "perfect" fit for a fresh start to his career.
"I think he brings a dynamic playmaker, somebody who runs great routes and can catch pretty much any ball. I'm super excited to get to work with him," Stroud said after the trade was announced.
"I loved him in college. He's probably the hardest worker I've ever been around in my life. And then there's who he is off the field. He's a great dude, a quiet guy, but you definitely feel his presence. I'm excited to get him here, get him learning and get him around the other guys. I think it's perfect for him. Fresh starts are good, so I'm excited to have him with us."
Having also played with Harrison Jr. for two years, Stroud was seemingly able to give a bit of input to the Texans' front office about what exactly they'd be getting in him if they traded for him. And pretty clearly, what he told them was enough to convince them to pull the trigger.
"Yeah, I had some conversations with different people, just telling them who he is as a person and a player and what I liked about him when I played with him," Stroud said. "I thought our front office did a great job allowing me to be part of it."
Harrison Jr.'s had a bit of a slow start to his 2026 campaign with the Cardinals, having brought in five receptions for 85 yards and a touchdown in the four games he's played this far; good for an average of 21.3 yards per game.
The hope is for Harrison Jr. that in Houston, those numbers can turn around for the better, and make for an ideal situation for not only his career moving forward, but also for what the Texans could use in their offensive arsenal.
As to what Stroud wants to see out of his newest offensive addition upon his arrival in Houston, he kept his expectations simple : he wants Harrison Jr. to be himself.
"Just being himself. I'm not an expectations-type person when it comes to others or even myself. I take things one at a time. The next thing I'm focused on is correcting things from this game."
After a Week 5 win against their division rival Titans, paired with a big-time trade to add a 2024 top-five pick to the roster, the Texans will hope to build on their current momentum for what will be a pivotal Week 6 game in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars—one where Stroud will likely have a new, yet familiar target to throw to.

title: Instant Grade: Texans Finally Land Marvin Harrison Jr. in Blockbuster Trade
full_text:
The deal is officially done: Marvin Harrison Jr. is a Houston Texan.
According to ESPN 's Adam Schefter, the Texans are acquiring Harrison Jr. from the Arizona Cardinals in exchange for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick. Houston also acquires a 2027 seventh-round pick from the Cardinals along with the wide receiver.
Trade: the Arizona Cardinals have agreed to trade WR Marvin Harrison Jr. and 2027 7th-round pick to the Houston Texans in exchange for a 2027 2nd-round pick and 2027 6th-round pick, per @rapsheet and me. pic.twitter.com/ziepfRIPr4
After much chatter had encircled the Texans' potential interest in a move to acquire Harrison Jr. heading into Week 5's action, Houston finally silenced that noise by pulling the trigger on a move to acquire the No. 4 overall pick from the 2024 NFL Draft.
And that move to acquire Harrison Jr. would actually be officially announced via Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans right after Houston's Week 5 victory over the Tennessee Titans.
Ryans was asked during his post-game media on three different occasions regarding a potential move for Harrison Jr.. He declined the first two times before letting the big secret spill walking out of his interview.
“You guys wanted to know, huh? Yes, alright, we traded for Marvin Harrison," Ryans said on Sunday afternoon. "See ya!"
#Texans coach DeMeco Ryans on trading for Marvin Harrison Jrm https://t.co/tXKpdIrbk4 pic.twitter.com/AI46f1R663
Now, the Texans' receiving core is able to look a little bit better, and of course, allows Harrison Jr. to reunite with his college teammate of two seasons from Ohio State, quarterback C.J. Stroud.
Let's break down the Texans' newest roster move by handing out an instant grade for the deal; evaluating just how Houston did in terms of the package they gave up for the Cardinals wideout, along with how Harrison Jr. might fit into the offensive equation overall.
In reality, this is a high-risk, high-reward move for the Texans offense to take on .
There's a world in which we look back on this trade as a genius investment for Houston to make at this point in the year. However, there's also a chance things turn in a much different direction.
Let's start with how the Texans can walk away from this trade as winners. If Harrison Jr. can enter the fold in Houston as not only an immediate impact player for this season, but also a pass-catcher that can be a valuable piece of their future endeavors offensively, this can be a massive victory .
It was only a few years ago that Harrison Jr. was not only viewed as a great receiver prospect, but practically a generational one. He had the physical traits, the college production, and of course, the NFL pedigree that would hint that his future is extremely bright in the league.
To this point, that NFL breakout for Harrison Jr. has yet to happen, which has really led to the Cardinals looking to move on from him in the first place.
But if Houston can discover some of his untapped potential as a complement lining up opposite Nico Collins, rekindle his connection with his college quarterback, while also having his rights for the next three years on a rookie deal, this can be a home run for the Texans' front office.
Let's keep in mind: Harrison Jr. has not been up to par in his NFL career.
He's continued to look less engaged and less involved in the Cardinals' offense each and every season, to the point where he's now recorded a total of 85 receiving yards through the first four games of his 2026 campaign. That's a far cry from his generational prospect expectations he entered the league with.
That blame could be put on the Cardinals for not putting Harrison Jr. in the best of situations throughout his tenure there. Perhaps it’s on the player himself.
But the fact of the matter is, the Texans are banking on their own development and their own offensive system to bring the best out of their newest trade acquisition.
Will the Texans be able to unlock Harrison Jr.’s true potential to take this offense to the next level? Only time will tell. But until we see how his fit in Houston really takes shape, a C grade feels like a nice middle ground that accounts for the benefits and risks of taking a swing like this.

title: 3 Biggest Texans Takeaways From Dominant 26-3 Win vs. Titans
full_text:
The Houston Texans have finally marked down their first win of the 2026 season.
After a dominant 26-3 victory over the Tennessee Titans in Week 5, the Texans finally ended their gloomy four-game losing stretch over the first four weeks of the season to have a much-better-looking result on the road in Nashville.
This time last week, it felt like the sky was falling in Houston. But now, this Texans team rises up to a slightly better 1-4 on the year, an even 1-1 within the AFC South , and now has a bit of momentum to bank on riding into the next couple of weeks before their bye.
Let's break down the Texans' Week 5 win by sorting through three of the biggest takeaways to gather:
There's little doubt that Week 5 in Nashville wound up being the best performance of C.J. Stroud's 2026 campaign so far.
After Stroud had a handful of solid performances through the first four weeks, yet couldn't see that success translate to a win on the books, this game was a much different story.
Not only did Stroud hold up his end for over 260 yards passing, two total touchdowns, and a fifth-straight game of no interceptions, but the supporting cast around Houston's quarterback carried their weight as well.
This throw by C.J. Stroud and catch by Kayshon Boutte  👏 @HOUvsTEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ivlTYQE2fM
Stroud also did a fantastic job of spreading the love all around the offense to a variety of playmakers from start to finish. Six pass-catchers on Houston's side of the equation recorded three receptions or more, with Xavier Hutchinson of all names leading the way with four catches for 65 yards.
Granted, this was a softer Titans roster compared to some of the teams Houston has seen over the past few weeks. Regardless, it was a get-right opportunity for everyone involved, and Stroud finally saw his strong performance result in the Texans' long-awaited first win of the 2026 season.
Not only did the offense hold their own throughout most of the day against their division rivals, but this was unquestionably the best performance this Texans defense has seen across their 2026 season as well.
Many fans expected to see more days like this from the Texans' defense entering the season: Tennessee was limited to under 200 yards of total offense, saw quarterback Cam Ward sacked four times, the Titans averaged just 3.2 yards per carry, and of course, Houston limited them to zero touchdowns and a slim total of three points.
Big man sack! 📺: @nfloncbs | @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/yuMEq8Wq2X
Again, the Titans could very well be the softest matchup the Texans play all season. Regardless of the level of competition Tennessee has to offer, though, this outing showed that Houston still has the potential of being a dominant defense on any given week––a credit to head coach DeMeco Ryans in his first weekend back as the team's defensive play-caller .
If there was one hole to poke through from the Texans’ dominant three-score victory, it would undoubtedly be the consistent penalty woes that Houston faced. Because, wow. Houston saw a ton of flags come their way over the course of their Week 5 matchup.
Houston had a whopping 11 penalties for 95 total yards recorded over the course of this one, much more than Tennessee's ultimate total of nine penalties for 83 yards. A lot of those errors would come on the offensive end, whether it be via false starts or offensive holding calls.
Because of those 11 flags thrown on the Texans, their season total for penalties now rises to 42; an average of over eight per game, and makes for a clear area that needs improvement moving into the next few weeks.
The Texans can get by with those mistakes in games like these where all three phases seem to otherwise be firing on all cylinders against a lackluster Titans roster. But against higher competition later down the line this season, those penalty woes can quickly come to haunt them and their aspired consistency on a down-to-down basis.

title: Texans RB David Montgomery Leaves vs. Titans With Injury, Ruled Out
full_text:
The Houston Texans' running back room suffered a notable injury in their Week 5 matchup vs. the Tennessee Titans .
According to an injury update from the Texans, veteran running back David Montgomery has been ruled out for the rest of the game in Tennessee with a groin injury.
Montgomery initially went down with the injury in the second quarter, which would inevitably leave him questionable to return heading into the half. In due time, the Texans would downgrade him to out.
. @ShariffLawFirm Texans Injury Update: #32 RB David Montgomery has been downgraded to out with a groin injury.
Before Montgomery left the game, he recorded five carries for 11 yards, with his longest run going for five yards; a similarly uninspiring performance that he's put together for the past few weeks.
And instead of getting a chance to build on those numbers, he'll see his day end a bit prematurely.
It's seemingly become a common trend for Texans players to suffer groin injuries over the past few weeks. It was only in Weeks 2 and 3 where Ed Ingram missed time with a groin issue, and last weekend against the Dallas Cowboys, Azeez Al-Shaair missed with a groin injury as well.
And now, Montgomery is the latest to add onto that list; another key starter for Houston on the offensive side, though hasn't had a sharp beginning to his Texans tenure like he would have hoped.
While Montgomery did chip in for three touchdowns in his Texans debut against the Buffalo Bills, he's followed up that performance with a combined 32 carries for 78 yards, coming out to an average of 2.4 yards per carry.
Based on what the Texans thought they were getting in Montgomery when trading Juice Scruggs and multiple draft picks for him from the Detroit Lions earlier this offseason, the veteran running back has fallen wildly short of those expectations this far .
And now, he could be at risk of missing some time moving forward, depending on how severe his groin issue is. At the very least, he'll be missing the rest of the game in Nashville.
The good news for the Texans is that they don't have many weeks on tap before their Week 8 bye week arrives. Houston has a trip to London in Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars, then will host the New York Giants the following weekend.
If Montgomery is deemed out for an extended period, he could have a nice three-week span to recover, and get right before the Texans are back playing in Week 9 against the Los Angeles Chargers.
For however long he's out––both for this game against the Titans and any time moving forward––you can expect Woody Marks to claim a lion's share of carries in the running back room, possibly with more work handed to veteran Dare Ogunbowale , who was signed to the active roster earlier this season, and is the only active running back on the roster for Week 5.

CB Collin Wright DE Chris Braswell DE Sabastian Harris LB Aiden Fisher OG Febechi Nwaiwu OT Nate Thomas TE Marlin Klein

title: How Texans’ Game vs. Titans Could Shape Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Pursuit
full_text:
Since news surfaced this weekend surrounding the Arizona Cardinals' intention to trade away wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., the Houston Texans have been largely viewed as the favorites in the mix to land him.
Rumors have connected the Texans with some of the most interest to land the Cardinals wideout, reportedly offering a future second-round pick to Arizona in hopes of landing him , and by the end of Week 5's action across the league, could have the former No. 4 pick on their roster.
But without a clear trade agreement in place for Harrison Jr. before Week 5 gets rolling, is there a chance that the Texans' matchup against the Tennessee Titans plays any role in a potential deal moving forward?
Considering where the Texans stand at this point in the season, it really wouldn't be too outlandish to say plans could shift on Harrison Jr., depending on whether they win or lose this weekend.
The situation around Harrison Jr.'s pending trade status is pretty bizarre as is: a player being inactive on gameday and on his way out in a potential deal, yet the trade package and team acquiring him are largely speculative.
Oftentimes, a player in this type of situation could've already been traded by this point in the week. But in Harrison Jr.'s case, along with what could be a pending offer on the table from the Texans, there has yet to be a clear agreement.
And this could be for a few reasons. On the Cardinals' side of things, they could simply be holding out and looking for the best package available in exchange for their former No. 4 pick.
While one team may have a second-rounder on the table, maybe another team coughs up more by the time this weekend's games end. For a premier asset like Harrison Jr., getting the best possible package will be a top priority for Arizona .
But for the Texans' side of things, there's a world where the outcome for Week 5's game against the Titans shifts their thought process of an acquisition entirely.
With a win in Nashville, the Texans can move forward as usual. They'd be 1-4, able to take a deep breath from their winless first four games, have some sense of momentum now built up, and feel a bit more confident that their second-round investment in Harrison Jr. can still be worthwhile to get wins on the board this season.
But with a loss against the Titans? The Texans then sink to 0-5. They'd find themselves in an even bigger hole than they are now, likely falling to the worst roster they've faced this season, and at a record that no team in NFL history has ever come back to make the playoffs from.
At 0-5, that win-now mindset that Houston entered the season with would be tough to continue to have. Sure, the Texans did come back from similar early-season struggles last year. But especially for the cost of a second-round pick, it makes a Harrison Jr. trade a whole lot less appealing.
So if you're a fan that wants to see Harrison Jr. in a Texans uniform by the time Week 6 rolls around, a win this weekend against Tennessee will be critical to see that dream come to fruition.
On the other hand, a loss might just leave Houston to have a major change of plans on how to move forward. So stay tuned to the results that come out of Nashville this Sunday.

title: Texans' 3 Keys to Victory vs. Titans in Pivotal Week 5 Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans have their Week 5 matchup against the Tennessee Titans right around the corner ; a game that's really a must-win for both sides as they look to escape their 0-4 record put together through four weeks.
But even while the Texans are viewed as the heavy favorites for this one, that doesn't mean this matchup will be a walk in the park.
For one, any divisional matchup can be due for some unpredictable outcomes . But we've also seen just how things can go wrong for this talented roster in the first quarter of the season for a winless start, thus giving us a blueprint on what Houston needs this weekend to ensure they get their first win on the season.
With that in mind, let's sort through three of the Texans' biggest keys to victory in Week 5 against the Titans, which could mark their seventh win in eight tries against Tennessee dating back to 2022:
The Texans finally got to see Nico Collins back in their lineup last week against the Dallas Cowboys , who returned from a two-game absence due to a hamstring strain. And in his first game back, Houston's No. 1 wideout proved exactly why he's an essential piece to their aspired offensive success.
Collins burst onto the scene with seven receptions for 118 yards and a pair of touchdowns; really for one of the best games of his entire Texans tenure, even in a losing effort. And in the process of that performance, he gave this offense a much-needed breath of fresh air.
We've witnessed how dreary this offense can be when Collins is not on the field as C.J. Stroud's top target. It's not pretty, nor is it a recipe for success. So building upon that momentum Collins saw last week feels like a good plan of attack to keep this offense from sinking as they did without him in Weeks 2 and 3.
There's no doubt about who the best player is that the Texans will be up against this weekend: it's First-Team All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who has a chance to create some real trouble for Houston if they're not careful.
Simmons has had a similarly dominant start to his 2026 campaign, recording 24 combined tackles, three TFLs, and two sacks. And throughout the past four weeks, we've seen just what a strong interior defense can do to this Texans offensive line with the likes of Dexter Lawrence, Ed Oliver, and DeForest Buckner.
The Titans are a team that can be easily overlooked. But doing that for Simmons could be a fatal mistake for the Texans and their porous interior offensive line. So ensuring he's a center focus from start to finish will be key for Houston to keep their game script on track.
The Texans' run game has been largely the same story over the past three weeks : lacking consistency, explosiveness, and the juice needed to propel this offense to be a little more well-balanced.
Houston has failed to reach over 70 total rushing yards across the last three weeks, and their running backs have combined for less than 3.0 yards per carry across that stretch.
And without that consistency on the ground, it tends to be a major limitation for how dynamic this Texans' offense can be. That simply can't be the case moving forward this season, so maybe this outing against the Titans can be a different story.
The Titans' defense does rank top 10 in the NFL for yards per carry allowed (3.7), but they do also lead the league in carries allowed, and are 24th in total rushing yards allowed. There are holes that Houston can attack in the run game, and will likely need to in order to get the most out of their offense.

title: How to Watch, Stream Texans' Week 5 Game vs. Titans
full_text:
The Houston Texans are on for their Week 5 action against the Tennessee Titans ––one that has some steep stakes in play for both sides as they look to claim their first win of an otherwise turbulent 2026 campaign.
For the Texans, they're coming off some rough losses on their end over the past four weeks. Most recently, they fell to their in-state rivals, the Dallas Cowboys, 30-34 , sinking them to an even deeper hole record-wise than they were last year as they now stand at 0-4.
So this week is important as ever for the Texans to take advantage of. Because if they don't, an 0-5 record could simply be too big of a hole to climb out of moving deeper into the season.

title: Six Most Revealing Quotes After Colts’ Disappointing Loss to Steelers
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts had opportunities to leave Pittsburgh with a win on Sunday. Instead, they left with a 34-22 loss to the Steelers and a list of issues that need to be addressed heading into Week 6.
Indianapolis moved the ball between the 20-yard lines but struggled to turn those drives into touchdowns. Meanwhile, the defense gave up two explosive touchdowns while tackling problems persisted.
After the game, head coach Shane Steichen, quarterback Daniel Jones and running back Jonathan Taylor offered insight into what went wrong and what the Colts need to improve. Here are six of the most important quotes from Indianapolis' Week 5 loss and what they reveal about the team moving forward.
Steichen Sounds Off on Red-Zone Woes
The Colts' red zone struggles were arguably the difference maker between a win and a loss. Indianapolis scored a touchdown on only one of its three trips inside Pittsburgh's 20-yard line, settling for field goals on two other possessions. Those missed opportunities proved costly in a 34-22 loss.
Following the game, head coach Shane Steichen acknowledged that the Colts needed to improve in those situations, including in the way he managed the offense.
“We’ve to do a better job. I’ve got to do a better job of calling plays. We’ve got to do a better job of executing. Credit Pittsburgh in those situations, but we've got to do a better job overall and get it cleaned up so we can score touchdowns down there.”
Steichen's willingness to include his own playcalling in the problem is notable. The Colts had entered Week 5 with one of the league's more productive red-zone offenses, converting 75% of their trips into touchdowns through the first four weeks. Against Pittsburgh, however, they failed to finish drives even when they had opportunities from close range.
The coach did not place the blame solely on execution or the Steelers' defense. By acknowledging his own role, Steichen made clear that the solution must involve both better decisions from the sideline and better execution on the field, not one or the other.
The red zone offense will be an area to watch in Week 6. The Colts don't have a red zone problem, at least not yet, and Sunday's performance showed how quickly stalled drives can quickly turn into a larger issue.
Colts' Offense Asking Too Much of Spencer Shrader
Spencer Shrader did everything Indianapolis could have asked of him against Pittsburgh. The kicker connected on all five field-goal attempts, tying a franchise record for field goals made in a game. Yet his production could not compensate for an offense that repeatedly failed to reach the end zone.
Running back Jonathan Taylor recognized the value of Shrader's performance but also emphasized that the offense must do more to support its special teams.
“That's definitely a lot to put on [Spencer] Shrader. We know, obviously, he's been playing amazing. But that's not something you want to keep putting on him...We want to play complementary football. Special teams has been doing a great job, like we just talked about with Shrader, but offense has to do their part as well.”
Taylor's comments reinforce the point Steichen made about the red zone, but they also offer a different perspective. The running back praised Shrader while acknowledging that the offense cannot continue asking its kicker to bail them out.
That admission carries additional weight after a difficult afternoon for Taylor himself. He finished with 45 rushing yards on 15 carries, averaging just 3.0 yards per attempt.
The Colts need more consistent production from their offense, particularly when drives reach scoring territory. Shrader has shown he can deliver points, but Indianapolis can't rely on field goals to win games
Pierce's Absence Looms Large
It's been rough sledding for the Colts' passing game without Alec Pierce, whose ability to stretch the field gives Indy a dimension that is difficult to replicate. With Pierce unavailable, quarterback Daniel Jones was asked about the team's ability to generate downfield opportunities.
Jones acknowledged that Pierce brings a special skill set while emphasizing that the offense must find other ways to threaten defenses vertically.
“He's one of the best in the league getting the ball down the field. So, yeah, (we've) got to find ways to do it and find opportunities. The red zone stuff, go back and look at the tape and see where we may have had opportunities to get the ball down the field.”
Jones finished with 267 passing yards, completing 24 of 44 attempts. He did not throw a touchdown, however, and Indianapolis struggled to convert yardage to points.
Pierce's absence does not explain every problem from Sunday, particularly the failures in the red zone. Still, Jones' comments suggest the Colts' passing attack is capped without their primary deep-ball option.
It's on the coaching staff and Jones to identify new ways to create down the field.
Jones Wants Downs More Involved
Josh Downs' involvement is another question for an Indianapolis passing game that looked sloppy on Sunday. Downs finished with just three catches for 47 yards.
Jones was asked about the receiver's role and the challenges of getting him the ball, acknowledging that defenses are particularly aware of Downs on third down. But he also took responsibility for finding ways to get the receiver more involved.
"I think they're certainly aware of him, particularly on third down," Jones said. "So, I think that's another thing that I'll go back and look at where I can be better, and where there may be opportunities to get him the ball.”
Jones' response is useful because he did not suggest that Downs' limited production was solely the result of defensive attention and is instead an opportunity for Jones to self-evaluate and figure out how to get more out of Downs.
Indianapolis needs answers when defenses hone in on their top receiving threat. That could mean finding Downs in different situations, adjusting how the offense creates opportunities or making better use of the openings that are available.
Jones' comments are not an admission of a major disconnect between him and Downs. They do, however, identify a matchup the Colts need to evaluate as they look to make their passing game more productive.
Colts Have a Tackling Problem
The offensive struggles were not the Colts' only concern in Pittsburgh. Indianapolis was also plagued by horrendous tackling problems, which helped Steelers' running back Jaylen Warren score twice on big plays.
After the game, Steichen was asked about the recurring tackling issues and acknowledged that the team needed to take a closer look at the problem.
“It's something we've got to look at hard for sure," he said. "We do tackling drills every day in practice, individuals. We've just got to hammer it home.”
Steichen's response, particularly the detail about tackling being emphasized in every practice, raises concerns. The coach did not offer a specific explanation for the missed tackles, instead emphasizing the need to reinforce fundamentals, and doesn't seem to have any idea of how to move forward.
With another divisional game approaching, improving the defense's ability to finish plays will be just as important as cleaning up the offensive mistakes.
Colts' Ground Game Hits a Wall
The Colts' inability to establish a consistent ground game added another challenge to an offense that struggled to finish drives. Taylor managed just 45 rushing yards on 15 carries, and Indianapolis finished with 66 rushing yards as a team.
With Pittsburgh limiting the ground attack, Jones was asked how the offense adjusts when the run game is not producing the results Indianapolis wants. His answer pointed to a broader responsibility for the entire unit.
“There are games like that," he said "Sometimes the run is working and the pass isn't working as well. Sometimes it's the other way around. So, we've got to be able to handle whatever kind of game it is and find ways to get in the end zone.”

title: Top Takeaways From Colts' Loss Against Steelers: Is This Team Beyond Saving?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are back under .500 (2-3) after a 34-22 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers (3-2) in Week 5.
The Colts continued their poor history playing in Pittsburgh, with this loss marking their sixth consecutive road loss to the Steelers.
Perhaps you could chalk this loss up to fate, given that the Colts haven't left Pittsburgh victorious since Peyton Manning was leading the charge, but this loss in particular felt more like a Chris Ballard-era loss than anything else .
Indianapolis looks like the same disappointing product that Ballard and Co. have churned out throughout their tenure, and I'm breaking down why the Colts' most recent loss in Pittsburgh is more of an indictment of the regime's culture, or lack thereof, than anything else.
The Indianapolis Colts' offense has been average so far in 2026, and that's not what you want to see from a team whose head coach is in year four of overhauling that side of the ball.
Head coach Shane Steichen has been deemed one of the NFL's top offensive minds since he became an offensive coordinator, but his on-field product continues to leave a lot to be desired.
Steichen finally found his ideal quarterback in Daniel Jones to lead the Colts, but their offensive marriage has taken a drastic step back in their second season together.
The rushing attack has been underwhelming, the passing game ineffective, and as a result, the Colts have been trying to climb out of deficits they've helped create, as opposed to hanging onto leads they've established.
The Colts have been looking to reclaim their early-season efficiency from 2025, but too often, they have looked like a shell of themselves.
Starting quarterback Daniel Jones's lack of ball security has been a big reason the Colts' offense has been so inconsistent.
Jones and Co. did not turn the ball over against the Pittsburgh Steelers, which was a much-needed change of pace after the first four weeks, though they struggled in areas they've otherwise excelled in.
The Colts proved to be one of the most efficient red zone-scoring offenses through four weeks of play , but they took a step back in Pittsburgh.
Jones and Co. were just 1-3 on red zone opportunities against the Steelers, and stalling drives overall resulted in five (successful) field goal attempts from Spencer Shrader.
The Colts' offense scored just one touchdown against the Steelers, and now Shrader has accounted for 59% of the team's overall points output over the past three games.
Indianapolis' revolving door of subpar passcatchers has forced Daniel Jones to either hit tight end Tyler Warren in the flats, force-feed Josh Downs whenever the opportunity arises, or turn to longtime veteran Laquon Treadwell when the rough gets going.
Not having Alec Pierce has given us a Colts offense that features no legitimate downfield threat, and even though Indianapolis has tried to put a band-aid on said issue by signing veteran free agent Darius Slayton, injuries have thwarted their attempts altogether.
With a shrunken field to work with through the air, Jones and Co. have faced box-heavy opposing defenses who have made stopping running back Jonathan Taylor their top priority, and it's working.
Taylor did find success in Week 4 against the Commanders, rushing for 4.8 yards per carry and scoring two touchdowns on the ground, but too often, he has been kept at bay.
Jonathan Taylor has averaged less than four yards per carry in three of the Colts' five games so far in 2026, and has yet to notch a 100-yard rushing game.
Regardless of whose offensive scheme the Colts are working with, the offense has run through Jonathan Taylor in each of the six seasons since he was drafted in 2020.
If general manager Chris Ballard and Co. want to finally right the ship they've sunk on numerous occasions, opening up the offense with legitimate passcatchers is a must, though that now seems like an impossible task as we inch closer toward the trade deadline.
Lou Anarumo's Colts defense started off the 2026 campaign on a horrific note as they allowed the second-most yards of an NFL team through two games (1,029), but they started to trend upward after back-to-back wins in Weeks 3 and 4, two performances where they allowed just 540 total yards.
However, those two recent showings in question were also against two of the league's worst offenses.
The Colts beat up on an already uninspired Texans offense in Week 3, and their matchup saw Houston without their top two receiving options.
It was an even more lopsided matchup against the Commanders, as both top quarterbacks, Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota, were unavailable for the majority of the contest. Not only that, but Washington was also without their top receiving option in veteran wideout Terry McLaurin.
The Colts' defense allowed 352 yards of offense and 34 points against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 5, and they now look much closer to the first two-week version of themselves, as opposed to the latter half that had at least handled opposing offenses.
Expecting the Colts' defense to fully rebound after the opposing offenses they faced was never the right mindset , and their performance against the Pittsburgh Steelers reminded us why.
The linebacker room is full of subpar players, the secondary is comprised of strong coverage defenders but lacks playmakers, and the pass rush looks as nonexistent as it has throughout general manager Chris Ballard's tenure.
Anyone with a semblance of a pulse on the state of the Colts understands that this has been the case for the better part of the 2020s, but Chris Ballard's roster construction has reared its ugly head, perhaps more than thought possible.
The Indianapolis Colts entered their Week 5 matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers with a 2-2 record after putting together back-to-back wins against the Houston Texans and Washington Commanders.
However, despite establishing a small winning streak to even up their overall record, the Colts look as lost as they have under general manager Chris Ballard.
We are in year ten of the experiment, and a lack of enthusiasm and effort remains at the forefront of issues stemming from Ballard's reign.
Whenever there's been an inkling of adversity coming this era's way, the Colts have sat down and accepted their fate.
Against the Pittsburgh Steelers, these issues have once again reared their ugly head.
For example, the Steelers had history and prep time on their side entering Week 5's matchup. The Colts have failed to win in Pittsburgh since 2008, and the Steelers had ten days of rest going into it thanks to playing Thursday Night Football the week prior, while the Colts had a short turnaround after playing overseas.
Any other team may get the benefit of the doubt, but this regime is far past the art of excuses.
Indianapolis Colts Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon famously emphasized that general manager Chris Ballard, head coach Shane Steichen, and the rest of this regime are entering 2026 with a sense of urgency that has never been higher.
But through five weeks, any outsider would not see this version of the Colts as looking any different than they have for the past decade.
The Colts continue to seem destined for mediocrity, with their alleged playoff aspirations feeling like wishful thinking more than a convincing mindset.
It felt as if the Colts needed to at least make the playoffs and/or win the AFC South for Ballard and Co. to make right in the eyes of ownership, but now it seems like even a playoff win won't get the job done - that's how broken this team's outlook feels.
Indianapolis starting the season 2-3, especially with the way it's played out, is by no means shocking.
Honestly, it was expected, but the Colts have shown nothing through five games that suggests we can envision, let alone bank on, a collective rebound, and that should serve as a placeholder grasp of Ballard and Co.'s outlook.
The Indianapolis Colts desperately need to tear their entire operation down to the studs and rebuild, full stop.…

title: 2 Winners, 4 Losers From Colts' Disappointing Loss in Pittsburgh
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts had plenty of chances to leave Pittsburgh with their third straight win. They just could not finish enough drives to make it happen.
Indianapolis finished with 332 yards, turned the ball over zero times and punted just once, but went 4-of-15 on third down and 1-of-3 in the red zone in a 34-22 loss.
The offense certainly wasn't horrible. The defense, however, looked much closer to the group we saw during the first two weeks of the season.
That being said, we have a few more losers than winners this week.
This was exactly the kind of receiving performance Tyler Warren needed.
Warren hauled in seven passes for 83 yards while also punching in a one-yard rushing touchdown, once again showing this coaching staff will find just about any way possible to get the ball in his hands.
His usage continues to be one of the more interesting parts of this offense, and when Jonathan Taylor couldn't get going, Warren became one of Indianapolis' most reliable options.
At this point, Spencer Shrader has a legitimate argument as the best kicker in football.
Shrader went a perfect 5-for-5 on field goals, including makes from 57 and 56 yards, tying the Colts' franchise record for field goals made in a single game.
He is now 16-for-16 on field goals this season.
When nearly every Indianapolis drive stalled before reaching the end zone, Shrader made sure the Colts still walked away with points.
Pittsburgh's run defense was exactly as advertised.
Taylor finished with just 45 yards on 15 carries, and when he gets bottled up like this, life becomes considerably more difficult for the rest of Indianapolis' offense. Taylor also averaged a lowly 0.47 yards before contact, his 4th-worst showing of his career.
The Colts moved the ball relatively well between the 20's. They just couldn't finish drives, something Taylor is usually able to help them do.
Future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson said postgame that he feels the Colts' rushing attack is  "capable of so much more" than what they've been doing. Indy's offense goes as far as Taylor's legs will take them, and they need to get back to leaning on him if they want to make any noise in the playoffs, let alone make it that far.
Indianapolis desperately needed its pass rush to make Aaron Rodgers uncomfortable, and Laiatu Latu was largely ineffective as a pass rusher.
Latu finished with zero tackles, zero sacks and zero quarterback hits while generating just one pressure on 28 pass-rushing snaps.
Yes, Rodgers was getting the ball out quickly. But this secondary is already vulnerable enough without opposing quarterbacks having clean pockets.
Bryce Boettcher didn't play much, but made a couple key mistakes when he did.
With Jaylon Carlies sidelined, Boettcher missed multiple tackles on 14 defensive snaps, including one on Jaylen Warren's 80-yard touchdown reception.
Limited opportunities make every snap matter, and that one hurt.
This was a rough afternoon for Bernhard Raimann.
Five of Pittsburgh's 11 total pressures were attributed to the Colts' starting left tackle, another problem Indianapolis couldn't afford while already struggling to establish its rushing attack.
The Colts didn't lose this game because of one player or one position group. But against a Pittsburgh team that made Indianapolis earn everything, too many individual battles went the wrong way.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly from the Colts’ Defeat in Pittsburgh
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts couldn't keep pace with the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, falling 34-22 to drop to 2-3 on the season.
There were a few individual performances worth recognizing, but the loss exposed several issues that continue to hold Indianapolis back. The Colts left Pittsburgh with plenty to address on both sides of the ball heading into Week 6.
Here’s a look at the good, bad and ugly from Sunday's loss.
It’s never really a good thing when the kicker is any team’s best player on a given Sunday; Spencer Shrader was lights-out.
Shrader had one of the busiest games of his career in Pittsburgh, making his only extra point attempt and going a perfect 5-for-5 on field goal tries with makes coming from 22, 28, 40, 56 and 57. His 16 points scored in a game are the second-most of his career and the most in a game so far this season.
Shrader emerged as a legitimate weapon for the Colts in the first month of the season. With another excellent performance against the Steelers, Shrader is making great headway towards becoming one of the league’s elite.
The Colts offense didn’t have many bright spots. But Tyler Warren was one of the few.
Warren led all Colts pass catchers, logging seven receptions for a season-high 83 yards and added a rushing touchdown, the Colts’ only trip to the end zone all day. In addition, Warren made some crucial blocks in short yardage situations and had some key chip blocks to keep Daniel Jones upright in the pocket.
We haven’t seen Warren impact the passing game much so far this season, but Sunday was an exception. His blocking, however, has been strong all year. With a banged up wide receiver group, we could very well see a much busier Warren in the next few weeks.
Daniel Jones himself wasn’t all that spectacular. The Colts signal caller completed 24 or his 44 pass attempts for 264 yards. No touchdowns to speak of, but no turnovers either. That’s at least a step in the right direction for Jones.
Taking care of the football has been an issue for Jones this year. He’s turned the ball over seven times through five games, with four interceptions and three lost fumbles. Protecting the ball was the main point of emphasis for Jones going into Pittsburgh, and he executed in that regard.
It was especially nice to see Jones be smart with the football in a game where he could’ve easily gotten aggressive playing from behind and put the ball in harm’s way.
Instead, Jones only took calculated risks. If he can continue protecting the football like he did against Pittsburgh, then the Colts offense will have a much better chance to find a groove.
The first two weeks, the Colts’ tackling on defense was putrid. The defense missed 28 total tackles across eight quarters.
The second two weeks were much better, reducing that number to four. But in Week 5, the defense reverted back to old habits.
Both of Jaylen Warren’s touchdowns for the home team were the result of poor and downright lazy tackle attempts. On the first, Bryce Boettcher went low and whiffed and Charvarius Ward took a terrible angle to the ball, allowing Warren to take the ball 80 yards to the house.
The second was worse. Warren should’ve been taken down for a gain of a few. Instead, Akeem Davis-Gaither flung himself right past Warren, who slipped through DeForest Buckner’s desperation try and split two safeties to find the open field and finish off the 50-yard score.
Per Pro Football Focus, Indianapolis finished with 8 missed tackles in Week 5, the third-most in a game this season. To state the obvious, that simply can’t happen, especially for a defense with bigger issues to worry about.
The tackling dilemma was only a symptom of a larger problem. Indianapolis struggled mightily to shut down Warren and the run game.
Warren finished with 188 total yards and two touchdowns, 101 of those yards coming on the ground. As a team, the Steelers averaged almost six yards per carry (5.8), the most yards per rush allowed by the Colts defense this season.
Warren really only had the one explosive play, and killed the Colts gradually as the game went on by extending drives and keeping the defense on the field for several minutes at a time. Closing down running lanes and finishing plays were just too tall of tasks for the unit.
For a defense that showed real progress against Houston and Washington, Sunday's performance brought them back to the starting line. The Colts need to find a way to make opponents work harder for their rushing yards, because if they continue allowing teams to run the ball effectively, the rest of the defense will be left with little margin for error.
Indianapolis had just as many problems defending the pass as it did stopping the run. The main issue was the failure to consistently pressure Aaron Rodgers. The 42-year-old was sacked just once and posted a 125.1 passer rating.
Lou Anarumo's defensive philosophy typically relies on tight coverage to give the pass rush time to get home. When the secondary can make receivers work to get open, it allows the defensive front to disrupt the quarterback.
Against Pittsburgh, those two units weren't in sync. Rodgers had too much time to operate and was able to take advantage of the opportunities the Colts gave him.
For a defense that has struggled to generate consistent pressure this season, Sunday's performance was another reminder that the pass rush and secondary need to work in tandem. Indianapolis can't expect to contain opposing offenses if the coverage is too loose for the rush to make an impact, or if the front can't capitalize when the secondary does its job.
The Colts' red-zone offense was one of the biggest reasons they couldn't keep pace with Pittsburgh. Indianapolis went just 1-for-3 on red-zone trips, settling for field goals on multiple occasions when it needed touchdowns to keep up.
The biggest missed opportunity came early in the fourth quarter. After Jonathan Taylor ripped off a 20-yard run to put Indianapolis at the Pittsburgh 10-yard line, Daniel Jones threw three consecutive incompletions. The Colts settled for a 28-yard Spencer Shrader field goal, leaving points on the table at a critical point in the game.
Pittsburgh then promptly drove down the field and scored a touchdown to put the game out of reach.
That drive summed up the problem. Shrader did everything asked of him, but the Colts shouldn't have asked that much of their kicker. Settling for field goals when the opponent is finding pay dirt will never be a winning strategy.
The Colts' pass rush entered Sunday as a major concern, and the game offered little reason for optimism.
A banged-up group of pass rushers managed just one sack, giving Rodgers the time he needed to pick apart the secondary. Indianapolis struggled to consistently collapse the pocket or force the veteran quarterback into uncomfortable situations, allowing him to finish with a 125.1 passer rating. The injuries up front certainly didn't help, but the lack of pressure remains a problem this defense has yet to solve.
The Colts need more from their defensive front. Indianapolis has to find ways to make life uncomfortable for opposing passers. Until that happens consistently, even improved coverage will have a difficult time holding up, and quarterbacks will continue to feast.
The Colts' passing game struggled to find consistency in Pittsburgh, and the injuries Indianapolis dealt with at wide receiver certainly didn't help.
Alec Pierce's absence still looms large. The Colts needed more from the rest of their receiving corps without him, but didn't get much. Josh Downs finished with three catches, while Laquon Treadwell caught just two of his eight targets.
Tyler Warren was a bright spot, leading Indianapolis with seven catches for 83 yards and adding a one-yard rushing touchdown, but the Colts can't rely on their star tight end to carry the passing game on his own.
The injuries provide some context for the struggles, but can't be an excuse. Indianapolis still needs more from the players…

title: 3 Matchups That Could Make or Break the Colts in Pittsburgh
full_text:
For whatever reason, the Indianapolis Colts just do not play well when they travel to Pittsburgh.
The Colts haven't won in Pittsburgh since 2008, including a 27-20 loss at Acrisure Stadium last season. But this time around, Indianapolis has a pretty clean path to finally ending that drought.
Both teams enter Sunday at 2-2, with Indianapolis sitting as a 2.5-point underdog ahead of the 1 p.m. ET kickoff on CBS.
This game should come down to creating pressure and forcing the other quarterback to make mistakes.
Here are three matchups that could decide it.
This one is pretty simple: Make Aaron Rodgers move.
Indianapolis enters Sunday with a 35% pass-rush win rate, which ranks dead last in the entire NFL, via ESPN. They are lined up against Pittsburgh's 10th-ranked pass-blocking unit, and generating pressure has to be the priority.
Rodgers has completed 88 of 153 passes for 999 yards, seven touchdowns and four interceptions, but he has already been sacked 13 times.
And at 42 years old, he isn't exactly escaping the pocket and turning broken plays into 20-yard gains anymore. Rodgers has just seven rushing attempts for 12 yards this season.
If the Colts can consistently win up front and force Rodgers to extend plays with his legs, Pittsburgh's offense becomes significantly more uncomfortable.
The formula isn't complicated. Get Rodgers off his spot, make him move and force him into poor decisions.
Gardner has himself a prove-it game after what happened in London.
He allowed four catches on five targets for 117 yards and a touchdown against Washington, including completions of 47 and 48 yards. Gardner later called his performance "unacceptable," and Sunday gives him an immediate opportunity to respond.
His job is usually pretty simple: Take away the opponent's No. 1 receiver.
This week, that means DK Metcalf.
Metcalf has 16 catches for 213 yards and a touchdown through four games, and he is coming off a 115-yard performance against Cleveland.
Indianapolis absolutely cannot allow Rodgers and Metcalf to get comfortable, especially on the deep ball. Gardner gave up a couple big shots in London, and I would imagine he is itching to pitch a shutout this time around.
This might be the most important matchup of the afternoon.
Jones has been far too careless with the football through four weeks, throwing four interceptions while also putting the ball on the ground multiple times.
Watt already has 4.5 sacks, a forced fumble, a fumble recovery and even a pick-six this season. If Jones gets careless with the football again Sunday, Watt is exactly the kind of player who will make him pay for it.
Jones has to know where No. 90 is at all times.
Get the ball out quickly or roll out to Watt's opposite side. Just don't give him the opportunity to completely wreck the game.
Indianapolis does not need to complicate its game plan this Sunday. Pressure Rodgers, don't let Metcalf beat you deep and keep Watt away from the football.
The formula is right in front of Indianapolis. Now it's a matter of executing it in a stadium that has given this franchise problems for nearly two decades.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts-Steelers Final Injury Report: Who’s In and Who’s Out for Week 5?
full_text:
The final injury reports are in ahead of the Colts and Steelers’ Week 5 clash on Sunday. Both teams go into the weekend with different questions they each need answered before kickoff as they each look to improve to 3-2 on the year.
Let’s take a look at both teams’ reports, determine who’s likely to play, who’s likely to sit out and what each injury means going into an important early-season bout between two conference foes.
Indianapolis Colts Final Injury Report
Indianapolis rules out four players, with no true surprises. That said, the Colts will be down two starters on defense. Defensive end Arden Key is expected to miss multiple games with his hamstring injury, with this week being the first. Linebacker Jaylon Carlies, who had an interception for the Colts last week, also suffered a rib injury that will keep him out of this Sunday’s contest.
Expect plenty of rookie action on Sunday as a result of these knocks. CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher to both take snaps at linebacker while the edge duo of Caden Curry and George Gumbs Jr. should see some playing time as well. Gumbs is yet to suit up for an NFL game, so his professional debut could be on the horizon.
Ashton Dulin will miss his third game of the season already, so the Colts will have to make things work on special teams without their top gunner. Tight end Will Mallory just had his 21-day practice window opened on Wednesday after starting the season on injured reserve, but him being ruled out against Pittsburgh proves the Colts are using an abundance of caution with him moving forward.
Center Tanor Bortolini went from limited on Wednesday to a full participant Thursday, and now logged another full practice Friday. He enters the weekend without an injury designation and will start. That’s an underrated development, as Indy’s offensive line has been stellar through the first month and losing continuity would be a big hit to the unit’s current positive momentum.
There’s three Colts listed as questionable this week, with two wide receivers. Keenan Allen is questionable for the second week in a row, but completed a full practice on Friday, which is a significant step towards suiting up this weekend. Darius Slayton is a new addition to the injury report late in the week having been limited on Friday with a knee injury. Given the issue appears to have just popped up, Slayton may have to wait yet another week to make his Colts debut.
Cornerback Charvarius Ward is trending towards playing. After two straight days being limited, Ward was a full participant in the week’s final session. The questionable tag does add a little uncertainty, but a week of progress indicates Ward should be good to go.
Finally, it’s worth noting that defensive tackle DeForest Buckner did not practice Friday due to rest. No reason to worry about the veteran, though, as he doesn’t have any injury designation.
Overall, the final report for Indianapolis could’ve been much longer. Twelve different names showed up on the practice report this week, but only seven enter Week 5 with a designation. The possibility of being down three wide receivers is far from ideal, making that group the main on to monitor ahead of Sunday. On the practice squad, the Colts could turn to Nick Westbrook-Ikhine like they did last week should they need extra bodies.
For defensive practice squad elevations, Carl Lawson is likely to get the nod. WIthout Key, the Colts defensive end room lacks significant experience, so getting the 31-year-old into the mix could prove beneficial.
Pittsburgh Steelers Final Injury Report
Not as long a final list for the Steelers, but a top-heavy report. Worst case scenario, Pittsburgh could be without four starters. Michael Pittman Jr.’s foot injury got worse throughout the week, so he won’t be playing his former team. No Jamel Dean hurts the secondary, especially with Jalen Ramsey also carrying a questionable tag. If both can’t go, the Steelers will have to turn to their backup cornerbacks Daylen Everette and Sean Murphy-Bunting, who was signed off the Buccaneers’ practice squad earlier in the week.
Safety DeShon Elliott’s 21-day practice window was opened this week but he’s yet to be activated off injured reserve, so he’s unavailable to dress until that transaction occurs.
Rico Dowdle was limited all week and is officially questionable with the toe injury that’s kept him out of Pittsburgh’s last two contests as well.
Comparing the two reports, I’d give the Steelers a slight advantage, although Pittsburgh’s secondary concerns and Indy’s injuries at wide receiver make for an interesting storyline entering the game. Those matchups on the outside could have a major influence on the eventual outcome, so how effectively each team takes advantage of the other’s personnel concerns could be a deciding factor.

title: Colts Are Keeping Themselves Alive By Dominating In These Key Areas
full_text:
Despite having as many wins as they have losses, the Indianapolis Colts have gotten off to a rocky start to the 2026 regular season.
The 2-2 Colts struggled immensely on defense to start the year, specifically during the team's first two matchups against the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs, but have since found their footing with back-to-back wins over the Houston Texans and Washington Commanders.
However, both the Texans and Commanders sported subpar offensive units, with injuries giving the Colts advantages defensively, so there's reason to believe they'll go back to struggling against more respectable offenses.
Furthermore, the Colts' offense has largely kept them in each of their four games so far in 2026, though inconsistency sprouting from turnovers and a revolving door of pass-catching options has kept them from putting together an efficient operation.
With that said, the Colts have managed to, for the most part, stay competitive through one month of regular-season play thanks to their top-tier execution in a few areas of the game that are typically overlooked.
Without further ado, let's break down the three areas in question where the Colts are raising their overall floor.
The Indianapolis Colts have struggled to replicate their efficient output from a season ago through four weeks of the 2026 regular season, but when they've gotten into the red zone, it's almost a guarantee that they're scoring.
According to Sumer Sports via Locked On Colts' Zach Hicks, the Colts' offense ranks in the following red zone categories entering Week 5:
3rd in total EPA (Expected Points Added) 4th in EPA/play 5th in overall success rate 5th in EPA/pass 4th in pass success rate 3rd in EPA/rush
According to Team Rankings, the Colts rank 6th in the NFL in red zone touchdown rate. Indianapolis is scoring a touchdown on 75% of its red zone trips.
Head coach Shane Steichen's Colts offense doesn't have an issue with scoring in the red zone; they have a problem getting into red zone territory altogether.
They are tied for the 17th-most red zone scoring attempts (3.0 per game) with several teams, which shows that they have untapped potential offensively.
If starting quarterback Daniel Jones can limit his turnovers, and if pass protection gets sorted out, the Colts' offense can begin to unlock its potential.
Fourth-year special teams coordinator Brian Mason has only improved his unit with each year in Indianapolis.
So far in 2026, the Colts' special teams unit looks like one of the best in the entire NFL - and that's without having longtime special teams ace Ashton Dulin available for half of their games.
Mason made the impossible decision of choosing between Spencer Shrader and Blake Grupe to become the team's starting kicker before the regular season arrived, and his choice has aged flawlessly.
Spencer Shrader was named the Colts' starting kicker ahead of the season after dominating the team's preseason slate, and he's gotten off to a tremendous start in 2026.
Shrader missed his first kick of the new year, an extra point attempt in the team's season opener, but has been perfect since going 11-for-11 on field goal attempts.
The Colts' kicker has nailed each of his four 50+ yard attempts so far this season, including a 53-yard game-winner against the Houston Texans in Week 3, and the special teams unit as a whole (kickoff, punt, etc.) has been just as effective.
Indianapolis's rookie class has been a strong injection of talent to the special teams unit, with running back Seth McGowan flashing as a kick returner, and defenders Caden Curry and Bryce Boettcher showing up on kickoffs.
The Indianapolis Colts still have some things to clean up if they want to be treated as legitimate playoff contenders, but their special teams operation is not one of them.
The Indianapolis Colts have been the most disciplined team in the NFL through one month of regular-season play.
According to Tru Media analytics via Rotowire's Ian Hartitz, the Colts have been flagged for the fewest penalties on both sides of the ball through four weeks.
Colts have been flagged for the fewest penalties on offense *and* defense this season pic.twitter.com/1FyN2lIPmo
There's been plenty to critique so far this season, but playing disciplined football has not been one of them.
If anything, the Colts' disciplined play has been one of the main reasons they're sitting with a 2-2 record entering Week 5.
Football is a game of inches and margins, and the Colts' success in these three areas has allowed them to stay afloat as they iron out their deficiencies on both sides of the ball.

title: 3 Burning Questions Facing the Colts Heading Into Pittsburgh
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are back to .500 after winning two straight, but there are still some major questions surrounding this team heading into Pittsburgh.
The defense has taken a noticeable step forward. The offense has not, and Daniel Jones suddenly looks nothing like the quarterback Indianapolis saw last season.
Here are three questions the Colts need to answer against the Steelers.
Just to put it blatantly, Jones has not been good enough through the first month of the season.
He has completed 63.6% of his passes for 754 yards, three touchdowns and four interceptions, while also losing three fumbles. He has now thrown an interception in all four games.
That is a massive change from the quarterback Indianapolis watched last season, when Jones threw 19 touchdowns to eight interceptions, added five scores on the ground and finished with a 100.2 passer rating before tearing his Achilles.
The Colts gave Jones a two-year, $88 million deal this offseason that can climb toward $100 million with incentives because they believed that version of him was real.
Maybe we are expecting too much from a quarterback who returned roughly nine months after tearing his Achilles. Or maybe Jones' 2025 performance was simply an outlier?
Kirk Cousins struggled with inconsistency after returning from the same injury, so there is at least some recent precedent for a quarterback needing time to completely look like himself again.
Either way, Indianapolis needs Jones to start taking care of the football. If this becomes Giants DJ again, the Colts are in trouble.
Indianapolis allowed 41 points against Baltimore and 33 against Kansas City.
Since then? Seventeen against Houston and 13 against Washington.
That is progress, but I am not completely sold yet.
Houston is still searching for its first win of the season, and Washington was eventually forced to turn to seventh-round rookie Athan Kaliakmanis after Marcus Mariota left the game with a knee injury.
The defense looks much better, but I still want to see what happens when Indianapolis desperately needs a stop against an offense capable of putting real pressure on them.
Another storyline to watch is CJ Allen.
The Colts' first selection in April's draft has played just 11 defensive snaps through four games and did not see the field defensively in London. At some point, Lou Anarumo has to start easing the No. 53 overall pick into the rotation.
The Colts desperately need somebody who can stretch the field.
Jones averaged 8.1 yards per attempt last season. That number has fallen to 5.7 this year, and Alec Pierce's absence has completely changed the complexion of this passing attack.
That is where Slayton could come in.
The veteran has averaged roughly 15 yards per reception throughout his career and already has extensive history with Jones, catching 200 passes for 2,912 yards and 12 touchdowns with him in New York.
Slayton has yet to play a regular-season snap for Indianapolis, but said this week that he feels ready to go against Pittsburgh.
There is no guarantee he becomes the missing piece immediately, but the Colts need somebody who can threaten defenses vertically and give Jones a reliable veteran target in big moments.
Two straight wins have put Indianapolis back on track, but until these questions are answered, it is hard to know just how good this Colts team really is.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 4 Colts Rookies Who Could See More Playing Time Against Steelers
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' front office focused on injecting youth, speed, and experience via the draft into their roster for the 2026 season, and throughout four regular-season games so far, it looks like they've achieved that goal.
However, the Colts' eight rookies in question have hardly gotten an opportunity to show their worth . They've shown up when they've been called upon, but their number has only been called in spurts.
As a result of injuries to key starters, specifically on the defensive side of the ball, numerous Colts rookies have been granted a massive opportunity ahead of Indianapolis's Week 5 road matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
The Colts have historically struggled against the Steelers, and they haven't won in Pittsburgh since Peyton Manning was still leading the charge (2008), so this will be a tough environment for the rookies, but they'll take anything they can get as budding NFL contributors.
With that being said, let's break down the Colts' rookie defenders in question who are primed for an increased workload in Week 5.
The Indianapolis Colts infamously missed out on the Trey Hendrickson sweepstakes earlier this offseason, and this caused them to pivot their construction of their new-look pass rush by adding low-risk veterans and rookies as a result.
Veterans Arden Key and Micheal Clemons were brought in to replace the longtime rotational trio of Kwity Paye, Samson Ebukam, and Tyquan Lewis, but they're both out for the foreseeable future with injuries.
The Colts finished their defensive line room by drafting rookies George Gumbs Jr. and Caden Curry in the fifth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, but only the latter has seen any playing time through four weeks, and even then, Curry has mainly been a special teams contributor.
With Key and Clemons' injuries causing them to miss time, it'll be second-year defensive end Jaylahn Tuimoloau filling the void in the starting unit.
However, Curry and Gumbs Jr. both serve as the man up.
Veteran Carl Lawson was signed to the Colts' practice squad earlier this week, reuniting him with defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo from their days together in Cincinnati.
Lawson may very well see a gameday elevation to the active roster, given that Anarumo tends to favor familiarity and proven experience, but don't count out the rookie duo in question from getting some more run.
Defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo has been rolling with veterans Akeem Davis-Gaither and Jaylon Carlies as his starting linebacker tandem through four weeks, but injuries to both players have opened the door for rookies CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher.
Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee) did not practice on Tuesday but was a full participant on Wednesday; therefore, it's likely we still see him suit up on Sunday, but his place in the defense remains to be seen.
Davis-Gaither has served as the defense's green dot since Week 2, but now could be a worthwhile opportunity to have CJ Allen take over the MIKE linebacker role that Anarumo, Steichen, and Ballard all envisioned he'd become, and slide Davis-Gaither over to WILL linebacker.
Jaylon Carlies (ribs) has missed both practices ahead of the Colts' Week 5 matchup against the Steelers, putting him at risk of missing the game altogether.
If Davis-Gaither plays and Carlies is out, Anarumo may look to start Bryce Boettcher alongside Davis-Gaither, as the spot Carlies plays - WILL linebacker - is the role that Boettcher was envisioned to play.
However, there's still a chance that Anarumo and Co. look to ramp up Allen's workload by starting him at the WILL linebacker spot.
We'll have to see what Friday's practice brings in terms of gameday availability, but it's trending toward at least one rookie linebacker getting some serious first-team run for the first time this season.
