title: Shipley's Dozen: 12 Takes on Jaguars' Wacky Win Over Eagles, Parker Washington and More
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are no strangers to wacky games with heart-stopping ends, but Week 5 was something else.
The Jaguars managed to simply find a way to win against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5 in a thrilling 19-17 walkoff , but there was, well, a lot that happened between the first snap and the last one. We break down one of the craziest Jaguars games in recent memory in this week's Shipley's Dozen column.
I can say with confidence that I do not believe Parker Washington is going anywhere. That is not due to some insight or knowledge of his pending contract negotiations with the Jaguars. Instead, it is due to the fact that it becomes clearer and clearer with each passing game that the Jaguars' offense would likely be in big trouble without Washington. He is the Jaguars' top pass-catcher for so many reasons, but the most important one might be trust. Just look at the play he makes on his second touchdown, and look at the trust it took between him and Trevor Lawrence to make that play happen.
Washington is going to be a key piece of the Jaguars for a long time because, simply because it is not really possible to envision a Jaguars offense without him. Those are the kinds of players this regime does not let leave the building.
An unbelievably clutch play from Parker Washington. @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/C7Y6hQ0Coc
I thought the first half of football from the Jaguars' defense had some good things, but the two touchdowns they allowed were simply drives that should not happen considering the state of the Eagles' offense. The depleted Eagles put together a first-half scoring drive that ended with a two-yard Will Shipley touchdown, and the real issues for the Jaguars were on third-down. The Jaguars allowed conversions on 3rd-and-8, 3rd-and-10, and then 3rd-and-17 in the red-zone due to a Travis Hunter pass interference call. Add in a 62-yard touchdown allowed to Darius Cooper shortly thereafter, and the Jaguars had work to do.
But the second half went much differently. The Eagles gained just three first downs on their first six drives of the second-half, with five of those drives ending in punts and one ending in a turnover on downs. The Jaguars were especially effective in the fourth quarter, forcing three three-and-outs and allowing just three net yards on the first three drives of the game. The Jaguars did see the Eagles have a short drive for a field goal, but it was a nine-play drive that barely averaged four yards per play. The defense was perhaps the biggest reason the Jaguars won this game.
This has to be the biggest present concern for the Jaguars. They do have some offensive tackle depth, as evidenced by Walker Little stepping in and playing well during the second-half of the game. But Anton Harrison was carted off with a knee injury, and there was not much of an update for the Jaguars' blindside protector on Monday other than Liam Coen noting that he got an MRI but no results yet. Harrison missing extended time while Cole Van Lanen also goes through some of his own struggles would be bad timing with the Houston Texans coming up, and it would also mean the Jaguars would have to lean into offensive line depth like Daniel Faalele and, eventually, Patrick Mekari to help fill-in.
Jalen Huskey did not play a single defensive snap on Sunday, which seems ... odd. The Jaguars had Rayuan Lane fill in for Eric Murray and the second-year safety played 100% of the defensive snaps, while Kaevon Merriweather served as the third safety and played 21% of the snaps. Even with two safeties out with Murray and Ransaw, Huskey still didn't see the field. The Jaguars can get better production out of safety than they did on Sunday, and moving toward Huskey as at least the third safety could go a long way toward making that happen.
The Jaguars have long had a strong red-zone offense under head coach Liam Coen, but it was simply all over the place on Sunday. I think penalties were the biggest issue on the day, such as the false starts and delay of games. But I also think those are self-inflicted mistakes that the Jaguars can fix with improved execution. To me, the real concern in the red-zone was the fact that the Jaguars let Jalen Carter completely wreck the game. Carter is one of the highest-paid defenders in all of football for a reason, after all, but it felt like the Jaguars' inability to run the ball at Carter is what led to the ill-fated Bhayshul Tuten fly sweep. If the Jaguars can't block elite defensive linemen when they need just a few yards, that will be an issue that doesn't just go away or work itself out.
I have long considered the London games to be road games for the Jaguars, no matter how they are classified on the schedule. The Jaguars have to make their longest trip of the year to play the game, disrupting entire weeks of work in the process, and then they do not have a homefield advantage in any shape or form come game time. This was truer than ever against the Eagles, with the game feeling like an Eagles home came considering the crowd noise, especially when the Jaguars were inside the red-zone. Despite the Jaguars upheaving their travel plans for London each year, it is still a tough road test. That is an odd sense of irony that could come into play again next week against the Texans.
The Jaguars do not win this game without Heath Farwell's unit. The Jaguars did miss one extra point, but the Jaguars made all of their other kicks despite punter/holder Logan Cooke having to adjust to some high snaps from backup long-snapper Davon Hamilton and he was just one of several impressive special teamers. The Jaguars also saw Josh Cameron return a kick for a nullified touchdown, Cam Little make a 57-yard walk-off, and Ameer Abdullah and the kickoff return team producing one of the most important special teams plays of the last few years with his fourht-quarter kick return. Heath Farwell should wear this game proudly.
I was surprised the Jaguars went with man coverage as often as they did. They went away from it a bit after the first-half, but it was a big reason the Jaguars allowed a 62-yard touchdown to Darius Cooper. The way to beat Jalen Hurts is by using zone coverage to muddy the picture in the secondary, while man coverage provides him with the ready-made answers he needs. The Jaguars adjusted well, but they paid for it a bit at the start of the game. Man coverage allowed some of the biggest plays of the day, which is a stark contrast from other weeks in the season.
The Jaguars' defensive line playing well. They completely shut down the Eagles' rushing attack, while Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker combined for 10 pressures and four quarterback hits. The Jaguars had an easier matchup this week considering the state of the Eagles' offensive line, but they also did what they needed to when it came to taking advantage of the matchup. I thought this might have been the best game the Jaguars' front has had this year, and this comes a week after I thought the same thing.
Davon Hamilton. That's the tweet.
Jaguars walk off win in improbable fashion with game-winning Cam Little 57-yard field goal + backup long snapper Davon Hamilton: pic.twitter.com/BXhZmb9aSG
It says a lot about the AFC South that a 1-4 team is pretty easily still the second-best team in the division, but that is the case through five weeks. The Indianapolis Colts dropped to 2-3 after a loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers, and even with their win over Houston a week ago I do not think anyone can confidently say the Colts pose a larger threat to the Jaguars than the Texans do after Week 5. Perhaps that is because the Texans are next up on the Jaguars' schedule , but it very much so feels like the Texans are a better team as a whole than the Colts are.
8️⃣0️⃣ YARDS TO THE HOUSE @Nunless2 pic.twitter.com/veiSAV9F4M
The Texans still have their fair share of flaws, of course. Their win over the Tennessee Titans was expected in every…

title: 3 Things We Learned About the Jaguars vs. the Eagles: Trevor Lawrence's Fire
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars had to pull out all of the stops for their fourth win of the season, but they made it happen in Week 5.
The Jaguars survived an upset attempt from the Philadelphia Eagles thanks to Cam Little hitting a walkoff 57-yard field goal in a 19-17 win. But what did we learn from the Jaguars' narrow win, and what could it all mean moving forward?
Trevor Lawrence did a lot of good things on Sunday sans his second-half interception. He was faced with plenty of unfavorable 2nd- and 3rd-and-long situations due to the penalties for the second week in a row, but he made so many plays in and out of structure that helped the Jaguars move the ball. Had the Jaguars figured things out in the red-zone, the score would have more so reflected the performance that Lawrence had. But among all other things, Lawrence also showed some of the maturation as the general of the offense when he, well, was irate after yet another red-zone penalty.
Trevor Lawrence CRASHED OUT on his center 😭 pic.twitter.com/bUC2oV1z3Y
It was a sign of Lawrence's fire that, frankly, needed to be shown considering the situation. I have covered every single game of Lawrence's NFL career, and I never once saw him quite so frustrated and then let the rest of the offense know about it. Lawrence is a cool, calm and collected type of leader, and this isn't something he would have done a few years ago at least not in my eyes. Call it the Liam Coen impact, call it the natural growth of a franchise quarterback, but Lawrence showed the fire that many thought he was missing entering the NFL.
"I do like seeing him have that fire and that, you know, competitive edge. You know, he wants it to be good. He wants the operation to be clean. I think there was a lot of frustrations throughout that game that probably built up to be more emotional in that moment," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Monday
I thought Parker Washington had the best game of any Jaguars skill player, which is easy to say with two touchdowns and over 120 receiving yards. Washington is far and away the clear Jaguars' No. 1 receiver, even with his one-catch game in Week 4 in the rear view window. But after Washington, I think we are starting to see a second player establish himself on the Jaguars' pecking order in the passing game: Brenton Strange.
Over the last three weeks, Strange leads the Jaguars with 21 targets, 17 receptions and 195 yards despite ranking third on the team in routes in that span with 75. Strange has been effective for the Jaguars aside from a few uncharacteristic drops in that span. His increase in volumn does not seem like an accident, though, especially considering most teams are better at defending passes out wide than they are in the middle of the field.
Washington is the clear No. 1. Brian Thomas Jr. clearly is a small part of the offense. Jakobi Meyers has, so far, felt more like an auxilary option other than in Week 3. I think Strange is the No. 2 pass-catcher in the offense right now.
The Jaguars simply have to sort out their penalty issues. Some flags have certainly been silly calls by the officials, but some have been purely the Jaguars' fault. It is not the fault of the officials if the Jaguars are getting false starts and delay of games, which has happened far too often over the last two weeks especially. "The penalties are concerning when you start the season off in the first three weeks as the second-least penalized team in the NFL, and now over the last two weeks, we're arguably one of the most penalized teams in the NFL," Coen said.
The Jaguars have won each of their last 2 games despite 26 total penalties. They are the first team since the Seahawks in Weeks 10 and 11 of the 2011 season to win consecutive games with 13+ penalties in each game. Penalties are the major reason why the last two wins have had to come in one-score games, and the Jaguars simply have to figure out how to play cleaner football in all three phases. Penalties alone have wiped out three touchdowns and an interception for the Jaguars in the last two weeks. What happens when this happens against a good team and not just the Bengals or Eagles?

title: 5 Winners, 5 Losers From Jaguars' Close Win Over Eagles: Cam Little Wasn't the Only Game-Changer
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars just won one of the wackiest football games you will see in 2026, if not longer than that.
"One of the craziest games, maybe the craziest games I've ever been a part of, and I've been in some pretty wild ones," Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence said after the 19-17 last-second win over the Philadelphia Eagles.
"Just how cool is this sport? The game's never over, and I think the belief from our team, man, obviously didn't look great there at the end, but just the belief of our kickoff return unit, Ameer [Abdullah] being smart, breaking through, and still getting down at the second. So many things had to happen, right? I felt like we finally got a break at the end of the game, and that play went our way. Obviously, we had some bad stuff we've got to clean up. But just keep playing. It's not always going to be pretty. That's this league. It's tough to win. So, when you can win them, especially like that, you've got to enjoy it.
So, which players had the biggest hand in the Jaguars' dramatic win over the Eagles? And which players saw their stock maybe go down as a result of the game? We break it all down below.
Parker Washington had one of the best games in his entire career on Sunday, catching two touchdowns and hitting 124 yards in the process. Washington won on contested catches in the red-zone, after the catch in space, tough coordination catches near the sidelines, and seemingly everything in between. It has become clear that Washington is the alpha male of the Jaguars' passing attack, and he took it a step further on Sunday considering the stakes that came with both of his touchdowns.
Cam Little was terrific for the Jaguars on Sunday. He did miss an extra point that I think you can likely chalk up to the fact that the Jaguars had some errant snaps from backup long-snapper Davon Hamilton. But Little having the ice in his veins to make the 57-yard game-winner was everything the Jaguars have always needed from him. He has hit some big kicks before, but this one ensured the Jaguars enter Week 6 with a three-game lead over the Texans instead of a two-game lead.
Davon Hamilton was once again one of the Jaguars' most important players. Yes, he stepped in for the Jaguars im some big moments when thrust into the action as the long-snapper. But Hamilton once again had a terrific outing as the Jaguars' nose tackle that really set the tone. Hamilton manhandled the Eagles' offensive line on several reps in both the run and pass game, and it is fair to say the Jaguars do not win without his contributions on both defense and special teams.
Take away his interception, and I think Sunday was another good performance from Trevor Lawrence. He was under siege all day by a talented Eagles' defensive line and one of the best defensive coordinators in the NFL, but he managed to make big throws for the Jaguars on each of the game's most important drives. His second touchdown pass to Parker Washington is one of the best passes he has thrown all season long, and Lawrence was the biggest reason the Jaguars were in a position to win this game. Had the Jaguars not goofed on two red-zone trips, the score would have looked better to reflect the kind of performance that Lawrence had.
You can't talk about this win and not mention Ameer Abdullah , who is on his seventh team in 12 seasons. Abdullah has found a home in Jacksonville, though, and has been active in every single game despite the Jaguars having the No. 1 through No. 3 running back spots locked up. The Jaguars do not win this game without Abdullah's stellar kick return on the second-to-last play of the game, and he has earned the full-time kick returner role next to Josh Cameron.
Brian Thomas Jr. did not catch a pass for the first time in his entire career on Sunday. He was targeted three times, but one resulted in an interception after Trevor Lawrence underthrew the ball while getting hit. The other two targets came in the end-zone, and Thomas was not able to come up with either pass for a touchdown. He was out-produced in the passing game on Sunday by Travis Hunter, Nate Boerkircher, and Chris Rodriguez Jr. Things have just not panned out for him this season.
The Jaguars turned to Rayuan Lane to replace an injured Eric Murray on Sunday, and he certainly did not have the kind of game that will bring much confidence from those outside of the Jaguars' building. Lane had a good game against the run and as a blitzer, but it felt like he was getting picked on at times in coverage, and he also took a few angles that expose some of his flaws as a defender in space.
Anton Harrison lands here this week after being carted off the field with a knee injury in the third-quarter. The Jaguars' offensive line had its own share of issues in Week 5, but Harrison had appeared to be playing the best of any of the Jaguars' offensive linemen. If Harrison misses any extended time for the Jaguars, this is a very significant loss in both the run and the passing game. Harrison is the Jaguars' most talented offensive lineman, and his injury will be a big storyline to watch before they face the Texans' pass-rush next week.
The Jaguars saw Montaric Brown return for Sunday's game after missing last week's contest against the Bengals with an injury. It did not turn out to be the return anyone likely hoped, though, with Brown losing on the 62-yard touchdown allowed to Darius Cooper. Brown did not play another snap in the game, either, with the veteran cornerback getting re-added to the Jaguars' growing injury list in the secondary. It has become a season to forget so far for Brown.
There just was not much out there for Chris Rodriguez Jr. on Sunday. He did have a key block on Ameer Abdullah's kick return before Cam Little's game-winning kick, but he also had a few not-so-great reps on offense. He very nearly fumbled the ball at the goal line before the end of the half, though I think he gets a semi-pass considering the Jaguars never scored on that drive anyway. But the offense just looked out of sorts each time the Jaguars had him as the focus over Bhayshul Tuten, and his missed block on fourth-down at the end of the first half is the main reason Tuten didn't score.

title: Ameer Abdullah's Signature Moment Becomes Latest Example of Jaguars' Maturation
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are 4-1, and it took every single member of the active roster to make it happen in Week 5.
That included veteran running back Ameer Abdullah, who quietly made one of the biggest plays of the season with his fourth-quarter 53-yard kick return to set up a game-winning field goal in the Jaguars' 19-17 win over the Eagles. In the process, he became the latest example of the Jaguars' maturation as a franchise.
Abdullah's kick return set the Jaguars and kicker Cam Little up to win the game with a 57-yard field goal , and it showed all of the things that have made Abdullah valuable since the Jaguars signed him as a free agent late in the offseason: toughness, smarts, experience, and an ability to still make explosive plays. The fact that Abdullah had the burst to get the ball where he did is impressive. The fact he knew to get down with one second left is even more impressive.
JAGS HUGE KICK RETURN. They're in range for one more shot at a field goal! @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XSWbKBTvW2
Abdullah was seen as an afterthought perhaps externally when the Jaguars signed him, but he had stellar performances in training camp and the preseason to put himself in a position to make the Jaguars' roster. He is amongst the oldest and most experienced players on the roster, and he has clearly made his impact felt.
"He's that dude. He's one of the first in the building every single day, him and Parker. Ameer, to get in our building this spring, Ameer had four votes -- four or five votes to be a captain. He made such an impression on this team right away, right from the beginning," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game.
"He takes care of his body, takes care of his mind. He prepares to be a starter. He's been one of the best teammates. He's just such a great human being and a guy that I cannot say enough about, has gone through so much in this last six months actually. I pray for him. I love him to death. I'm so happy that he's a Jaguar, and I'm very proud of him today."
This Jaguars regime has mastered finding edges by uncovering diamonds in the rough, something that the best franchises do every single year. Their scouting shows up not just in the win-loss column, but in the fact that players like Abdullah have continued to help the Jaguars pick up wins during the Liam Coen era, which has seen the Jaguars go 17-5 in 22 regular-season games.
The Jaguars have been one of the NFL's best franchises since Coen, general manager James Gladstone, and executive vice president of football operations Tony Boselli took over, and Abdullah has become the latest example of why they have thrived. Abdullah had touched the ball 18 times (12 on offense, six kick returns) before Sunday, but he was always ready. Despite having a marginal role, he proved to be a difference-maker between the Jaguars being 4-1 and the Jaguars being 3-2.
Abdullah is far from the only diamond in the rough the Jaguars have mined. Sixth-round receiver Josh Cameron is another one. LeQuint Allen, Quintin Morris, Dennis Gardeck, Danny Striggow, BJ Green, and Matt Dickerson a year ago, too. The Jaguars have proven that they can fill the back-end of their active roster with talented players who can help them win games, which is what allows them to make moves like contract extensions and the Travis Hunter trade.
The Jaguars have matured into a real-deal football team. They are doing the things that the best franchises have always done, and Abdullah is a shining example of why it is working.

title: Game Balls from Jaguars' Nailbiter vs. Eagles: Unlikely Hero Emerges
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- There are team wins, and then there is whatever the heck just happened between the Jacksonville Jaguars and Philadelphia Eagles in London.
The Jaguars had their entire active roster step in and make an impact in Sunday's 19-17 last-second win over the Eagles , making it the kind of performance where every single player on the roster can confidently say they left their fingerprints on it.
"Mental toughness. It's kind of what we talked about all week, staying the course. One second left on the clock, guys competing to the end when things weren't really going your way," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game. "It wasn't clean, a lot of penalties, didn't execute in the red zone. Let them off the hook a lot on third and long. It just was a weird kind of vibe game, weird. Guys stayed the course and made plays, we had D-Ham [DaVon Hamilton] snapping again. It was just kind of wild we were in that position. Nobody flinched. Nobody blinked. Nobody blamed. Guys stayed the course and ended up squeaking away with a win."
So, which Jaguars deserve game balls for their performances against the Eagles? We break it down below.
This one was relatively easy. An argument could be made for Trevor Lawrence, of course, but Parker Washington was a one-man wrecking crew against the Eagles. Washington led the Jaguars in receiving for the third time in five games, catching six passes for 124 yards and both of the Jaguars' touchdowns. Washington created the plays for the Jaguars in both instances, with Washington scoring a 51-yard touchdown that was almost all yards after the catch. His second touchdown was then a spectacular one-handed catch in the end-zone on a fourth-quarter 27-yard touchdown that was also on fourth down.
51-YARD TOUCHDOWN FOR PARKER WASHINGTON @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Gf38EGe1Qr
Washington has been the Jaguars' go-to receiving in big-time situations, and he had ice water in his veins in the game's biggest moment on Sunday. Games like this one are exactly why the Jaguars will make him a big-money reeiver much sooner rather than later.
It's a big time moment and big time play. We needed a play right there. First, I'm looking, I was looking in the air. I was like, ‘where is the football?’ I'm like, I know I'm supposed to be getting it," Washington said after the game. "Then as soon as I saw it, I was like, okay, there we go. Just being able to make that play, that's what it's all about. That's what the off-season is for. That's what all the training, that's what the training camps, OTAs, that's what it's all about. So, just making that play and being a guy that your team leans on in a big time moment, that was special for me.
The Jaguars' defensive line needed to take over this game, and I think you can certainly make the argument that Josh Hines-Allen did exactly that. While the Jaguars may have only sacked Jalen Hurts once, there is zero question what kind of impact Hines-Allen had. The Jaguars' veteran pass-rusher had one of his most disruptive games of the year, recording two quarterback hits to lead the team while also recording a team-leading two tackles for loss against the run.
Other defenders like Ventrell Miller, Davon Hamilton, Travon Walker, and Antonio Johnson deserve some consideration as well, but this was a vintage Hines-Allen game. As long as you do not hyperfixiate on sacks, then it is hard to not appreciate the kind of physical and dominating performance Hines-Allen had on Sunday.
There are a few different ways to go with this one. Cam Little made a stellar 57-yard field goal, Ameer Abdullah had a massive kick return, Josh Cameron got jobbed on a kickoff return touchdown, and Davon Hamilton stepped up at long-snapper. With all of that in mind, I think this one has to go to Logan Cooke. The fact the Jaguars did not have an errant snap was 100% due to Cooke, who stepped up on every single Hamilton snap to mostly positive results. A lesser performance as a holder, and the Jaguars could have been in trouble.
"It's not like a ton of live reps by any means. It's mostly in a walk-through setting. Whether as a defense on the other side, but without a true live rush all the time. And I don't know if Logan handles that many snaps like that throughout the course of a week," Coen said. "I think those guys do a nice job of mixing it up in practice and being able to give him some of that kind of hot potato drill if you will. Logan's one of the best athletes on our team in terms of hand-eye coordination. He's one of the better golfers. He can throw it. He's just such a good hand-eye coordinated athlete that he was huge today. He was massive."

title: Good, Not So Good From Jaguars' Late Win Over Eagles: OL Concerns Have Set In
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars somehow found a Week 5 win against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday.
The "somehow" label, of course, is a result of the Jaguars putting together their worst performance of the season in their 19-17 win over the Eagles. So, what were the ups and downs of the Week 5 victory? We break it down below in this week's Good and Not So Good.
I thought this would be a good game from Trevor Lawrence , and it was outside of his interception to Quinyon Mitchell. But you can't talk about Lawrence's performance against the Eagles and not mention his connection with Parker Washington on two of the game's most important plays. Washington has become more and more invaluable to the offense every week outside of his career-low day against the Bengals last week, and this duo is what really got the Jaguars over the hump.
Lawrence connected with Washington on both of his touchdown passes, with Washington leading the Jaguars in receiving for the third time in five games. You can just tell that Washington and Lawrence have a different connection than the rest of the pass-catchers in the room, and that connection is what helped the Jaguars improve to 4-1 for the second year in a row. Washington is going to be a very rich man sooner than later.
PARKER WASHINGTON, WOW. JAGS TAKE THE LEAD. @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ubE4xivDcD
We have never seen a Jaguars run defense like this one. The Jaguars once again completely shut down the opposing rushing attack, but they might have been at their season-best with their domination of the Eagles up front. The Eagles' running backs combined for 16 carries for 20 yards, though Will Shipley did score on a two-yard run. But when the Jaguars needed to make a stop, they made it.
The run defense is a big reason the Jaguars' defense was so much better in the second-half. They consistently forced negative runs on early downs to put prressure on the Eagles' passing game, and it led to a number of failed Eagles' drives. This is an even better run defense than it was a year ago, which says quite a bit.
I know the Jaguars missed an extra point, and also had a few short punts and a few too many long returns allowed. With that said, the Jaguars do not win this game without the special teams. Heath Farwell's unit was needed to ensure the Jaguars left with a win, and they made several impact players to go along with a few that might have gone a bit unseen.
DaVon Hamilton stepping up at long-snapper was huge. So was Logan Cooke getting some of his high snaps down. Cam Little kicked a bomb on the game-winning 57-yard field goal, but that was only made possible thanks to a stellar Ameer Abdullah return that was set up by blocks from Quintin Morris, Josh Cameron, Chris Rodriguez Jr., Tanner Koziol, and Jahlani Tavai.
JAGS HUGE KICK RETURN. They're in range for one more shot at a field goal! @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XSWbKBTvW2
Josh Cameron has been one of the Jaguars' best rookie performers all season long, and he took it another step in Week 5. He had a stellar kick return touchdown called back on a questionable call, while he also had a few big plays for the Jaguars as a pass-catcher, run-blocker, and as a blocker on special teams. Cameron has gotten better and better for the Jaguars with every performance this season, and Week 5 was another big step forward.
Josh Cameron Takes It To The House To Start The Kickoff, OMG. That’s A Statement. 🔥 pic.twitter.com/PhXI3oACqv
The numbers might not be pretty for Bhayshul Tuten's day, with the Jaguars' lead back rushing 22 times for just 72 yards with a season-worst 3.3 yard per carry average. But when watching the game live, it was clear that those numbers could have been much, much worse if Tuten was not creating yards on his own and surviving his fair share of negative runs and contact being made behind the line of scrimmage.
Tuten had several zero-yard or one-yard runs that looked like they were about to be stopped a few yards in the backfield, and I would venture to guess a big chunk of his yards came after contact. Tuten played very, very well on Sunday, even if the numbers might not have reflected that on the box score at the end of the day.
The Jaguars' offensive line had some big questions to answer this week, and it is hard to say they passed the test. It felt like it was a rough game for all five linemen at different points, with Ezra Cleveland and Cole Van Lanen giving up sacks, Robert Hainsey having issues with delay of games, and with Emmanuel Pregnon getting three holding calls. Add in Anton Harrison getting carted off with a knee injury, and it is a hard day for the Jaguars' offensive line.
Jalen Carter has been dominant in the first half of this game. 4 tackles, 2 sacks, 2 forced fumbles @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/oJIA9Heufp
I do not think I have ever seen a worse Jaguars game in terms of offensive performance in the red-zone. The Jaguars turned the ball over twice despite getting the ball to the Eagles' one-yard line, and there were numerous reasons why: penalties, missed blocks, drops, odd play-calls. The Jaguars did everything wrong that they could do in the red-zone on Sunday, and it almost cost them a game they had no business losing.
"We need to make some of those plays that we had opportunities to make in the red zone that we didn't," Liam Coen said after the game. "So I think [Trevor Lawrence] was frustrated, but man, I never felt him waver. I never felt him get nerved up or anxious. He was frustrated, but he kept coming off the sideline like we're just shooting ourselves in the foot. Statistically, when you felt the flow of it, it never felt like it wasn't we couldn't get going. We were getting going. It was like positive, negative, positive, negative. So as frustrating as it is, it still leaves you hope because you're moving the ball. It just wasn't really pretty.
Eagles deny the Jaguars at the goal line! Eagles head into the half with a 14-7 lead. @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/K1f1ZnsWCj
The Jaguars allowed over 25% of their allowed yardage on one play: a 62-yard touchdown to Darius Cooper that made up pretty much the entire value of the Eagles' passing game. The pass defense deserves credit for forcing Jalen Hurts to be 20-of-39 for 158 yards (4.05 yards per attempt), but the long bomb given up to Cooper was a mess from a few areas: there was no point to show Hurts man since he is much worse against zone; Montaric Brown got beaten badly on the rep; Backup safety Rayuan Lane completely whiffed with his angle and missed tackle.
DARIUS COOPER, 62-YARD TOUCHDOWN EAGLES TAKE THE LEAD. @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/eKpCwhW8QZ
This was the 36th game of Brian Thomas' career, and it was the first one that he ever got completely shut out in. That is saying something considering he had just three catches in his last two games combined, but his role and production somehow got diminished even more this week. The unfortunate part of this game, though, is that it isn't like Thomas wasn't given the chances to succeed.
Thomas should not get dinged for the Trevor Lawrence interception; Thomas actually had Quinyon Mitchell beat deep. Thomas also had a block that helped spring Parker Washington on his first touchdown. With that said, Thomas led the Jaguars in end-zone targets Sunday but failed to come down with either. One got broken up and went off his hands in the first-half, while a second one was caught but saw Thomas fail to get two feet down. We are not trying to bang the Thomas Jr. Trade Drum , but this one was rough.

title: 10 Observations on Jaguars' Stunning Walk-Off Win Over Eagles in London: Cam Little Saves the Day
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Well, that was a lot.
The Jaguars had a heart-stopping last-second 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles in London thanks to Cam Little's game-winning 57-yard field goal. So, what did we see during the madness and what does it all mean?
Simply put, this was almost the worst loss of the Liam Coen era. They have lost close games before. They have even been blown out before. But this kind of mistake-filled game against an Eagles team that walked into the game with more injuries to key players than not, and there is no excusing where they almost were ... until Cam Little and Ameer Abdullah saved them.
It is hard to pinpoint exactly where the Jaguars were at their worst today. The third-downs to Jalen Hurts, the penalties, the blown red-zone trips, Liam Coen's play-calls, whatever ... but Cam Little did Cam Little things, and he got the Jaguars to their most miraculous win of the Liam Coen era after they almost had their worst loss. Hat tip to Abdullah for the return to set it up, too.
Parker Washington was, more often than not, the best player on the field on Sunday. Washington scored both of the Jaguars' touchdowns, with a 51-yard catch-and-run from Trevor Lawrence setting the Jaguars up with a 7-0 lead early in the game. Washington wasn't done there, though, and he continued to show off the value he brings to the Jaguars throughout the game.
Washington made by far the biggest play of the game with his 27-yard touchdown catch on fourth-down in the fourth-quarter, making a spectacular one-handed catch in the end-zone when the Jaguars simply needed someone to make a play. Washington is the most valuable pass-catcher the Jaguars have, and they need to lock him up much cooner rather than later.
The Jaguars turned the ball over twice on downs after getting the ball to the Eagles' one-yard line. That happening once is brutal. But it happening twice is something that just should not happen to any team, let alone to a team that has legitimate aspirations of a deep playoff run. The Jaguars didn't convert a single one of their first three red-zone trips, a brutal outcome for a team that had been so good in the red-zone to start the season.
On the first of the three failed red-zone trips, the Jaguars had Chris Rodriguez nearly fumble, a Brian Thomas Jr. drop on the touchdown, and then a brutal fourth-down fly sweep to Tuten that honestly would have worked if the Jaguars did not have Rodriguez attempting to make the defining block on the edge against Pro Bowl linebacker Zack Baun.
On the second of the three failed drives, the Jaguars had 1st-and-10 at the Eagles' 14 before an Emmanuel Pregnon holding forced them into 1st-and-20 and derailed the entire drive, leading to a Cam Little 34-yard field goal. Then there was the third drive, where the Jaguars again had first-down at the Eagles' one-yard line before a false start and two delay of games paved the way 4th-and-5. It was simply a brutal day of red-zone offense.
Considering the fact that the Eagles went weeks without any success at all on third-down, it is a bit jarring to see how much success the Jaguars let them have. Jalen Hurts converted a 3rd-and-8 and a 3rd-and-10 in the first-half on their first scoring drive, and they then convered a 3rd-and-17 in the red-zone after a pass-interference on Travis Hunter. Hurts' 61-yard touchdown pass to Darius Cooper was also on third down, and Hurts was 6-of-9 for 119 yards and a touchdown on his first nine third-down drop backs.
Hurts was able to dice up the Jaguars in man coverage, and their blitzes continued to be ineffective as they had been in past weeks. The Jaguars simply had too many downs where they looked like the Eagles were putting them on their heels when they were supposed to be at their best. The Jaguars idea of bending but not breaking only works when the defense refuses to bend on must-win downs, and that didn't happen enough on Sunday.
The Jaguars entered Sunday knowing they had some issues in the secondary due to injuries, and those issues certainly showed up and made an impact early on. Rayuan Lane was getting picked on in coverage by the Eagles, with their offense mostly flowing through the middle of the field where Lane was occupying coverage. Lane also took a bad angle on Darius Cooper's 62-yard touchdown as the high safety.
Speaking of the Cooper touchdown, that was a rough, rough rep for cornerback Montaric Brown. Brown was active after missing last week's game with a hamstring injury, but he allowed a ton of explosive receptions over the first three weeks. He was the cornerback who Cooper beat on his touchdown, which was on 3rd-and-10. Brown simply has had the worst start of a season he has had since becoming a full-time starter, and it cost the Jaguars a touchdown.
The big question facing the Jaguars' offensive line dating back to even last season is whether they are up to the task of slowing down blue-chip defensive linemen. The inability to do so at times has led to some of the only losses of the Liam Coen era, such as last year's losses to the Seattle Seahawks, Los Angeles Rams, and the Houston Texans and this year's loss to the Denver Broncos. That same issue was flagged several times against the Eagles, with star defensive tackle Jalen Carter dominating the game at times.
In the first half alone, Carter had two strip-sacks and a tackle for loss against the run. The Jaguars need to prove they can handle the NFL's elite defensive linemen, but this game was not a sign that they are yet ready to do that. Carter was a game-wrecker that the Jaguars were not ready for, and that could be a concern moving forward.
Then there is Anton Harrison. The Jaguars' starting tackle was carted off the field during second half on what appeared to be a non-contact injury. The Jaguars have some offensive line depth with experienced tackle Walker Little stepping in, but it is hard not to be concerned about the status of Harrison and the Jaguars' left tackle spot moving forward.
I don't know what the answer is for the NFL, but they have a massive referee problem that Roger Goodell needs to somehow curb. The officials threw four (four!) penalties on the opening kickoff alone, and one of them was a brutal holding call on Branson Combs that negated a Josh Cameron touchdown. The replay after the return was ... not kind to the officials if that is the kind of holding that will draw a flag.
The officials continued to be flag-happy throughout the game, much like they were last week. The NFL is throwing an egregious number of flags this season, and far too many of them are simply calls that should never have been made by the zebras. Throwing a bad flag on an exciting opening-game touchdown while in front of an international crowd that you are trying to sell the game to sums up the NFL's referee problem.
If you had to list the most valuable members of the Jaguars' roster thus far this year, it would not take you long to get to nose tackle Davon Hamilton. The seventh-year veteran has been a big part of what the Jaguars do on defense for years, but he played at a Pro Bowl/All-Pro level all season for the Jaguars, and this continued into Week 5 against a banged-up Eagles offensive line. These are the matchups Hamilton needs to win, and he certainly did that.
Hamilton showed up early for the Jaguars, getting a quarterback hit to force a Jalen Hurts incompletion on the first drive. Hamilton then served as the focal point to the Jaguars' run stuff of Will Shipley on fourth-down, which set up a shorter field for the Jaguars that ended up in the Parker Washington 51-yard touchdown and a 7-0 lead. Oh, he was also the freaking long-snapper.
The Jaguars' offense just can not get out of its own way sometimes. The Jaguars have been able to generate explosive plays at a high clip, but penalties and their own miscues have given the Jaguars some fits over the last few weeks. Yes, the officials are out of control, but the Jaguars also got in their own way early,…

title: Jaguars Announce Full Inactives Before Eagles Battle: Secondary Takes Big Hit
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' secondary is officially a bit depleted entering Sunday's Week 5 matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles.
The Jaguars announced their entire list of inactives ahead of the London battle with the Eagles , and it features a key name in the defensive back room: Eric Murray.
The complete list of Jaguars inactives entering Week 5 is as follows: safety Eric Murray, wide receiver CJ Williams, cornerback Alijah Huzzie, cornerback Jaylon Jones, defensive lineman Daniel Faalele, defensive end Wesley Williams, and defensive tackle Albert Regis. Jones and Huzzie just joined the Jaguars this week after Jacksonville signed them as defensive back depth, while Faalele and Wesley Williams have been inactive each week this season. CJ Williams has been a healthy scratch since Week 1.
Regis is also a healthy scratch this week, with the Jaguars carrying extra defensive backs in practice squad cornerback Jabbar Muhammad and practice squad safety Kaevon Merriweather. Linebacker Jalen McLeod is also active and will play a role on special teams.
But it is the status of Murray that is most concerning for the Jaguars. Murray has played a significant role as a starting safety for the Jaguars since he signed with the team last March, and the Jaguars will now have a new safety starting across from fourth-year safety Antonio Johnson. Whether that player will be second-year defensive back Rayuan Lane or third-year rookie Jalen Huskey remains to be seen, but the fact is the Jaguars are now without two of their top-3 safeties in Murray and Caleb Ransaw.
“Eric means a lot to us. Eric is one of the guys you would kind of put him in a classification of he's a coach on the field," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said this week. "You guys probably know that from being at practice. He's just really good communicator, knows the ins and outs of the defense and can kind of see problems before they start on the field. He's been great that way all the way through, the entire season last season, the beginning of this season. He's been a big part of our success."
Now with Huskey or Lane in the mix at the starting safety spot, the Jaguars will have to be at their best if they hope to improve to 4-1. This is the kind of game that will test the depth pieces the Jaguars have developed over the last two seasons, and it starts and ends with how the Jaguars see their safeties step up with Murray out of the lineup.
"Other guys, if they have to step up and do that, I have total confidence that they will, because we've really got a good bunch of communicators back there," Campanile said. "And that's one of the things we're always looking for at that position. A guy who has position flexibility, one. And then two, smart guys,  guys that love to play, that love to learn and obviously, know the ins and outs of all the calls, learn football.”

title: 3 Jaguars X-Factors vs. the Eagles in Week 5: Who Must Slow Down Jalen Hurts?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- For the Jacksonville Jaguars, Week 5 is a big one.
The Jaguars have a chance to knock off the Philadelphia Eagles and improve to 4-1 with a win in London, and here are the X-Factors who will have to step up to ensure it happens.
Arik Armstead is coming off his best game of the season , and he is now set to face off against an Eagles team that has so many moving pieces along the offensive line. The Lane Johnson retirement is the biggest noteworthy change for the Eagles' front line, but they also have several things getting juggled along the interior offensive line due to injuries and the Cam Jurgens trade. Right now, they are hurting and the Jaguars need to take advantage of it.
That means this should be another week where Armstead takes over as a pass-rusher, just like he has over the last two weeks. Armstead has 10 pressures over the last two games, and this is a game that should be set up for him to another impact performer in Week 5. The Eagles have a history of developing offensive linemen, but Armstead can test that and help the Jaguars slow down Jalen Hurts.
The best parts about the Eagles' defense normally comes down to their pass defense: a very strong trio of defensive backs with Quinyon Mitchell, Tariq Woolen, and Cooper DeJean along with a host of pass-rushers like Jonathan Greenard, Jalen Carter, Moro Ojomo, Nolan Smith, and Jalyx Hunt. That means they might offer the Jaguars some actual resistance when it comes to their Trevor Lawrence-led passing attack, which could put this game in the hands of the rushing attack and Bhayshul Tuten.
Tuten has been one of the NFL's most effective running backs to start the 2026 season, and this could be a game that sees him have his true breakout performance. That game would have been last week if not for a few penalties and two called-back touchdowns, but I think the Jaguars are ready to lean on him and let him lead the way to a win.
Foyesade Oluokun has been a very strong veteran performe r for the Jaguars this season, getting high marks in metrics in both run- and pass-defense. This culminated with him making one of the most important plays of the season thus far with a red-zone interception of Joe Burrow last week, and the Jaguars will once again need him to set the tone against the Eagles. While Jalen Hurts is unlikely to test the Jaguars often in the middle of the field, Oluokun can still make an impact.
With the Eagles set to be without both Saquon Barkley and Tank Bigsby at running back this week, that means the Jaguars' run defense will face off against backup running backs Will Shipley and Dameon Pierce. The way for the Jaguars to beat the Eagles is to force Jalen Hurts into a dropback-heavy attack by suffocating their run defense, and Oluokun is set to be a pivotal part of the Jaguars' hopes to do that.

title: Why the Jaguars Must Keep Close Tabs on the Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Compensation
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Marvin Harrison Jr. is on his way out of Arizona, and the outcome of his exit could be of some importance to the Jacksonville Jaguars.
That is not just because the most rumored landing spot for the former top-5 pick is to the AFC South rivals in the Houston Texans, who the Jaguars play in London in Week 6. Instead, the eventual conclusion of the Harrison trade saga and its final compensation for the Cardinals could be of great interest for the Jaguars moving forward.
Simply put, whatever the Cardinals end up getting for Harrison could indicate what the Jaguars could get if they end up wanting to trade away their own third-year wide receiver. The Jaguars continue to look no closer to considering trading wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., which is not surprising. Thomas' snap counts and role in the offense have fluctuated through the first month of the season , though the Jaguars have always seemed content on sticking by Thomas even if is not a high-volume producer in their deep passing game.
This is not an argument for the Jaguars to deal Thomas, though I do think the Harrison trade could make it clear that it could still end up being the most advantageous move for the Jaguars ahead of next month's trade deadline. Whatever the Cardinals end up landing for Harrison over the next few days could make that even clearer.
There have been several reports that the Cardinals' asking price for Harrison is a second-round pick. If this is the case, then that would set a clear floor for what kind of value Thomas may offer on the trade market before the November deadline. That is simply the result of Thomas being a much more valuable player than Harrison; if Harrison can fetch a potential top-50 pick, then what the heck could Thomas land the Jaguars?
Simply put, Thomas has been a much better player than Harrison to start their careers. He outpaces Harrison in games played, AV (approximate value), receptions, receiving yards, catch rate, yards per target, yards after the catch per reception, and passer rating when targeted. Even with Thomas looking like the third or fourth pass-catcher in the pecking order this year, he still has more catches and yards than Harrison, who has run more than double of the amount of routes Thomas had.
In short, there is zero comparison for Thomas and Harrison. Both are young, former first-round picks from the same class, but Thomas has been the significantly better NFL receiver to start their careers. That means whatever the Cardinals get for Harrison should be nothing more than the start of the conversation if the Jaguars ever see teams make offers for Thomas.
It does not appear the Jaguars have any interest in moving Thomas, so it doesn't make much sense for the Jaguars to shop him. But that could not stop other teams from calling about him, and the Harrison trade compensation should help inform those teams what a meaningful call would really look like.

title: While the Chiefs Enjoy a Bye Week, the Rest of the AFC West Has Plenty to Prove
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are 4-0 and the only undefeated team still standing in the AFC . That, of course, means the Chiefs are in command of the AFC West while the Las Vegas Raiders try to hold on to their second-place standing and the Denver Broncos look to improve on their .500 start.
Oh, and the Los Angeles Chargers would probably like to win a game sooner rather than later, too.
With the Chiefs enjoying their bye week, let's take a look at Sunday's pair of games containing AFC West squads, plus two primetime matchups with other AFC contenders.
The Raiders acquited themselves admirably against the Chiefs last week, taking their first loss of the season in decidedly un-Raider-y fashion. (Un-Raider-y isn't a word, but you know what it means!) In some ways, I'm more convinced that the Raiders are a legitimate playoff-adjacent team now than I was before their loss to the Chiefs. However, they're not getting a break from their upcoming schedule anytime soon.
Las Vegas gets the New England Patriots in Foxborough this week before hosting the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams in the next two weeks. The Raiders don't need to win all of those games to retain their new semi-contender status, but they can't lose four consecutive games and still be taken seriously in the second half of the year.
New England, on the other hand, is coming off an impressive win over the Bills in Buffalo last weekend, stabilizing the team after a blowout loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 3.
The Raiders may still be a year of progress away from true contention, but Chiefs fans should obviously be pulling for the Patriots in this one.
these posts came a week apart life comes at you fast and all that pic.twitter.com/pVD2tc26og
Even with impressive home victories over the Jaguars and Rams in Weeks 2 and 3, the vibes around quarterback Bo Nix and the Broncos' offense seem to have taken a considerable shift after last week's loss at the San Francisco 49ers. For what it's worth, I still think the Broncos are the second-best squad in the division and should be expected to return to the playoffs again this season, but that confidence would be severely shaken if the winless Chargers can pull off the upset in LA.
The Chargers have been one of the biggest disappointments in all of football this season, and they're running out of time to do something about it. After hosting the Broncos, the Chargers will head to Kansas City in Week 6 before "visiting" the Rams after their Week 7 bye. If there's any life left in the Chargers at all, they'll need to prove it against Denver.
Not that Chiefs fans need my guidance here, but a Chargers win would be good for both the Chiefs' lead over the Broncos and for a week of NFL comedy.
Beyond the AFC West, two of the Chiefs' top AFC rivals will go up against a pair of 2-2 NFC teams in primetime. The Baltimore Ravens (3-1) will face the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday Night Football, while the Bills (3-1) will travel to Los Angeles to take on the Rams for a Monday night showdown.
It's far too early in the year to be seriously considering playoff seeding, but any extra wiggle room for the Chiefs' hunt for the No. 1 seed would be beneficial, especially with Kansas City's Thanksgiving showdown with the Bills looming large.
Chiefs fans should enjoy the experience of rooting for Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson in their new homes on Monday Night Football while pulling for the Falcons to take a game from Baltimore on Sunday night.
Happy Championship Sunday! pic.twitter.com/Mw7LIStU11

title: Chiefs’ Pass-Rush Unit Could Return a Sneaky Weapon From Injury Soon
full_text:
Much has been made of the Kansas City Chiefs' defensive line failing to record a sack in each of the past three games. However, Steve Spagnuolo's unit could be getting a huge boost in the upcoming weeks.
Following Kansas City's bye, the Chiefs will finally be eligible to get 2025 second-round pick Omarr Norman-Lott back on the field. He's been on the PUP (Physically Unable to Perform) list since training camp and was required to miss the opening four contests of the year, but Week 6 marks the first point at which he can return to game action. The University of Tennessee product tore his ACL in Week 7 of last season and has been rehabbing ever since. There was hope he'd progress to full health and participate in offseason sessions, but the front office elected to place him on the PUP list to allow him extra time to recover.
It's been almost a full year since Norman-Lott suffered the injury. Barring any setbacks, it shouldn't be too long before we see him active again. Of course, every ACL tear is different, and not everyone can make a nine-month return like Patrick Mahomes did.
Head coach Andy Reid alluded to Norman-Lott "potentially" returning after the bye in late September. It was the first positive injury update the Chiefs had received on him in quite some time.
Andy Reid also says Chiefs DT Omarr Norman-Lott is a possibility to return from IR after the bye week. Reid says he’s doing more and getting closer to a return.
The Chiefs certainly won't be in any rush to bring Norman-Lott back from a serious knee injury at 4-0. Once they open his 21-day practice window, KC must either activate him during that span or transfer him to the IR for the remainder of the season.
As a rookie, Norman-Lott played sparingly but was an effective interior lineman. Across five contests, he finished with one sack, four solo tackles, and one tackle for loss, earning a 54.2 Pro Football Focus (PFF) grade. While Norman-Lott plays on the inside, his profile is more as a pass rusher than a run defender. He's extremely explosive for his size and has a relentless motor when getting after the quarterback, boasting an impressive 18.9% pass-rush win rate as a senior in college.
As we've noted in recent days on Chiefs at SI, the pass rush hasn't really been as invisible as it seems. It especially started to come alive in the second half of the victory over the Las Vegas Raiders. However, Norman-Lott's return to the squad could open up a plethora of possibilities for the defensive line rotation.
The Chiefs drafted another defensive tackle early in this year's draft, selecting former Clemson standout Peter Woods with the No. 29 overall pick . He and Khyiris Tonga have split snaps throughout the season, with both playing a little under 50% of the defense's reps. Norman-Lott could slot in during passing downs to rush the quarterback alongside Chris Jones on the inside.
When Coach Reid speaks to the media on Monday, we could get more clarity on Norman-Lott's status. It's been quiet on the injury front for ONR lately, but the Chiefs could have a secret weapon in the pass rush ready to deploy when he's healthy.

title: Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams Star in a Bright Future for the Chiefs' Cornerback Room
full_text:
It was a bit of a surprise when the Kansas City Chiefs traded up to obtain the No. 6 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, then even more of a surprise when they used that selection on LSU cornerback Mansoor Delane . Immediately, Delane rightfully had sky-high expectations as the new face of the Chiefs' secondary.
Delane was limited throughout the majority of training camp due to a shoulder injury and then played just three snaps (including an interception of Bo Nix) in Weeks 1 and 2 due to an issue with the same shoulder. Even with just two full games under his belt, Delane looks to be worth that draft selection, and he's not alone as a rising star in Kansas City's overhauled cornerback room.
As any Chiefs or Los Angeles Rams fan knows by now, the Chiefs traded away cornerback Trent McDuffie to the Rams this offseason, and Jaylen Watson reunited with McDuffie after leaving for LA in free agency. That left a significant void for the Chiefs to fill at corner.
To begin 2026, veteran cornerback Kristian Fulton was entering the second year of his two-year deal with the Chiefs after a disappointing 2025, and '25 third-round draft pick Nohl Williams was looking to follow his promising rookie campaign with a more consistent workload in his sophomore season.
Delane, Williams and Fulton all hit the ground running .
Highest graded CBs in man coverage this season Mansoor Delane         93.8 Kristian Fulton             92.8 Nohl Williams               91.8 Trent McDuffie            90.9 Travis Hunter               90.3 pic.twitter.com/4Tv5R4kLLU
Delane has been excellent , even when asked to take on difficult coverage responsibilities, as he was asked to do at times against Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers. He's also been a missile in run defense, playing with speed and physicality that fits Steve Spagnuolo's defense perfectly.
Mansoor Delane with one of the GREATEST two-play sequences you’ll see from a rook. Registers a TFL on Ashton Jeanty, and follows it up with CLAMPING Brock Bowers. The Chiefs rookie CB NEUTRALIZING some of the NFL’s top weapons 😳🔒 pic.twitter.com/oHzd3YU6qM
Delane has the fifth-highest overall cornerback grade from Pro Football Focus through the first four weeks of the 2026 season, while Fulton lands at No. 11. Williams appears at No. 41 in overall PFF grading but lands at No. 23 with his coverage grade alone.
good player this Mansoor Delane https://t.co/HNmzmM6Pbj pic.twitter.com/XPGheGgX3M
The one area of concern in the Chiefs' cornerback room comes in the slot, where veteran L'Jarius Sneed has provided some value and some tough snaps in his second act with the team. Sneed has the second-worst PFF grade among qualifying cornerbacks (No. 102 of 103), but he's been a positive force against the run and as a blitzer.
Sneed began the season in excellent fashion against the Denver Broncos in Week 1 before being routinely bested by Indianapolis Colts receiver Josh Downs in Week 2. I'll argue that it's a bit too early (and a bit unnecessary) to rush to end the Sneed-reclaimation experiment, but he's certainly struggled more than the team's trio of outside corners to begin the year.
I'd be interested to see Delane get a bit of work in the slot if that would enable Williams and Fulton to hold the outside corner roles in nickel packages, but I'd also understand some hesitance, as Delane's potential value is probably highest as a shutdown outside corner, and he's still acclimating to the NFL game (though you wouldn't know that if you only watched him play).
What other options could the Chiefs have?
Rookie defensive back Jadon Canady was a healthy scratch in Week 4 as safety Chamarri Conner returned to the lineup, while slot corner Kader Kohou remains on the practice squad, so neither Canady nor Kohou seem particularly close to challenging Sneed for those slot corner reps. Versatile DB Chris Roland-Wallace took a season-high 29 defensive snaps against the Raiders, but Sneed has taken more than 72% of the defensive snaps in every game so far this season.
Ultimately, the Chiefs' slot corner position will require more monitoring (and, ideally, better play) in the weeks to come, but the Delane/Williams outside duo—with room for cameos from Fulton this season—appears to be one of the NFL's most promising young pairings.

title: Chiefs RB Kenneth Walker Welcomes Potential Tyreek Hill Reunion in Kansas City
full_text:
While the Kansas City Chiefs are off to a 4-0 start heading into the bye, the front office is actively looking to bolster the roster. Kansas City will likely be without wide receiver Tyquan Thornton for the remainder of the regular season and could miss wide receiver Rashee Rice for some time as well.
KC has been linked to several wideouts, but the most obvious addition could come in the form of a reunion with Tyreek Hill . The speedster is coming off a dislocated knee last season and could make his return to the NFL with the team he started his career with. Rumors have been swirling between Hill and the Chiefs for quite some time. It's the worst-kept secret that Kansas City is showing interest in the 32-year-old. Recently, one of the AFC's biggest stars revealed his thoughts on Hill potentially returning to play for Andy Reid.
In an interview with Yahoo Sports on behalf of Orgain, running back Kenneth Walker III was asked what he thought about Hill potentially rejoining the Chiefs. The NFL's leading rusher is all for bringing "Cheetah" back.
"I've seen his speed. Everybody knows Tyreek Hill is just straight speed, and he's just an athlete in general," Walker said. "And just watching him over the years, I'm like, 'He's one of the best players that really played.' So, it's cool to see that. I think it's cool and it would be a great addition to our team."
Through the first four games of his Chiefs tenure, Walker has truly been an MVP candidate . He's currently sitting at 537 rushing yards with six total touchdowns. Chiefs fans knew he was talented when he signed with the franchise in March, but no one could have expected this level of production.
Part of the reason why Walker believes a reunion with Hill would work, as he later explained in the interview, is that it would make the Chiefs' offense more versatile. Between Patrick Mahomes' arm talent, Walker's dynamic running style , and Hill as a downfield threat, opposing defenses would have a difficult time containing those three players at once. While the backfield is set in Kansas City, the wide receiving corps is far less certain. The aforementioned injuries to Rice and Thornton will hinder KC, leaving the team with Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals, Cyrus Allen, Nikko Remigio, and a potential practice squad elevation for next week's group of wideouts.
There's more at play than Brett Veach simply signing him to a cheap one-year contract, though. Hill is currently battling a civil assault and battery trial in court and has a pending Personal Conduct Policy investigation from the NFL. The Chiefs are already starting to look at other options, including former Chief champion Justin Watson .
Hill is coming off a devastating injury himself and hasn't played in an NFL game in over a year, but he's only two seasons removed from leading the league in receiving yards. If he's even 80% of his old self, he'd be a tremendous help to this offense, and Walker's comments reflect that.

title: Reported Chiefs Interest in WR Reunion Underscores a Harsh Reality
full_text:
Although the Kansas City Chiefs are on a bye week, many folks are still talking about the lone undefeated team left in the AFC. Some of that is for good reason, but there's also a glaring hole on the roster that needs to be addressed at some point.
With wide receiver Tyquan Thornton suffering a dislocated ankle in Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders, it'd likely behoove general manager Brett Veach to add another pass catcher. The only issue is that the in-season talent pool doesn't contain many quality options, leaving the franchise in a tough spot.
The most recent bit of Chiefs-related wideout news sums that up pretty perfectly. According to Pete Sweeney of the Kansas City Star , Veach and Co. are "among several teams" interested in free agent Justin Watson.
The Chiefs are among several teams interested in WR Justin Watson, per source. Watson played for Kansas City from 2022-24 and is a three-time Super Bowl champion, having beaten the Chiefs with the Bucs before being part of their back-to-back title teams.
Watson being the latest name tied to KC emphasizes just how dried up the market is. Barring a trade that would almost surely cost NFL Draft capital, he's right in the thick of the tier of players the team could be vying for. Does a reunion with the three-time Super Bowl champ make any sense? Let's break it down.
They oftentimes come off as buzz phrases in Chiefs circles, but they do matter to the organization and come in handy given the timing of any potential signing once the season's rolling. Veteran experience, familiarity with the scheme, attention to detail, alignment versatility and more all carry significance. Watson checks each and every box there.
Now in his age-30 campaign, Watson has 1,716 regular-season offensive snaps under his belt as a member of the Chiefs and over 500 spanning five other years with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Houston Texans. Thinking from a Thornton-esque perspective regarding the operation of the offense, the former fifth-round pick also possesses proven chemistry with quarterback Patrick Mahomes on vertical passing concepts.
Watson carried a 17.2-yard average depth of target in Kansas City from 2022-2024. He averaged 13.9 yards before the catch per reception and owned an 89.8 passer rating when targeted. According to Pro Football Focus , Watson spent between 63.9% and 68.8% of his time lined up out wide over his three Chiefs seasons. Thornton was at 62.5% in 2025 and is at 70.9% in 2026.
It also doesn't hurt that Watson is a bigger-bodied player than most of the current Chiefs receiver room (6-foot-2, 215 pounds), is a willing and (mostly) capable blocker and can play special teams. Things like that stand out to the coaching staff and front office, for better or worse.
Simply put, Watson just wasn't a very good player during his time with the Chiefs. According to SumerSports , his 50.94% catch rate ranked sixth among all Kansas City wideouts in 2023. The following year, he owned an 0.72 yards per route run figure that was dead last in the group and trailed sixth-place Marquez Valdes-Scantling (0.89) by a decent margin.
The advanced data not being in Watson's favor doesn't stop there. NFL Pro pegs him as posting a -9.8% catch rate over expected in 2022, then a -1.3% mark in 2023 before it spiked to +6.0% in his final Kansas City season. He was worth 17.2 EPA in the latter campaign, but that can't be a reliable expectation baseline for the current year.
Other factors must also be considered, even with Thornton set to miss most or all of this season . What's the latest with Tyreek Hill? The Chiefs have been linked to him at every step over the last few weeks, although his ongoing legal situation muddies those waters quite a bit. Would a Watson addition put that potential acquisition on ice?
What about costing players like second-year man Jalen Royals and rookie Cyrus Allen developmental reps? Is Watson that much better than either option at this stage in his career? So many moving pieces make this far from a no-brainer of a decision.
Now on the wrong side of the aging curve, it's fair to question what Watson has left in the tank. His Texans tenure was virtually silent, but it's also not like he forgot how to function in a Kansas City-style offense after the end of the 2024-25 campaign. As long as there's still some speed, he can execute the same type of role he used to have.
If the Chiefs did sign Watson, this writer doesn't believe head coach Andy Reid and company would be quite as compelled to put him on the field as often as a JuJu Smith-Schuster. Additionally, Watson doesn't carry any off-the-field baggage and isn't recovering from a major injury, so he'd be a more immediate plug-and-play (and keep in the lineup) fit than someone like Hill.
At the end of the day, Watson might just be a more appropriate Thornton replacement than multiple internal options or free agent avenues. Even if he isn't a clear-cut needle-mover, it may not hurt to bring him in and see what he's got as a part-time player. An emphasis should be placed on the part, though, coming with the understanding that the double champion with the Chiefs wouldn't be saving the receiver room.
Again, that's an unfortunate reminder of where things are at. Help could be on the way while still not solving the current problem to the optimal degree.

title: The Chiefs' Pass Rush Has Room to Improve, But It's Probably Been Better Than You Think
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs haven't recorded a sack in three games. At face value, that's an alarming statistic that paints a grim picture of the team's pass rush. After a longer look, there are plenty of reasons to be optimistic that the team's defensive line will be able to put it all together after the bye week.
Using this week off to take a longer look at a few key position groups that will determine where the Chiefs go in the next act of the season, Kansas City's D-line has some work to do, but they have been better than their box score indicates.
First, find the Chiefs in this chart of key pass rush stats. (There's a lot of information for all 32 teams, so we'll break down the important parts next.) Surface-level, what do you see?
Key pass rush stats: pic.twitter.com/uq0LEa6pEK
There's a whole lot of green (which is good) throughout the Chiefs' row, with two dark purple (bad) cells. Why?
In that chart, the Chiefs are No. 6 in the NFL in pressure rate, No. 8 in quick pressure rate, No. 13 in non-blitz pressure rate and No. 8 in average time to pressure. Those are the numbers of a top-10 pass rush unit! Then, the purple boxes.
The Chiefs are No. 31 in sack rate (2.5%) and dead last, No. 32, in pressure-to-sack ratio (5.7%). The KC D-line is creating pressure at a top-10 rate, but they've been one of the worst-finishing teams on those opportunities. Ultimately, I think that paints a relatively positive picture of the pass rush, and it certainly beats the alternative.
Those numbers are supported by other individual stats, like the fact that George Karlaftis was credited with a whopping seven quarterback hits against Kirk Cousins by Pro Football Focus ( a performance supported by a longer look at the film ), giving him a total of 12 quarterback hits this season , despite getting zero sacks out of those hits.
Most QB hits this season, via @PFF George Karlaftis - 12 Greg Rousseau - 12 Dallas Turner - 9 Cameron Thomas - 9 Maxx Crosby - 9 Resulting Sacks Greg Rousseau - 6 Dallas Turner - 6 Maxx Crosby - 3 Cameron Thomas - 2 George Karlaftis - 0 pic.twitter.com/CdsAVfNdmt
Regarding the other defensive ends, rookie second-round pick R Mason Thomas has also flashed far beyond his one sack would suggest , while former first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah (lined up over the center in the clip below) has had some of his best reps as a pro throughout the start of this season.
The way R Mason Thomas can accelerate towards the QB is just nuts. pic.twitter.com/ZsjpPTFvY6
Even second-year third-round pick Ashton Gillotte's season benefits from a deep dive into more advanced metrics, as Gillotte's "DIPRA" (defensive impact per rush attempt) is 10th-best in the league through four weeks.
The defensive tackles, particularly superstar veteran Chris Jones and first-round rookie Peter Woods, haven't had a series of game-wrecking moments so far this season, but Woods has shown tremendous physical tools , and Jones has been on the injury report with a calf issue to begin the year. I'm still very optimistic about Woods, and I'll wait a few more weeks before I'm willing to worry about Jones in his age-32 season.
Defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga has been a positive force against the run, and second-year lineman Omarr Norman-Lott is still on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list due to his ongoing recovery from last season's torn ACL.
Yes, the Chiefs' pass rush still needs to turn pressures and hits into sacks, but they appear to have the players to get to the quarterback; that's a much better problem than the issues they had last season.

title: How Does the Chiefs' Wide Receiver Room Stack Up at the Bye?
full_text:
On Sunday in Las Vegas, the Kansas City Chiefs' offense felt like it was hitting its stride, particularly in the deep passing game. Explosive plays had returned both on the ground and through the air, giving the Chiefs multiple ways to burn opposing defenses. Then, on one of those deep completions, wide receiver Tyquan Thornton suffered a serious ankle injury, ending Thornton's two-touchdown, 111-yard day on a somber, season-threatening note.
For now, the Chiefs will at least be without Thornton for the foreseeable future , while Rashee Rice also exited the Raiders game with a tweaked hamstring. Even if the Chiefs do complete the much-speculated reunion with Tyreek Hill , he reportedly wouldn't be ready to return to the field until November . So, how will the offense adjust in the meantime?
Every *catchable* target for Worthy through 4 weeks. *Two route-pass location miscues not included, plus final pass vs LV + Best in open space & on the move (crossers and crossers) - 15/19 balls were caught against the body, double underhand - Rarely working back to the ball pic.twitter.com/d5x7D51rCf
Even as fan sentiment regarding third-year first-round wide receiver Xavier Worthy has shifted from excitement to frustration, the 23-year-old speedster is still the Chiefs' best chance to create explosive plays from the wide receiver position .
Yes, he's had his struggles with the deep ball. No, he hasn't yet found a way to turn his record-breaking speed into consistent NFL production. Yes, he still has a skillset that doesn't exist elsewhere on the roster (or many places throughout the NFL).
Worthy has already consistently been the Chiefs' most-used wide receiver by snap count (now at 80% of the offensive reps through four games), and the Chiefs' coaching staff has the benefit of an extra week to review Worthy's strengths and weaknesses while retooling the receiver room. For better or for worse, Worthy is even more important to the Chiefs now than he was before the season began.
Cyrus Allen target on third down.. like the idea of using him on possible M2M reps. Go get the DE’s hands down on a quick pass tho. pic.twitter.com/3Jbg3cqvkC
Elsewhere, Kansas City has no choice but to bring at least one of their most recent wide receiver draft picks into the fold. Second-year fourth-round pick Jalen Royals has played 60 offensive snaps through four games, with 38 of those reps coming in Vegas. Royals didn't take an offensive snap in Week 1 and has just three catches on the season, but he has been the team's No. 4 receiver so far.
Rookie fifth-round pick Cyrus Allen was the recipient of a massive amount of training camp hype , but he's taken only 10 snaps so far in the regular season —fewer offensive reps than defensive tackle/occasional fullback Khyiris Tonga.
Even with Allen's preseason hype, it always made more sense for him to be a late-season climber after he becomes more familiar with the offense and as the coaches and quarterback develop more trust in him. Now, however, the once-long runway could be shortening. If the Chiefs truly believe in Allen's skillset, the Chiefs' thinning receiver room needs playmakers wherever they can be found.
