title: Saints DC Doesn't Hold Back in Response to Troy Aikman
full_text:
New Orleans Saints defensive coordinator Brandon Staley pushed back Thursday against criticism from ESPN analyst Troy Aikman , who said during a 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons that Staley "didn't have any answers" for Atlanta's rushing attack.
The Saints (1-3) surrendered five rushing touchdowns and 205 yards on the ground while playing without linebacker Kaden Elliss and edge rushers Carl Granderson and Anfernee Jennings . Staley acknowledged his responsibility for the outcome, but stated the comments bothered him "because they're not true."
“I did hear those comments, and I have no idea what he’s talking about.” #Saints DC Brandon Staley addresses Troy Aikman’s comments from Monday Night’s broadcast. pic.twitter.com/mukvaI6DMO
Bijan Robinson had 19 carries for 145 yards and two touchdowns while Brian Robinson had 14 carries for 62 yards and three touchdowns.
"It was a tough night for us, and certainly, I'm responsible. I'm calling the defense, but we've got a great group of guys," Staley said. "No one defended that runner last year better than us. He's a hell of a player. But our group defended him twice last year better than anyone through his time in the NFL."
Staley said he had heard Aikman's comments but had "no idea" what he was talking about as he alluded to how the Saints held Bijan Robinson to just 33 and 70 yards in both meetings last season.
With 2:43 left in the third quarter of the "Monday Night Football" broadcast, Aikman weighed in, highlighting missing personnel up front.
"Brandon Staley, he just simply doesn't have any answers. And I think he knew it when we talked to him coming in," Aikman said. "I think he knew. He didn't tell us, but the guys that are out ... their big edge rushers and guys who can play the run and set the edge, they're not on the field, and they just don't have that star defender that can erase mistakes for other people.
"This was a matchup issue coming into this game, and it's proven true."
Aikman also criticized the team's effort on Atlanta's fifth rushing touchdown and the third by Brian Robinson, noting that players were "standing around watching the play, missed tackles, just bad football."
Addressing the defensive breakdown, Staley noted that Bijan Robinson's 59-yard run on the third play was a "shock to everybody," but defended his unit's overall effort.
"There were plenty of good moments in there in the first half, but after that possession, it was really up and down," Staley said. "We did not play a good game after that fourth-down penalty. We never got our rhythm back as a defense. And that's what stood out to me. And that's why I say it was very uncharacteristic of us because, since I've been here, we've been very steady. But that game got away from us."
"Our guys have played the right way," Staley added regarding effort. "And mainly that's assignment, technique, effort, all in one. I think the other night, we were missing two out of the three. Our effort was there."
"We're focusing on Minnesota, learning the tough lessons from the other night," Staley said as the Saints prepare to host the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. "We've got the right guys to bounce back."

title: Kellen Moore and Saints Have a Serious Problem After Falcons Humiliation
full_text:
Before the season, the New Orleans Saints had high expectations after a strong finish to the 2025 season and with one of the best young quarterbacks in the league, Tyler Shough .
However, the second season of the Kellen Moore era has not gotten off to the start the organization wanted. After a 1-1 start featuring an upset win over the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2, the Saints have lost their last two games—falling in a fourth-quarter collapse to the Las Vegas Raiders and getting blown out by the Atlanta Falcons on Monday Night Football.
The loss to Atlanta has seemingly broken the dam. It was an embarrassing 45-24 loss on a night commemorating the 20th anniversary of Domecoming. TV networks, the city, the franchise and the league designated the game as a celebration of the night that rebirthed New Orleans.
Then, the Saints laid an egg in front of 73,000 fans, with former players such as Drew Brees and Steve Gleason and members of the 2006 team watching by a national audience.
What is going on with the Saints?
Slow starts remain a defining flaw of the Moore era for the Saints.
In 2025, New Orleans was outscored 122-29 in the first quarter. This minus-93 differential routinely forced the team to play from behind, despite second-half improvements after Shough took over at quarterback.
The issue persists in 2026. A Week 3 touchdown pass from Shough to Juwan Johnson against Las Vegas provided the Saints with a 6-3 first-quarter lead—their first under Moore and their first since Dec. 8, 2024, ending a 23-game drought.
However, the momentum proved brief. Against Atlanta on Monday night, New Orleans fell behind 24-7 at halftime following an early Falcons touchdown, a quick three-and-out, and a lone second-quarter score, ultimately losing 45-24.
Moore noted postgame that the team has tried various approaches to resolve the issue but has not yet found a solution.
"We have tried a number of different things," Moore said. "Obviously, we have to solve this. We have to find a way."
Dating back to 2025, the Saints continue to struggle early, leaving them constantly playing catch-up.
The Saints' secondary entered the season with legitimate questions, and four games have done little to provide answers.
New Orleans has talent on the back end, but the unit has struggled to prevent explosive plays and has compounded those mistakes with penalties, missed tackles and breakdowns at critical moments. Those issues were on full display against Atlanta, when Michael Penix Jr. needed only 20 attempts to throw for 223 yards and a touchdown. He averaged 11.2 yards per attempt and completed 75% of his passes despite Atlanta leaning heavily on its running game.
Cornerbacks Kool-Aid McKinstry and Quincy Riley had particularly difficult nights. According to Pro Football Focus (PFF) data, Riley allowed four receptions for 58 yards and a touchdown as the nearest defender, while McKinstry allowed two catches for 60 yards and committed two penalties. They finished with overall PFF grades of 28.0 and 29.5, respectively.
The problems extend well beyond one game.
Through four games, McKinstry has been targeted 22 times, allowing 13 receptions for 209 yards and one touchdown. He has surrendered four first downs while forcing four incompletions.
Riley has faced 21 targets, allowing 11 receptions for 142 yards and three touchdowns. He has allowed three first downs and forced three incompletions. The three touchdowns allowed are particularly concerning considering Riley has been targeted only 21 times.
The Saints haven't received much better production from their safeties.
Jonas Sanker has been targeted 19 times and allowed 17 receptions for 161 yards and a touchdown. He has yet to force an incompletion or allow a first down, according to PFF's charting.
Veteran Justin Reid has also struggled to consistently hold up in coverage. Opposing quarterbacks have completed 13 of 15 passes for 111 yards and a touchdown when targeting him. Like Sanker, Reid has not recorded a forced incompletion or allowed a first down through four games.
Combined, McKinstry, Riley, Sanker, Reid and Julian Blackmon have surrendered 57 receptions on 79 targets for 657 yards with seven touchdowns and only one interception. That is a 70.1% completion rate, with the five defensive backs combining for only seven forced incompletions.
If there is one defensive problem that should concern the Saints even more than their secondary, it's their inability to stop the run.
The warning signs were already there before Monday night. New Orleans entered Week 4 allowing 128.7 rushing yards per game, 27th in the NFL. Atlanta then turned that weakness into a full-blown disaster.
The Falcons rushed for 205 yards and five touchdowns on 35 carries, averaging 5.9 yards per attempt. Bijan Robinson accounted for 145 yards and two touchdowns, while Brian Robinson Jr. added 62 yards and three scores.
Worse, the Saints were overwhelmed immediately.
Bijan Robinson ripped off a 59-yard touchdown on Atlanta's third offensive play, setting the tone for an evening in which New Orleans never found an answer. The Falcons didn't need deception or a complicated offensive formula. They repeatedly attacked a defensive front that couldn't maintain its gaps or consistently finish tackles.
And this wasn't an isolated performance. New Orleans has now allowed 165, 108, 113 and 205 rushing yards through its first four games. That's 591 yards overall, an average of nearly 147.8 yards per game, which is 30th out of 32 teams in the NFL. The only two teams that have a worse rushing defense than the Saints are the Dallas Cowboys and NFC South rival Carolina Panthers .
There is a difference between losing games and losing the fanbase. Moore may be dangerously close to the latter.
Monday night's 45-24 loss to the Falcons felt like more than another defeat for a Saints team that has fallen to 1-3. New Orleans was embarrassed at home by its biggest rival on a night meant to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Domecoming, and the frustration inside the Caesars Superdome was impossible to ignore.
Fans can tolerate a rebuilding team. They can understand injuries, growing pains and a young roster making mistakes. Who Dat Nation can tolerate a close loss where the Saints fight until the final whistle, especially given the key injuries the team faced entering the game.
What becomes much harder to accept is a team consistently looking unprepared, undisciplined or incapable of matching its opponent's intensity.
That's where Moore's problem begins.
Moore was hired to give the Saints a new direction after years of stagnation. Instead, the results are beginning to look painfully familiar.
Four games should not determine a coach's future, particularly one overseeing a roster with obvious deficiencies. But patience around Moore could disappear quickly if performances like Monday's continue, especially since everyone, from the city of New Orleans to the NFL and television networks, designated that night for New Orleans to celebrate one of the city's and franchise's greatest moments.
This loss is something that they will not forget, and given their reactions across social media , it has not been pretty.
Saints fans aren't simply asking for wins right now. They're looking for evidence that the franchise is actually headed somewhere.
Against Atlanta, they didn't get much of it.

title: Isaiah Likely Makes Giants History in Wild Tie vs. Commanders
full_text:
New York Giants tight end Isaiah Likely has been making sure his on-field production matches every penny the franchise paid him to come over from Baltimore with head coach John Harbaugh during the offseason.
The 6-foot-4 Likely, who traded in Ravens purple for a blue uniform and a three-year, $40 million contract in free agency, has wasted no time making his mark in his Giants tenure.
Harbaugh and the Giants wanted Likely to be a complementary, versatile receiving threat for their initial starting quarterback, Jaxson Dart, and Matt Nagy’s offense. Still, he has gone far beyond that, logging a team-leading 33 receptions on 47 targets for 284 yards and four touchdowns.
The catch total puts him in rare company in Giants lore: he is the first tight end in franchise history to record that many catches through his first five games.
The feat came on the strength of Likely’s breakout effort in the Giants’ roller-coaster 27-27 Week 5 overtime tie against the Washington Commanders, one where the tight end hauled in a career-high 11 catches for 94 yards and two touchdowns to help the team overcome a 14-point second-half deficit.
At the same time, his performance wasn’t enough to counteract other missed opportunities that kept Big Blue from beating its division rival and widening its lead in the NFC East.
“I honestly was shocked,” Likely said about the final result. “I never tied up before in my NFL career, really in any game.”
“I mean, we had the game right there—unfortunate errors. You know, obviously there are plays that we all can have back to really end the game from there. It wasn’t a win, it wasn’t a loss, obviously, but it definitely was a blessing.”
The Giants’ odd blessing of leaving Northwest Stadium with a tie came down to tough conversations and a whole lot of grit.
That started in the team’s much-needed halftime break, when New York trailed the Commanders 12-3 after Dominic Zvada missed a pair of field goals and Jameis Winston fumbled, while the offense managed just 72 passing yards and 26 rushing yards.
Knowing those numbers stemmed purely from a lack of execution, the Giants took advantage of their chance to regroup and made the adjustments that led them back to the fruitful football they missed in the first 30 minutes.
“[We had] great feedback at halftime,” Likely said.
“Player dialogue, coaches’ dialogue, and really just getting behind your brother. Jameis [Winston] had open ears. He understood that the job in the second half was to get us back in the game, and that’s exactly what he did.”
The Giants returned with renewed offensive energy in the second half as Winston connected with Likely for two scores.
The first came on a 13-play drive that featured three late downs, two penalties, and a near interception by Commanders cornerback Amik Robertson that a pass interference penalty wiped out, putting the Giants within three yards of the end zone for a quick strike to cut the deficit to 19-13.
Likely’s biggest moment came when facing what felt like a must-have fourth-down conversion from the Washington 17, No. 9 put the whole team on his shoulders and didn’t settle for the first down, taking it all the way to the end zone.
“It was fourth down, so in my mind I’m thinking, we got to get in the end zone regardless,” Likely said.
“Knowing the situation, knowing the stakes, knowing that when I get the first down, I can be more cautious with the ball in my hands and try to get down if I can if I’m wrapped up, but, in my mind, I was thinking about scoring and try to go up.”
Likely’s second touchdown, which made him the first Giants tight end with nine or more receptions and two or more touchdowns in a single game, was a clear example of why the organization made it a priority to insert him into its offensive huddle and give him the chance to be a No. 1 option, something he couldn’t be behind Mark Andrews in Baltimore.
While his record start was enough to pull the Giants back from defeat in Washington, it didn’t serve as the centerpiece of a win that would have given the franchise its first 4-1 start since the 2022 season and a two-game lead in the division.
Likely and his teammates know they did their job to force a thrilling comeback when they should have been counted out, but they’ll have to wait for another chance to change the script in Week 6, when they welcome the New Orleans Saints to MetLife Stadium.

title: 6  Winners and 4 Losers From Giants' Wild 27-27 Tie With Commanders
full_text:
The 2026 New York Giants live in the land of chaos. Following game-ending interceptions in back-to-back weeks, Big Blue strapped its fans into a roller coaster that somehow ended in a 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders.
The tie came in part to Washington’s boneheaded final play of the game, in which it clearly looked as though the players on the field, and in particular quarterback Jayden Daniels, forgot that they were out of timeouts.
A scuffling Giants offense sprang to life in the fourth quarter, the team appeared to secure victory in overtime, and then one of the most mind-boggling displays of clock management spared it certain defeat. The John Harbaugh era is off to a wacky yet ultimately productive start.
While Giants fans try to process another emotionally draining game, we will acknowledge the winners and losers from this Week 5 stalemate .
Malik Nabers wanted the ball more and his wish was granted as he was targeted 20 times, a new career high. He could have snagged a couple more receptions, including the one he dropped, but the Giants’ star wide receiver erupted for the second week in a row, posting his second 100-yard receiving effort.
He is showing little effect from the season-ending knee injury he suffered a little more than a year ago. Nabers has displayed outstanding athleticism and explosiveness against the Commanders.
Nabers led the way with 11 receptions for 121 yards and a game-tying touchdown with less than two minutes remaining in regulation.
The former No. 6 overall draft pick also gave New York advantageous field position in overtime on a 28-yard reception. He has figured out Jameis Winston’s tendencies and is once again an unquestioned game-wrecker.
The veteran signal-caller fumbled, which led to a Washington field goal, and missed some other throws, but he is a backup, after all. Overall, Winston made plenty of winning plays and posted his best effort of the season.
Completing 33-of-54 passes for 326 yards and three touchdowns, the 32-year-old helped revive an offense that struggled for much of the afternoon. He led three straight touchdown drives in the second half and carried his signature fighting spirit on the sidelines.
Most importantly, Winston made fairly sound decisions. He put the Giants in position to win and further allayed previous concerns about his job status.
The NFL world expected a huge year two for Abdul Carter, and he hasn’t disappointed through the first quarter. The young outside linebacker couldn’t find consistent form in 2025, which can happen to rookies, but Carter is now stringing together big games.
The 22-year-old registered one sack, five total pressures , and a forced fumble that the Commanders ultimately recovered in overtime. He is stepping up in Brian Burns’ absence and operating as the most important member of the defense.
That’s exactly what the Giants expected when they selected him with the No. 3 pick last year.
Although New York’s starting tight end had some tough moments, most notably three penalties, he remains an igniter in the passing game. Isaiah Likely matched Nabers’ 11 catches, recording 94 yards and two touchdowns at Northwest Stadium.
The Giants spent $26 million guaranteed on Likely, hoping he’d stretch the field and help to expand the playbook. He has done exactly that in 2026. The former fourth-rounder is a safety net on critical downs and can also lift the offense to new heights.
When the Giants hired creative play-caller Dennard Wilson to be their new defensive coordinator, slot cornerback Dru Phillips jumped out as a potential breakout candidate. His intensity should pair well with an aggressive system, and it did on Sunday.
Phillips thrived in Wilson’s blitz-heavy scheme, posting two sacks on quarterback Jayden Daniels and five total tackles. Someone with his high motor shouldn’t fade into the background as he did at times last season. Wilson is wisely emphasizing the 2024 third-rounder’s versatile skill set.
New York allowing Daniels and Jacory Croskey-Merritt to rush for 185 yards combined, but DJ Reader largely held up his end. And he has done so throughout the season.
The 32-year-old, on a two-year, $12.5 million contract, notched three stops against the Commanders, per Pro Football Focus. He is steady and reliable, even when the unit as a whole is not cutting it.
It’s hard to pick on an undrafted rookie who was forced to brave tough weather conditions after sinking the first nine field goals of his NFL career , but I have no choice following his last blunder. But facts are facts: kickers are expected to do their job regardless of the conditions.
Zvada’s missed field-goal attempts from 50 and 57 yards are forgivable, especially in the rain. However, his 46-yard misfire in overtime cost Big Blue dearly.
The 2024 Big Ten Kicker of the Year was unshakable before this rough day in Maryland, so John Harbaugh has to hope he can brush it off and bounce back in Week 6 against the New Orleans Saints.
The NFC Defensive Player of the Month had become a frequent visitor to the winners’ lounge after a hot start to the season, but he wasn’t good enough against Washington.
Jevon Holland missed two tackles, including one that preceded a Jayden Daniels rushing score. He put himself in all the right spots in the first few games, so it was a little surprising to see him out of sorts here. He could regain momentum against an interception-prone Tyler Shough.
Although Cam Skattebo set up the Giants for the win by rushing for 33 yards on their final drive, he is one of the biggest reasons New York doesn’t currently own a two-game lead in the NFC East. You have to hold onto the ball.
The second-year running back fumbled at the Commanders’ 24-yard line in overtime, ensuring Big Blue wouldn’t leave Landover with a win. Daniels’ incomprehensible decision not to take a knee on the ensuing drive lowers the heat a bit, but Skattebo still made a brutal mistake.
New York’s backfield must fix its ball-security problem, or more game-changing turnovers will eventually follow.
Despite making some nice tackles, the 25-year-old still fell short in an important area. He took a bad angle on a Jacory Croskey-Merritt touchdown run, putting the Giants in an early 6-0 hole. Nubin still has upside, but he needs to become more fundamentally sound.
New York will not blossom into a true playoff-worthy squad until it consistently prevents monster gains and big scores.

title: NFL Insider Dishes on Giants’ Potential Trade Activity as Deadline Approaches
full_text:
So far, the NFL has seen a smattering of significant in-season trades. Among the most notable: the New York Giants acquiring quarterback J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings, the Baltimore Ravens getting center Cam Jurgens from the Philadelphia Eagles, and the Houston Texans landing receiver Marvin Harrison from the Arizona Cardinals.
But according to one NFL insider, what’s happened so far could be just the tip of the iceberg.
“I don’t think the trade market heats up for another two weeks,” Jordan Schultz said in an interview with the Locked On Giants podcast , dropping Monday evening.
“I do think it will be a very active deadline. I think most teams right now still feel like they have a great shot at making the playoffs. By the deadline, I think that number might dwindle. There’s still a lot of teams that wanna be buyers.”
The Giants, who have been aggressive in fine-tuning their roster via free-agent signings and the McCarthy trade, the latter made after the team lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season to a torn ACL, may not be finished, according to Schultz.
Rumors continue to swirl that the team could look to move outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux, who is currently playing out the option year of his rookie deal, via trade.
Schultz reported in the offseason that the New Orleans Saints had interest in Thibodeaux before pivoting to Tyree Wilson of the Raiders, presumably because the Giants’ asking price for their 2022 first-round pick was too high at the time.
But with Thibodeaux off to a sluggish start this season, even with more opportunities after Brian Burns’ season-ending knee injury, plus the rapid growth of rookie Arvell Reese and second-year man Abdul Carter, Schultz thinks the Giants could still move Thibodeaux via trade.
“I think there’d be a market,” Schultz said regarding Thibodeaux. “It’s interesting to me how most teams value mid-round picks at a very high premium. Most teams hate to give up picks anyway, but mid-round picks are of extra value — those third, fourth and fifth picks teams hate to give up.
“I think for Thibodeaux, that’s what it would be at this point. You know, he’s still a young player. It would either be an injury, a team that has an injured rusher, or the Giants just saying, ‘We wanna cut ties because we’re four and a half years into this thing and we, you know, don’t feel that he’s part of the future here.’
“I don’t know the answer to that just yet. I think there’ll be more clarity in the next couple of weeks,” he added.
If the Giants were to move Thibodeaux, their cap savings would come to approximately $867,705 for every week he is not on the roster. There would be no dead money involved in the trade either since he is in his contract’s option year.

title: Giants Reportedly Hosting Yannick Ngakoue for Workout
full_text:
The New York Giants may soon be making an interesting addition to their defensive front.
Just moments after battling the Washington Commanders to a 27-27 tie in Week 5 , NFL insider Jordan Schultz reported that New York will be hosting former Pro Bowl defensive end Yannick Ngakoue for a workout on Monday, Oct. 12.
Ngakoue, 31, last played in the NFL in 2024, when he suited up for six games with the New England Patriots after joining the team following his release by the Baltimore Ravens in November. During his stint in Foxborough, he registered nine total tackles. In all, he compiled 14 tackles and 1.5 sacks in 11 games that season.
The 6-foot-3, 250-pound defender sat out the 2025 season to let his body recover from injuries, most notably a lingering ankle injury that caused him to miss the latter part of the 2023 season. Per Schultz’s report, he is now fully healthy and ready to return to the field.
Ngakoue is a veteran of nine NFL seasons through 2024 with the Jacksonville Jaguars (2016-19), Minnesota Vikings (2020), Ravens (2020 and 2024, under Giants coach John Harbaugh ), Las Vegas Raiders (2021), Indianapolis Colts (2022) and Chicago Bears (2023), in addition to the Patriots in the latter part of 2024.
Ngakoue originally entered the NFL as a third-round draft pick (69th overall) of Jacksonville out of Maryland. Overall, he has played in 134 NFL games with 115 starts and has 238 total tackles, 70.5 sacks, two interceptions (one returned for a touchdown), 13 passes defensed, and 21 forced fumbles.
As the NFL’s Nov. 10 trade deadline approaches, several analysts have wondered whether the Giants may look to make changes along their defensive front, specifically regarding the future of outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux.
With outside linebacker Brian Burns out for the season due to a torn ACL, the Giants are relying on the depth of their front seven to provide additional help on the outside. Thibodeaux has been aligning at the edge, given his experience and skill set.
Still, Thibodeaux continues to struggle. Through New York’s first five games, the Oregon product has generated only seven pressures per PFF and has yet to register a sack in 203 defensive snaps. Against the run, he recorded two solo tackles. He logged only one tackle against the Commanders in Week 5.
If the Giants trade Thibodeaux, they would not incur any dead money because of his expiring contract. Though he and Ngakoue play similar positions, Thibodeaux has traditionally been a better run defender, while Ngakoue is at his best in pass-defense packages.
In the final analysis, it would not be inconceivable for New York, which currently has an open spot on its 53-man roster, to carry both players, helping bolster a front seven that has been playing aggressive football under first-year defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson.

title: Cam Skattebo Vows to Fix Ball Security After Overtime Fumble Against Commanders
full_text:
New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo walked both sides of the double-edged sword during the club’s Week 5 27-27 overtime thriller against the Washington Commanders.
On one end of the blade, Skattebo’s powerful rushing style helped him accumulate 59 yards on the ground for New York, including a 19-yard run that helped the offense approach field-goal range during its second possession in overtime.
Unfortunately, the other end saw the 24-year-old fumble the ball just five snaps later when Commanders defensive tackle Daron Payne stripped Skattebo on a rushing attempt. Washington recovered at its own 24-yard line, needing only a field goal to defeat the Giants .
However, in one of the more bizarre endings to an NFL game in recent memory, the Commanders’ bid to win ended on 2nd-and-8 at the Giants’ 24-yard line. Following a sack of Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, Washington failed to align for the final snap with 12 seconds remaining. Instead, the clock ran out, tying the game 27-27.
Though Skattebo and the Giants avoided defeat, the second-year running back realized his clutch-time commission of football’s cardinal sin would require immediate reconciliation.
“I fumbled the ball. We can’t have that. I understand that,” Skattebo said postgame. “I’m going to go into the film room and get it fixed. I felt like I had good protection. The kid made a [heck] of a play.
“I think in that situation what I think I could do differently is try not to get the extra yards because we’re already in a good position and continue to take care of the ball,” he continued.
“If I get tackled for a loss at one yard, then I get tackled for a loss at one yard.”
For a player who said he prides himself on “going for the ‘W,’” Skattebo learned a tough lesson about the fragility of defeat.
“I’m the player that tries to fight for as many yards as possible for this team,” he acknowledged. “It bit me in the [backside] there. I got to make sure I protect the ball for this football team. We win that game if I do.”
Skattebo’s charisma and playing style have rapidly made him a favorite among Giants fans. Selected in the fourth round (105th overall) in the 2025 NFL Draft, the 5-foot-11, 215-pound back compiled 410 yards (4.1 average) and five touchdowns in eight games last season.
Unfortunately, a dislocated ankle suffered in Week 8 prematurely ended what had become a promising rookie season.
After a strong performance during both training camp and the preseason, he returned to the gridiron in Week 1 to much acclaim. To date, he has carried the ball 81 times for 294 yards and one touchdown.
Still, Skattebo has fumbled the ball four times this season, including his Week 5 miscue against the Commanders. While he has taken accountability for his struggles, the Arizona State product knows true improvement won’t happen unless he performs better on the field.
“I think the players that come out of those things are the best players,” Skattebo said. “The people that can move past that and go into next week and take care of the ball and win the game. When their number is called again, they take care of it. I think that’s what makes the best players. So, when that happens, it’s going to happen.”
With the Giants now at 3-1-1, Skattebo would like nothing more than to help his team return to the win column when they host the New Orleans Saints (1-4) at MetLife Stadium in Week 6. For as much as he will learn from this experience, New York’s top rusher must execute at the highest level, a lesson he was destined to learn … win, lose or draw.
“It wasn’t a loss, and it wasn’t a win,” Skattebo said. “I think somebody explained it to us as a lesson. We could have fixed some things. I gave up the ball at the end there. We learned lessons today, especially I did. Once we get past that and we learn from those, get them fixed, and then it’s a different ball game.”

title: Giants Report Card: Offense, Defense Rally for 27-27 Tie With Commanders
full_text:
The New York Giants tied the Washington Commanders 27-27 in Week 5. Here are the grades.
The showing might have seemed ugly at times, but a closer look at the numbers tells a different story.
The Giants outgained the Commanders 408 to 378 in net yards. Big Blue was also 3-for-3 in the red zone, while Washington was 0-for-1.
Jameis Winston’s day started shaky, with 7-of-16 completions for 72 yards and no touchdowns. In the second half, he went 21 of 28 for 211 yards and three touchdowns, with his completion percentage improving by leaps and bounds each quarter.
Malik Nabers wanted the ball, and he was targeted 20 times, catching 11 for his second straight 100-yard receiving game, a showing that also included one drop. Tight end Isaiah Likely also had a busy day, catching 11 of 13 targets, including all three on third down.
The biggest gut punch, though, was the running game, and in particular the lost fumble in overtime by Cam Skattebo. It marked the team’s fifth fumble in as many games and its third lost fumble, both of which lead the league.
It’s bad enough that the running game struggled to get going, finishing with an average of 3.7 yards per carry (3.5 if you discount the quarterbacks’ contributions).
We’re reluctant to blame the Commanders on the fact that quarterback Jayden Daniels alone accounted for 103 of the team’s 202 rushing yards and two of its three touchdowns on the day (all on the ground), considering the Giants didn’t assign a spy on him (see coaching).
Take away Daniels’ rushing yards, and the run defense gave up only 99 rushing yards on 21 carries, 4.71 yards per carry, which looks a lot better than the 6.7 yards per carry the unit surrendered when you include Daniels’ yardage.
The pass rush added five more sacks to its season total, while the coverage allowed no touchdowns. Arvell Reese (13.3%) and Abdul Carter (15.6%) were among the Giants’ best rushers by pass-rush win rate .
Rookie kicker Dominic Zvada had a rough day at the office, missing three of his five field-goal attempts, all from at least 45 yards out.
Zvada wasn’t completely shut out of the field-goal conversion column, though. The rookie nailed 51- and 56-yard attempts. Chalk it up to the day’s wet, sloppy conditions.
Charlie Jones had a solid day of return work on both kickoffs (26.0 average) and punts (13.0 average). Jones showed decisiveness and acceleration on each return, which helped his offense get a decent starting field position each time.
Jordan Stout punted only twice, forcing one fair catch, while the lone returned punt went for only two yards. That’s a 57-yard gross average and a 56-yard net average for this field-position flipper.
It was disheartening to learn they didn’t call for a spy on quarterback Jayden Daniels on the quarterback runs, which included two rushing touchdowns, one of them a 38-yarder.
We’re still not sure what went into the decisions to insert quarterback J.J. McCarthy in the game when they did, as there didn’t appear to be a rhyme or reason behind it, but that might have been a result of simply taking what Washington gave them.
We're also not sure why the coaches asked Doinic Zvada to try the long field goals in the conditions, but we suppose at some point, the rookie is going to have to learn to deal with that in his career.
But to give credit where it’s due, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy adjusted the offense to a more uptempo pace in the second half, and the Giants became more productive as they fought back from a 14-point deficit.

title: Giants Comeback Effort Ends in 27-27 Overtime Tie with Commanders
full_text:
The New York Giants sure do keep things interesting on Sundays.
On a damp, rainy afternoon in Landover, Maryland, Big Blue battled through sloppy conditions and missed opportunities as they and the Washington Commanders put on a riveting second-half show, culminating in an incredulous 27-27 overtime tie at Northwest Stadium.
Giants starting quarterback Jameis Winston once again took Big Blue Nation on a roller-coaster ride, throwing for 326 yards with three touchdowns. Commanders starter Jayden Daniels — returning from an injury to his non-throwing elbow — completed 17 passes for 199 yards and two rushing scores.
However, a 12-second runoff at the end of the game’s extra period will be scrutinized for weeks.
With the tie, New York now moves to 3-1-1 on the season, while Washington drops to 1-3-1. Despite failing to secure the win, New York maintains sole possession of first place in the NFC East heading into Week 6.
The Commanders struck first with a four-play, 69-yard scoring drive on the game’s opening possession. Daniels connected with Commanders tight end Chig Okonkwo on two passes for 34 yards, helping set up a 33-yard touchdown run by running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Washington kicker Drew Stevens pushed his extra point attempt wide to the left, keeping the club’s lead at 6-0.
The Giants earned their first points of the day on their third offensive series, a five-play 22-yard drive with just over two minutes remaining in the first quarter. Winston found receiver Malik Nabers for a 20-yard gain on 1st-and-10 from their own 45, advancing into Washington territory. Rookie kicker Dominic Zvada capped the drive with a 51-yard field goal to cut the Commanders’ lead to 6-3.
Unfortunately, New York would be limited to just those three points for the entire half. On a day when establishing the run was vital to their success, the Giants couldn't find a rhythm. The club averaged only 2.2 yards per carry in the first half and managed just 77 yards of offense.
Perhaps their best opportunity to put Washington on its heels came with just over two minutes remaining in the second quarter. Facing a 9-3 deficit, Winston was sacked by Commanders linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson on 2nd-and-8 from their own 47. Chaisson also forced a fumble by the Giants’ quarterback, which defensive tackle Tim Settle recovered.
On the ensuing drive, Stevens made a 40-yard field goal to give the Commanders a 12-3 lead at the two-minute warning.
The Giants tried to close the gap as time expired in the second quarter on Zvada’s trusty leg. New York’s rookie hooked the 57-yard attempt sharply to the left. As a result, Washington took their 12-3 lead into halftime.
New York opened the third quarter with a seven-play, 30-yard drive, highlighted by a 14-yard connection from Winston to Nabers. The Giants’ rookie redeemed his shoe by booting a 56-yard attempt through the uprights, cutting the Commanders’ lead to 12-6.
Washington, however, did not allow the Giants very long to rest on their laurels. The Commanders traveled 77 yards on five plays, including a 17-yard connection from Daniels to receiver Antonio Williams. Daniels then took advantage of a gaping hole in New York’s run defense for a 38-yard touchdown run. Stevens’ extra point extended Washington's lead to 19-6.
Determined to find the end zone, the Giants finally earned their first touchdown of the day on a 13-play, 63-yard drive to close the third quarter. Despite losing starting right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor to a calf injury, Winston rallied his offense. After a would-be interception by Washington defensive back Amik Robertson was overturned as defensive pass interference, Winston found tight end Isaiah Likely for the three-yard touchdown pass — cutting the Commanders’ lead to 19-13
The Commanders took back control of the game, as Daniels led his team on an eight-play, 81-yard drive. Washington’s third-year quarterback once again took matters into his own hands for a 26-yard rush for the score. He then connected with receiver Terry McLaurin for the Two-Point Conversion and a 27-13 lead.
Still, New York would not go quietly into the murky air in Landover. Winston led New York 75 yards on nine plays, highlighted by a 21-yard completion from Winston to tight end Theo Johnson. The Giants starter once again found his favorite target, Likely, for 17 yards and the touchdown — slicing Washington’s lead to 27-20.
The Giants made it an official comeback on their ensuing offensive series. Winston used just over three minutes to lead his team on a 10-play, 72-yard drive to tie the game. Nabers hauled in the 17-yard pass for the touchdown, tying the game at 27-27 with under two minutes remaining.
LEEEEEEEEEK 🔥 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/cw4k9WPpp6
With the Commanders’ last drive resulting in a necessary punt, the Giants erased a 14-point deficit to force overtime, with the score tied at 27.
The Giants started the game’s extra period with the ball. Winston took 2:03 off the clock to lead New York 39 yards on eight plays. Unfortunately for Big Blue, Zvada couldn't connect on his 46-yard field goal attempt, giving Washington the ball at their own 36-yard line with 7:57 remaining.
The Commanders, however, could not capitalize. The four-play, 13-yard drive ended in a punt — giving the ball back to the Giants at their own 9-yard line.
Winston connected with Nabers on an eight-yard completion and a 28-yard deep ball, the latter coming on the heels of a 19-yard run by Cam Skattebo. The Giants had the ball on 1st-and-10 at the Washington 24-yard line.
Ultimately, the comeback could not be completed. While running up the middle, Skattebo fumbled the ball after Commanders defenisve tackle Daron Payne stripped it. Payne and defensive tackle Shy Tuttle moved into position to repossess the ball, which Tuttle eventually recovered.
However, in what could only be described as one of the most incredible endings to an NFL game in recent memory, the Commanders’ bid to win ended on 2nd-and-8 at the Giants’ 24-yard line.
After Giants defender Tremaine Edmunds sacked Daniels, Washington couldn't align to take the final snap with 12 seconds remaining. Instead, the clock ran out, resulting in a 27-27 tie.
A wild finish to Giants-Commanders game pic.twitter.com/0QvJGVIPbG
Giants’ starting left tackle Jermaine Eluemunor suffered a calf injury with just over six minutes remaining in the third quarter and did not return to the game.
Rookie cornerback Colton Hood absorbed a hit to the head that bloodied his nose and forced him out of the game late in the third quarter. He was immediately taken for evaluation for a concussion.
At the start of the fourth quarter, Giants safety Tyler Nubin also took a hit to his head/neck area. Nubin left the field of his own accord, and he was declared questionable to return with a neck issue.
Giants kicker Dominic Zvada snapped his perfect streak of field goals by missing a 51–yard attempt with 7:15 remaining in the first quarter. Zvada entered the game at 9-for-9 on field goal attempts this season and leads all rookies in points scored with 32.
Despite taking a 17-16 lead on kicker Jake Elliott's 48-yard field goal with eight seconds left, the Philadelphia Eagles fell to 2-3 after Jacksonville Jaguars’ return man Ameer Abdullah returned the ensuing kickoff for 53 yards. Kicker Cam Little connected on a 57-yard attempt as time expired to give the Jags a 19-17 victory over the Eagles at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, England.
The Dallas Cowboys (2-3) suffered a 24-16 defeat to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers earlier this week in prime time. Bucs running back Bucky Irving ran for 165 yards, including a 72-yard run to set up the touchdown that put Tampa Bay ahead for the win.
The Giants return home to the friendly confines of MetLife Stadium to host the New Orleans Saints (1-4) in a Week 6 matchup. The Saints will arrive on the heels of a 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Kickoff is set for 1:00 p.m. ET.

title: Three Key Giants Exit Week 5 Game vs. Washington with Injuries
full_text:
The New York Giants have once again been hit by the injury wave, as a trio of key contributors has exited their Week 5 showdown with the Washington Commanders.
At the time of the injuries, New York trailed Washington 27-13 at Northwest Stadium.
With 6:42 remaining in the third quarter, Giants starting right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor suffered a calf injury. The veteran lineman was helped to the sideline where he was checked, before being taken to the locker room for further evaluation. He was soon thereafter listed as questionable to return.
Just moments after Eluemunor left the game, New York’s rookie cornerback Colton Hood appeared to take a head hit on the kickoff attempt as time expired in the third quarter.
Hood stayed down before being taken to the sideline, nursing a visible bloody nose. The Giants’ defensive back was taken to the locker room to be evaluated for a concussion.
The Giants drafted Hood No. 37 overall in the second round of April’s draft. He entered the game after appearing in all four games and compiling seven total tackles. Hood had logged three tackles at the time of his injury.
At the start of the fourth quarter, Giants safety Tyler Nubin also took a hit to his head/neck area with 13 minutes remaining. Nubin left the field of his own accord, and he is questionable to return with a neck issue.
The Giants entered this matchup without defensive lineman/outside linebacker Chauncey Golston, who was placed on injured reserve (IR) earlier this weekend.
Golston suffered a neck injury in last week’s win over the Arizona Cardinals. The 28-year-old also missed five consecutive games in 2025 due to a neck injury. It remains unclear as to whether the reason for his absences last year is the same issue bothering him this season.
Safety Jason Pinock was also ruled out after failing to clear concussion protocol in time to be activated for Week 5. Pinnock left the Giants’ Week 4 victory over the Cardinals before the start of the third quarter to be evaluated for the head injury.
On the positive side, left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin), tight end Isaiah Likely (knee/groin), tight end Chris Manhertz (shoulder), and running back Cam Skattebo were upgraded to full practice participants earlier this week and were active for this game against the Commanders. But Thomas has looked as though he’s labored all game long.

title: Giants vs. Commanders Live Blog: Updates, Analysis and Reaction From Week 5
full_text:
The New York Giants and Washington Commanders share one of the league’s oldest rivalries, with two teams that regularly slug it out for the ‘W.’
They’ll do so again today in what is predicted to be wet and miserable weather—perfect football weather, some might say—at Northwest Stadium, home of the Commanders.
If the rain forecast holds, it will mark the second week in a row the Giants play in sloppy, wet conditions.
“I feel like we've gotten a lot of practice. Our very first camp practice was in the rain,” said head coach John Harbaugh.
“We should be fine. But we're still going to be intentional about it and focused on it. Ball handling, throwing the ball, catching the ball. And footing, too. Footing is another big deal. It's even a bigger deal on a grass field like that. We're going to have to really be thinking about our footing.”
They better be thinking about that and more because the Giants are up for a chance to keep a hold on sole possession of first place in the division and to take a 2-0 lead over their division opponents.
“Yeah, I think you take notice. It's talked about, probably not too specifically,” said Harbaugh when asked if he pays attention to what’s going on in the division at this point.
“It's more like you talk about it probably at work with your colleagues and friends and stuff. ‘You see the game last night?’ You kind of keep track of a little bit of the division, certainly more than the other teams that you're playing against.”
The Commanders, meanwhile, are back from their 30-13 loss to the Colts in London with a banged-up football team looking to steady its ship against a divisional foe they've beaten in the last four meetings, two by one score or less.
But in some good news for the Commanders, they will have Jayden Daniels, their starting quarterback, back in the lineup after a two-week absence due to a left elbow injury that will now require Daniels, whom head coach Dan Quinn said will have no restrictions, to wear a protective brace.
Can Daniels, who has been a nuisance to the Giants defense in the past because of his dual-threat ability, keep tormenting Big Blue? Or will the Giants offense have a huge, productive day against a struggling Commanders defense?
Follow along with our live blog, featuring a curated collection of observations, highlights, and more leading up to and through the game.
And don’t forget to check New York Giants On SI after the game for our complete postgame coverage.

title: Giants, Commanders Inactives: McLaurin Active; McCarthy Moves Up to QB2
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy is officially No. 2 on the quarterback depth chart.
McCarthy will serve as the backup quarterback behind starter Jameis Winston in this week’s game against the Washington Commanders. Jake Haener, who was signed to the 53-man roster from the practice squad this week, will be the emergency quarterback.
McCarthy, who is on a crash course to learn the Giants’ offense, drew rave reviews from offensive coordinator Matt Nagy this week when asked how he has been progressing in learning the system.
“I would say it’s an A-plus. He’s doing really well. That’s as best as I can put it,” Nagy said. “You look back seven days ago when we were up here having the same conversation, he’s much further along, which is, again, a credit to our position coaches and (quarterbacks coach) Brian Callahan, (offensive quality control coach) Mike Snyder.
“These guys are spending a lot of time putting time in with J.J. and with Jake (Haener) just in case. At the same point in time, J.J. is spending a lot of time trying to learn everything. So, that part has been great. Proud of him, but this is just the beginning. But I’d say A-plus right now.”
Head coach John Harbaugh admitted that the team had a package of plays for McCarthy in its offensive game plan last week against the Cardinals. It’s believed that the same package, and then some, is still in place for this week’s game against the Commanders. However, whether they’ll actually roll any of those plays out largely depends on the flow of the game and how Winston does. Winston is seeking his third straight win as a starter, something he hasn’t done since 2021 with the Saints.
Speaking of Haener, he will be the emergency quarterback after being signed off the practice squad earlier this week. League rules require the emergency quarterback to be on the 53-man roster rather than a standard practice-squad elevation.
As for the Giants’ inactive list, their lone injury-related scratch is safety Jason Pinnock, who remains in the concussion protocol after getting dinged in last week’s win over Arizona. Pinnock’s absence likely means an increased role for Ar’Darius Washington on defense.

title: 5 Studs & 3 Duds in Jets' Season-Saving Win Over Browns in Week 5
full_text:
It wasn't pretty. It wasn't sexy.
But at the end of the day, a win in the NFL counts the same no matter how it was achieved. The New York Jets understand that better than anyone after their 17-12 comeback victory over the Cleveland Browns on Sunday.
In a rain-soaked contest in which the Jets tried to end a three-game losing streak, New York outplayed the AFC North-leading Browns before a 29-yard touchdown pass from Deshaun Watson to Denzel Boston gave Cleveland the lead in the final quarter.
After a Jets fumble, the Browns fumbled the snap on a punt, setting up Gang Green's offense to take the lead for good. Now, at 2-3, the Jets will try to build on this win.
And there were plenty of studs that helped them along the way.
When a team drafts a player with one of the top five picks in an NFL Draft, the hope is that they will have a "Welcome to the NFL" moment, a game where he proves exactly why he is a top prospect in the league. After four weeks, Jets fans were getting impatient that second-overall pick David Bailey hadn't had that moment .
Bailey was the best player on the field on Sunday, totaling three sacks, four quarterback hits, and seven pressures. Even better, Bailey made several excellent plays against the run that stymied the Browns' rushing attack.
So far this season, Bailey has recorded five sacks and leads the team in pressures. On Sunday, he proved why the Jets made him the second overall pick.
After missing the last two games, Mason Taylor returned and added another wrinkle to their offense. Many wondered how Taylor's play would mix with first-round rookie Kenyon Sadiq.
Overall, though, the tight end position was quite disappointing on Sunday.
Taylor caught just three passes for 24 yards. He laid some strong blocks in the running game, but needs to be more impactful in the passing game. The day wasn't much better for Sadiq either. The rookie made two catches for three yards and lost a fumble in the red zone. In fairness to him, he did get hit hard and had to leave the game with a concussion. But a turnover like that cannot happen.
New York will need more impact plays from this tight end room.
How about the Jets kicker? The weather was atrocious, and Jason Sanders was abysmal all training camp. Yet at the start of the fourth quarter, Sanders nailed a 54-yard field goal in the pouring rain. It was an important field goal, as it put the team within striking distance when the Browns responded with a touchdown.
So far this season, Sanders has been quite good so far this season. He looked like his old All-Pro self.
The drought finally ended, but it's not like the team has seemingly turned the corner with their four-minute offense. The only reason the Jets finally got the job done after going eight straight games without scoring in the final four minutes of the first half and regulation was Cleveland's fumbled punt.
They executed enough to score a touchdown, but they failed to score going into halftime after committing several penalties again, and they couldn't even drain the clock when they got the ball back with the lead in the closing minutes of action. Just because the defense wrapped the game up on its own doesn't excuse the offense.
The group needs to be better when it matters most.
Several young players had great games for the Jets. Chief among them was running back Braelon Allen . He went over 100 yards on 24 carries, including the game-winner from 23 yards out. His best run, though, came when he ran over a Brown and broke it outside for a big gain.
This performance showed how good Allen could be going forward. Getting him to run downhill changes how this running game could look. In fact, this was the best he's looked in his career.
I wouldn't say Stephens had a bad game. However, I'd say he was beaten on the two plays that mattered most at the time. He was called for pass interference on Cleveland's last scoring drive that kept the ball in the Browns' hands.
He also gave up the touchdown in single coverage. If the Browns hadn't fumbled their punt and the Jets hadn't scored, Stephens' play would be highlighted worse than people realize.
For the most part, though, the former Baltimore Raven has been quite good this season. He'll need to be better on Sunday, though.
Garrett Wilson had another dominant game. Ho hum - it must be Sunday.
Wilson's seven-catch, 104-yard day led the way for New York's offense, which included a 32-yard touchdown in which Wilson spun away from a would-be tackler to get into the end zone. He is New York's best offensive weapon and remains the go-to guy this season .
New York's pass rush was exceptional on Sunday. As a collective unit, they recorded eight sacks. Even with how good the group was, though, fourth-round rookie Darrell Jackson Jr. really stood out on his own.
The Florida State product recorded his first career sack on Sunday, but he also had two pass deflections late in the fourth quarter. If he continues to play as he did on Sunday, he will become a consistent player on New York's interior defensive line.
And one of the better late-round picks made in the last few years.
Thomas could have had a game-ending interception on the final drive, but he'll have to settle for a key pass breakup. So far this season, the second-year cornerback has played very well and easily looked like the team's best cornerback on Sunday.
His size and physicality are a perfect fit for the blitz-heavy approach that the Jets want to run with Aaron Glenn. If Thomas continues to perform like he has this season, it will only enhance the team's outlook moving forward.

title: David Bailey Speaks Out on Jets' Role, Development, and More
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- Perhaps expectations were too high for second overall pick David Bailey coming into the NFL.
After being taken as the first non-quarterback of the 2026 draft by the New York Jets , Bailey dominated training camp in such a flurry that many wondered how good the Texas Tech product could be right away.
Through his first four NFL games, Bailey hasn't popped off like other rookie defensive players, but he also hasn't been bad either. If anything, the rookie has gone through the usual peaks and valleys that hit most high-talent rookies.
Even if he doesn't get caught up in the predictions from fans and media members.
"I'm not really too worried about expectations," Bailey said after practice on Friday. "I'm probably just more worried about like how I can help the team."
As he prepares for his fifth NFL game, and with the Jets sitting at a 1-3 mark, the team will be looking for Bailey to produce more than he already has. Confident as always, it appears Bailey is ready to show out again.
Coming into this season, the Jets seemingly had a different role for Bailey than the one where he dominated at Texas Tech. With the Red Raiders, Bailey led the country in sacks and was one of the most formidable edge rushers out there.
Now, the size and speed of the NFL game has the 23-year-old adjusting to new things.
"It's definitely just different," Bailey said. "There's a lot of factors that you gotta take into level competition, new defense. I'm working with new people...But you know at the end of the day it's just football. I still feel comfortable."
One of those adjustments is no longer being an everydown pass rusher. Over the last several games, the Jets have used Bailey in pass coverage at times. It has perplexed some fans who have wondered why the everydown edge rusher is not being used in the situation he was drafted for.
To his credit, it's not like Bailey hasn't had experience in that role.
"Definitely did that a lot in my Stanford days," Bailey said of dropping into coverage. "Playing kind of like that SAM linebacker role, obviously didn't do it too much at Tech."
Of course, for a team that has struggled so mightily to pressure the quarterback, one would imagine getting more pass rushing reps for Bailey would be smart. The rookie has recorded two sacks but none of them have come off of beating a tackle to the spot. They have come courtesy of his high motor.
And while that is something the Jets love to see from a young player, it highlights how much more he needs to grow.
One area of Bailey's game that has been unequivocally improved compared to his college days has been in run defense. At Texas Tech, Bailey wasn't seen as a run stuffer. If anything, the Red Raiders would use him more as a situational pass rusher than actually focus on the run.
Through four games in the NFL, though, and Bailey's run defense has been a welcome surprise. Pro Football Focus has graded out Bailey as the 14th best run stopping edge rusher in the league.
The youngster was quick to credit his coaching staff for getting him ready to improve in that area.
"That just came down to kind of like the work that I was putting in with my D-line and Coach Dunbar," Bailey said. "It just kind of came down to like it wasn't a question whether I could do it, just whether like I had all my tools in place."
Bailey's sack totals will eventually come in droves as he gets used to the NFL game. But his high motor and improved run defense could be what makes him a complete player moving forward.
So what happens next? What do the Jets need to do with Bailey in order to get the most out of him.
Speaking to defensive line coach Karl Dunbar, it's clear the Jets are on schedule with Bailey. He hasn't looked like a superstar yet, but he's improved to the point where he'll only get better with the more games he plays.
"I think he's on par for what we're trying to ask him to do," Dunbar said. "I think he does a great job of getting to the passer. These last couple of weeks, you wouldn't think you'd have tight ends and running backs chipping the rookie, but he's getting that work."
New York does not have many competent edge rushers outside of Bailey on their roster. Will McDonald has struggled , and the free agent acquisitions of Kingsley Enagbare and Joseph Ossai have yet to be truly impactful against opposing teams.
It's why the Jets want Bailey not just to win one-on-one matchups, but to play within the structure of their defense.
"(We're) trying to let him understand how he has to work with other guys and just can't be trying to beat everybody by himself. It's a four-man rush. It's not a one-man rush, a two-man rush," Dunbar said.
Through four games, Bailey has shown enough for Jets fans to realize there is a good player in here. When he reaches his potential will determine greatly on whether the team is willing to work with him in his more natural environment.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Mason Taylor Dishes on Return to Jets After Injury
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- When Mason Taylor first entered the 2026 offseason, the expectation was that he would take a significant jump in his second season. After all, this was a player who was not only a second-round pick in 2025, but finished in the top two with the New York Jets in receptions and receiving yards.
Then the injury bug hit him.
As it did to start his rookie campaign, Taylor suffered a thumb injury that kept him out for the last two weeks of the season. New York lost both of those games, and currently sits at 1-3 on the year. But with Taylor set to be back from his injury on Sunday, the team's expectations for him have not changed.
"Just because things happened with him (Taylor) within this season as far as injuries, that doesn't mean that my expectations have dropped at all," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "He's a really good player, so I look forward to seeing how he progresses as he gets back out there."
As Taylor gears up for Sunday, though, one constant message has stayed true to him since he got to the NFL.
It was early in Glenn's press conference Friday morning. The Jets head coach announced that Taylor would be back after a two-game absence . Speaking to Jets on SI after practice, the second-year tight end's smile was evident.
He was back doing what he always wanted.
"I mean, I'm excited to get back out. It was tough watching  the team not be on the field with them," Taylor said. "So definitely looking forward to it."
Taylor joins a Jets offense in desperate need of his talent. While the emergence of rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq has been celebrated, and with Garrett Wilson remaining an elite player, the Jets have also been ravaged by injuries.
Going into Sunday, the team will be without Breece Hall, Omar Cooper Jr. Adonai Mitchell, and Dylan Parham. That's a third of New York's starting offense being unable to go. Taylor will be an instant weapon—one that has plenty of chemistry with the quarterback as well.
“We put a lot of work in the offseason, he was always willing to get out there, it was super hot, but he didn’t mind it,” Jets quarterback Geno Smith said of Taylor in the offseason. “South Florida kid, seemed to be that way. But he’s a guy who I think is going to be a great player in this league for a long time.”
Things are different than when Taylor first went down, though. And while the group is happy with each other, New York's logjam at tight end means the LSU product will need to compete for snaps and targets at his own position.
When the Jets brought in Taylor, the hope was that he would be the organization's starting tight end for years to come. A year later, and New York drafted another tight end, this one in the first round and with more athleticism than the son of the Hall-of-Fame edge rusher.
Kenyon Sadiq's role on the team is growing, especially after the first 100-yard performance from a tight end in over a decade for Gang Green against Detroit two weeks ago. Watching from the sideline couldn't have been easy for Taylor.
But there isn't even a remote sense of jealousy coming from him.
“I think it's awesome to see what he's done, and I know he's going to keep doing that," Taylor said. "We all have certain roles to play. I'm going to go fit my role in some way.”
New York drafted Sadiq with the hope that he and Taylor would form the best 1-2 tight end duo in football. Injuries have kept the two off the field together, but there's hope that, with Taylor back, a new dimension of the Jets' offense can be brought to the field.
As long as Taylor heeds the words of both his father and coach.
"Just stay the course," Taylor said. "I know AG says that a lot. Stay the course. Don't waver. So that's what I'm going to do. I'm not going to flinch, and I'm going to go out there on Sunday and play like I've never been out."
If Taylor is healthy, he will change how the Browns attack the offense on Sunday. It will be up to him to prove he is worthy of a return to his starting spot.
And worthy of getting plenty of targets as well.

title: Too Soft? Jets' Players Defend Practice Plan Despite Backlash
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- Are the New York Jets soft?
Since head coach Aaron Glenn was hired by the team, he brought a specific swagger and intensity into the organization. Through 21 games, though, his 4-17 record is among the worst for coaches during that same time in NFL history.
Glenn did himself no favors this week either. The head coach called for a walkthrough for the entire team on Wednesday. Instead of trying to physically prepare the group for Sunday, the team chose to try and stay healthy.
Will it work? Time will tell.
But it's clear that the Jets did their research on making sure their process is best served to stay healthy.
And it has nothing to do whether they are soft or not.
The allegations were apparent from the moment the Jets walked into the facility on Wednesday. Their head coach has switched the practice around to have Wednesday become a walkthrough and nothing more.
But a walkthrough practice? In Week 5 of the NFL season?
Teams who do this normally are doing it towards the end of the year. The fact New York did this so early in the season is where some of the "soft" moniker came from. But speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Glenn's plan was clear.
And it had everything to do with their performance last Sunday.
"Defense had a good amount of plays, and plus I want this to be a recovery day anyway," Glenn said. "Just to make sure we take care of our bodies and get ready to go through this week on a good note to play against a good team."
New York's defense was on the field for 93 total plays including penalties in their loss. Even the most shaped up defense can crack under the weight of that many snaps. Does it still make the team soft, though? Even when the team needs to start racking up wins?
It was abundantly clear from the Jets locker room: the amount of injuries and plays run by the defense led to the walkthrough on Wednesday. Glenn wanted to make sure his team would be fresh for the start of October games.
In doing so, he pleased some of the more aging veterans on the team like Harrison Phillips.
"Our team here has done a fantastic job of kind of modifying based on snap counts and how we do our lift structure during the week and our practice plan during the week to help mitigate that," Phillips said.
New York has still managed to find a way to be banged up as a collective unit. Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper Jr. and Dylan Parham are just some of the team's concerning injury list.
But for the players who are suiting up, like Phillips especially, they have appreciated the team's focus on health so far this year. And it could serve them well when the weather gets colder and the elements become even more of a factor.
"I feel normal like any other normal week," Phillips said. "I think a couple of weeks ago we had 30 snaps or something like that, and now we had 80. I actually feel the same today than on both those weeks."
Ninety-three plays is never easy. But if Phillips and other players are pleased with their preparation going into Sunday, then the ruling on if the Jets are soft or not will be clearer.
As angry as fans are about the team's 1-3 start, there's just no correlation to a team going through a walk-through on Wednesday to being flat on their face during Sunday's contest. If New York were to struggle against the Browns, that wouldn't be an indication that they didn't prepare enough.
It would come down to execution and in-game coaching: two things that have plagued the roster so far under Glenn.
No NFL team or player is truly "soft." No practice habit is "soft" either. NFL teams who go lighter on the practice field to keep players healthy are just as smart as others who demand full-body practices each and every session.
If Glenn and the team's medical staff felt this was the right course of action, then there isn't much to get too worked up over. After a rough Week 4, some members of the defense could use that extra rehab time.
And if the Jets can beat the Browns on Sunday, no one will ever remember the walkthrough practice the team went through anyway.

title: Exclusive: Braelon Allen Breaks Down His Confidence in Jets’ Playoff Outlook, Breece Hall’s Impact & More
full_text:
Through his partnership with Q30 Sports Science, I had the opportunity to interview New York Jets running back Braelon Allen.
The company’s product, Q-Collar, is a device worn around the neck that is designed to help protect the brain from repetitive head impacts. Q-30 describes it as acting like a seatbelt for the brain.
Allen first heard about the Q-Collar while in college, when he saw former Carolina Panthers linebacker Luke Kuechly in ads for it. After seeing those ads, Allen reached out to the company to try the product, which has since been a staple of his routine.
“I absolutely love the products,” Allen said. “It’s hard for me to play without it."
Allen plays one of football's most physically demanding positions and has made protecting his body and mental health a long-term priority.
“Obviously, I want to be as healthy as possible… I try to do everything that’s in my power to make sure that happens, and Q-Collar is a great way to do that in terms of my mental health and protecting my brain.”
Allen knows firsthand just how quickly things can change on the field.
Last year, his second season was cut short after suffering a season-ending MCL injury during a kickoff return against the Miami Dolphins.
The injury required surgery, marking the first time he had undergone a major procedure. Despite the setback, Allen said he had a strong support team around him throughout his recovery, and the process went well.
Nearly a year later, with running mate Breece Hall sidelined due to a quad injury , Allen took on a larger role in the offense, posting career highs in both rushing attempts (14) and rushing yards (59) in the Jets’ 23-12 loss to the Bears.
While Hall’s absence gave Allen a bigger workload, the two have developed a close bond that extends beyond the field. “He’s one of my best friends,” Allen said.
Hall has been a valuable influence on the former Wisconsin Badger, as Allen credits him with helping him develop as a pass catcher and pass protector.
While both backs offer different skill sets, Allen feels that they complement each other well. The pair showed their potential in Week 1, combining for 142 rushing yards and a touchdown in New York’s victory over the Titans.
Since that win, however, the Jets have dropped the last three games. Their Week 4 loss to the Bears was demoralizing, as New York’s offense possessed the ball for just 17 minutes.
Despite this, Allen believes the Jets have the pieces to turn things around. When asked what the offense does well, he explained that the team has shown it can succeed through the air and on the ground, but needs to put everything together in the same game.
He pointed to the Week 1 win over Tennessee as an example of what the offense is capable of when everything clicks.
Ultimately, Allen’s ambitions align with Gang Green fans: winning. When asked what he wants the next chapter of his career to look like, his answer was straightforward: “Getting this team to the playoffs and having winning seasons as a New York Jet."
Allen made it clear that he wants to do his part to help the Jets reach that goal.
“I just want to do my part to help us win and continue to push us to the top,” Allen said.
Despite New York’s slow start, Allen remains focused on helping the team turn things around. With plenty of games ahead, he still has time to help turn the Jets' season around and achieve his goal.
And it starts against the Cleveland Browns Sunday afternoon.
